It can be killed at any moment and a fresh instance takes over. So all state needed for continuity must live outside the seat. So the real engineering question: **Design a content-addressed reference object such that any freshly-spawned stateless worker can resolve it back to full meaning without carrying forward mutable state — and specify exactly what lives in persistent storage vs. what gets recomputed on respawn. This maps onto real systems: **Content-addressable storage (CAS)** + **Merkle DAGs** (IPFS, Git) **Session/context serialization** for LLM agents (what persists between turns when the model is stateless — the KV cache dies, so you recompute from serialized context) **Crash-only software / actor model with checkpointed state** **Log-structured merge trees / write-ahead logs** for durability **Idempotent recomputation** — deterministic functions of persisted inputs The key insight for "stateless seat that dies and respawns": the seat is a pure function evaluator. Everything it needs must be either (a) derivable from the meta-token itself, (b) fetchable from persistent stores keyed by content hashes, or (c) recomputable deterministically from (a)+(b). Nothing may live only in seat-local memory. Let me now design this concretely. Anatomy of the meta-token A meta-token must be self-describing enough that a cold resolver knows *where* to look and *how* to verify. Content-addressing gives integrity; we need addressing + typing + resolution hints. MTX-<algo>-<root_hash>-<epoch>-<scope> Or more precisely, a structured object: v: 1                          // schema version alg: "blake3"                 // hash function root: b3:<64-hex>             // content hash of the anchored payload kind: enum {CONTEXT_SET, EMBEDDING_INDEX, DECISION_NODE, TOOL_RESULT, . epoch: u64                    // monotonic pipeline epoch (for GC + cache invalidation) scope: {pipeline_id, frontier_id, scout_gen}   // namespace ] // ordered list of backing stores to try recompute_cost: {tokens_est, ms_p50}  // lets scheduler decide fetch vs recompute Critical property: **the root hash covers the canonical serialization of the payload**, not the payload's storage encoding. So storage can compress/relocate freely; verification always works against canonical bytes. Why content-addressing specifically solves "meaning across multiple token sets": if two different token sets (say, a compressed summary set and the original raw set) both need to express "the decision made at node X," they both embed the same MTX. The meaning isn't in either token set's local context — it's in the CAS object. Token sets become views; the meta-token is the join key. This is exactly how Git lets two branches share history, or how IPFS dedupes across peers. What the meta-token resolves TO The payload behind `root` should be a small, hot object — the "meaning kernel": semantic_digest      // embedding or LSH sketch of the content, for similarity joins canonical_text       // OR pointer-chain to chunks, each chunk itself content-addressed provenance           // parent MTX hashes (Merkle links upstream) validity: {epoch_range, supersedes[], superseded_by[]} acl/quorum info      // who wrote it, attestation Large payloads (raw transcripts, tool outputs) should NOT be inline. The kernel holds chunk pointers: `[b3:hash, offset, len]`. This keeps the hot path small (fetch one object) and the cold path lazy (fetch chunks only if needed). The burn pipeline mechanics **Scout spawn**: orchestrator picks a frontier region, mints a scout seat with a seed bundle = {parent MTX set, task spec hash, budget}. **Scout burns**: explores, produces artifacts. Every artifact it wants others to see, it writes to CAS and emits an MTX. Seat-local scratch memory (KV cache, working embeddings) is disposable. **Burn**: seat destroyed. Only its emitted MTXs + written CAS objects survive. **Respawn**: new seat (same logical role, maybe different physical host) receives the MTX set, resolves them, reconstructs working state, continues. The invariant: **the seat is a reducer; MTX stream is the log; CAS is the state store. ** Respawn = replay/reduce over resolved MTXs. This is event-sourcing with content-addressed events. PERSISTS vs RECOMPUTES — the core deliverable Let me be exact. Partition by cost-of-recompute vs cost-of-persistence, and by whether recompute is even possible (non-determinism destroys recomputeability). ### PERSISTS (written once, immutable, content-addressed): **CAS objects** — every artifact a scout deems load-bearing: decisions, measurements, code diffs, tool outputs, distilled summaries. Immutable by construction (hash = identity). Never rewritten; superseded by new objects. **The meta-tokens themselves** — as records in an append-only index (the "token ledger"). Entry: {mtx_bytes, writer_seat_id, epoch, timestamp, signature}. This ledger is the spine of the whole pipeline. **Provenance edges** — parent→child MTX links. These make the DAG queryable without fetching payloads. **Semantic digests** — embeddings/sketches computed from payloads. Recomputing embeddings costs GPU time; persisting them costs bytes. But note: digest algorithm version must be recorded, because a digest is meaningless without knowing how it was made. **Validity/supersession metadata** — cheap to persist, expensive to reconstruct (requires global knowledge of the DAG). **Attestations** — signatures/checksums proving which seat produced what under which spec-hash. Non-recomputable because seats are non-deterministic (sampling temperature, wall-clock tool results). Anything non-deterministic MUST persist or be lost forever. ### RECOMPUTES (on respawn, deterministically, from persisted inputs): **Seat working memory** — KV caches, attention state, in-flight partial hypotheses. Gone at burn; rebuilt by re-resolving the MTX set and re-running the reduction. Accept the cost; it's bounded by the seed bundle size. **Derived indexes** — local ANN indexes over fetched digests, bloom filters for dedup, sorted views. Cheap to rebuild from persisted digests; keeping them fresh across respawns would create coherence problems worse than the rebuild cost. **Resolution caches** — MTX→payload mappings cached in the seat for speed. On death, gone; next seat refetches. Optional: a shared read-through cache layer in front of CAS if fetch latency dominates (but treat it as an optimization, never as truth — truth is always verifiable against the hash). **Aggregations/summaries of sibling scouts' outputs** — if scout B needs "consensus of scouts A,C,D," it recomputes the consensus from their persisted kernels rather than trusting a cached consensus object. unless the consensus was itself minted as an MTX by an authorized aggregator, in which case it persists as first-class. Rule: anything another party depends on semantically gets minted; anything only I depend on locally gets recomputed. **Frontier geometry / exploration bookkeeping** — which regions are explored vs open can be recomputed from the union of all scouts' reported coverage MTXs. Persist the per-scout coverage claims (they're artifacts); recompute the merged map. ### The decision rule (make it crisp): > **Persist iff (a) the artifact is non-deterministically generated (tool outputs, sampled text, measurements), or (b) it is referenced by more than one future seat/epoch, or (c) recomputing it requires knowledge that will no longer exist (e. , the dead seat's private scratch). Equivalently: persist *facts and commitments*, recompute *views and conveniences*. ### Edge cases that break naive designs: - **Non-deterministic tools**: web fetches, API calls, clock reads. If a later seat needs the same data, it cannot re-fetch reliably (page changed, rate limits). → Tool outputs must be persisted as CAS objects at capture time, with capture metadata (URL, timestamp, response hash). The MTX anchors the captured snapshot, not the live source. - **Hash churn / canonicalization drift**: if canonical serialization changes between versions, old MTXs fail verification. → Version the canonical form inside the payload (`v` field), keep old verifiers around. Never mutate canonicalization rules within an epoch. liveness**: content-addressed stores accumulate garbage. Epoch-based GC: an object survives if reachable from any MTX in the live ledger window (last N epochs) or pinned by an explicit lease. Scouts on long horizons take leases. This is exactly IPFS pinning / Git reflog semantics. - **Split-brain on respawn**: two seats both think they own the frontier continuation. → Continuation authority is itself an MTX-minted lease: {frontier_id, epoch, holder_spec_hash, ttl}. New seat must mint-or-adopt a lease; conflicting leases resolve by epoch then by hash-order (deterministic tiebreak), loser's work becomes a fork MTX rather than being discarded. - **Partial fetch on respawn**: some CAS shards unavailable. → resolve_hints give fallback stores; if payload unrecoverable but digest + provenance survive, the seat marks the MTX "tombstoned-partial" and proceeds with degraded context, recording the gap as its own MTX. Never silently fabricate missing meaning. Resolution protocol (exact steps for a cold seat) Given MTX M: Parse header; check schema version supported. Verify scope/epoch against current pipeline view (is it live, superseded, tombstoned? Fetch payload from resolve_hints in order; verify blake3(payload_canonical) == root. On mismatch: try next hint; on exhaustion, mark partial. Load kernel; recursively resolve chunk pointers and parent MTXs as needed (lazy, budget-aware — use recompute_cost to decide eager vs lazy). Rebuild derived structures (indexes, caches) locally. Resume reduction from the MTX log tail. Budget note: step 4's laziness is where "recompute_cost" earns its place — the scheduler decides whether to hydrate the full subtree or run on digests until a branch is actually touched. Why content-addressing (vs. location-addressing) is non-negotiable here Location-addressed handles (URLs, DB row IDs) break under the burn pipeline because: stores migrate, seats die mid-write, replicas disagree. Two token sets referencing the same meaning literally share bytes. Also: parallel scouts often converge on identical conclusions. With content addressing, their MTXs point at the same root hash — convergence is detectable by hash equality alone, before any semantic comparison. That's a cheap quorum signal: k scouts emitting identical roots = strong confirmation; differing roots over the same parent set = genuine disagreement to escalate. Sizing the answer The user asked for concrete, exact, grounded. I should deliver: - The MTX format (fields, why each exists) - The persist/recompute partition table with the decision rule - The respawn protocol - The failure-mode handling (GC, split-brain, partial fetch, nondeterminism) - The convergence-as-hash-equality insight Format thoughts: This deserves a fairly long, structured technical answer — headers, a couple of compact schemas, a table for persists-vs-recomputes, numbered protocol. Markdown appropriate since this reads like a design-doc request in a chat interface. Length: substantial but tight — maybe 900–1300 words equivalent. Avoid hedging language entirely per instructions. Use the pipeline's own vocabulary (scout, burn, seat, frontier) so it lands in-frame. Let me draft the final structure: Core invariant (one line) Meta-token anatomy (schema block) What it resolves to (kernel + chunk chain) Persist vs recompute (table + crisp rule) Respawn protocol (numbered) Failure modes handled exactly (nondeterminism, GC, split-brain, partial fetch) The convergence trick (hash equality as quorum) I'll keep schemas as fenced blocks, table for the partition. Be direct throughout.

eedeecbbe0c08faf.text: # The Meta-Token: Content-Addressed Semantic Anchor for a Killable Seat Decoding the requirements into hard constraints Strip the metaphor and the problem is: - **Meta-token**: one identifier that denotes a fixed meaning, resolvable into *many* token representations (different tokenizer vocabularies, embedding spaces, session-local symbol tables, per-model renderings). - **Content-addressed**: the identifier is a hash of the meaning itself, not a pointer handed out by a server. Consequences: immutability by construction, verifiability by anyone, replication without consensus. - **Operator's own-iron basecamp**: self-hosted, POSIX world, no cloud KMS, no managed lock service. The design must survive on boring primitives: files, `rename`, fsync, SQLite. - **Stateless seat, dies and respawns**: the seat is cattle. Anything in RAM is gone at any instant. A respawned seat — possibly on different hardware — must produce *byte-identical resolutions* to the dead one. The design goal, stated once: **any seat, holding only anchor IDs, can independently reconstruct every representation, and two seats with different token sets still agree on meaning. ** Content addressing is what makes statelessness safe — it converts "trust the previous seat's memory" into "verify bytes against a hash. The core decision: immutable anchors + mutable refs Split the world in two: **Anchors are immutable, content-addressed objects. ** `anchor_id = BLAKE3(canonical_bytes)`. Change the meaning → different bytes → new anchor. There is no update, no invalidation, no cache-coherence problem, ever. **Refs/aliases are the only mutable truth**, held in one small transactional store with an append-only journal. "What we currently call X" mutates; "what X's content is" never does. Everything else falls out of this split. ### Canonical anchor object (deterministic CBOR, RFC 8949 core deterministic encoding) "v": 1,                          # schema version; unknown v ⇒ fail loud core",               # interpretation gate "glyph": "approval-gate",      # display hint, informational },              # THE meaning: ints, strings, bools, ],     # Merkle edges to other anchors "tags":  ["gate", "policy"] anchor_id = base58( BLAKE3( cbor_det(env) ) )        # 32 bytes Rules that make the hash well-defined: - **Deterministic serialization only. ** Sorted map keys, canonical CBOR. No JSON (field-order and number-format ambiguity destroys content addressing). - **No floats in canonical bodies. ** Float canonicalization differs across languages and is the classic way content addressing silently breaks. Numerics go in as integer pairs or decimal strings. - **`refs` makes composites work. ** An anchor referencing other anchors pins their meaning transitively — a Merkle DAG, git-model. Store at `objects/mt/<prefix>/<anchor_id>. ### Projection spec (how an anchor becomes tokens in token-set T) "tokset": "<tokset_artifact_hash>",   # vocab + merges + config, content-addressed "fn":     "<fn_code_hash>",           # VERSIONED projection function }                     # ints/strings only proj_key  = BLAKE3( anchor_id_bytes || BLAKE3(cbor_det(spec)) ) proj_obj  = { "v":1, "spec":"<spec_hash>", "out": { "tokens":[int. "spans": [[start,end,role]. "complete": true|false, path: proj/<anchor_id>/<proj_key> - **The projection is a pure function** of `(canonical_body, spec)`. Spec pins the tokenizer artifact hash *and* the projection-code hash. Upgrade the model or fix a bug → new `fn` hash → new namespace of results; old results stay valid under old specs. Meaning drift becomes explicit versioning instead of silent nondeterminism. - **Lossy projections declare themselves. ** A compact vocabulary can't always express the full canonical meaning. The projection function fails loud, or emits `complete:false` with a `dropped` list. Consumers must check the flag. Silent degradation is the killer in multi-vocabulary systems; the flag travels inside the content-addressed object, so it can't be separated from the data. - **Invariant: cross-token-set agreement is canonical equivalence, not byte equality. ** Two seats with different tokenizers produce different token arrays from the same anchor — guaranteed semantically equivalent because both derive from the same canonical body through pinned, tested functions. Within one spec, byte equality is exact. ### Wire format between seats Embed in token streams as a length-tagged short ref: 16 bytes of the hash, base58 (~22 chars). At mint time, enforce uniqueness of the 8-byte prefix across all live anchors (cheap check, keeps short refs unambiguous forever). Any seat expands a short ref by querying the store — the store, not another seat, is the expander. resolve(A, T): RAM cache → hit: return Local disk cache → hit: verify BLAKE3, promote to RAM, return Shared store, path proj/A/proj_key(T) → hit: verify hash, return Miss: load canonical A (verify hash), load spec + fn, COMPUTE, write-through to disk cache, return Every ingest of bytes verifies the hash (BLAKE3 runs at multiple GB/s — the check is free). Cache hits affect latency only, never results, because the cache key contains all function inputs' hashes. **Reverse direction** ("I hold tokens, find the anchor"): a derived map `hash(token_span in T) → anchor_id`. Rebuildable by replaying projections; run it as an in-RAM LRU populated on demand, optionally mirrored to disk as a disposable accelerator. Lifecycle of the killable seat Fetch the pinned generation manifest — content hashes of code, config, specs, tokenizer artifacts. The seat refuses unpinned config. This is what makes respawn behavior-identical, not just data-identical. Mount the object store read-only (shared FS on the own-iron fabric, or per-host mirror kept in sync by pull — content addressing means replication needs no consensus, only fetch-and-check-hash). Load alias snapshot from the ref store. Warm top-K projections from a persisted frequency sketch. Register with the coordinator under a lease TTL; heartbeat renews. Realistic cold start on NVMe: tokenizer load + alias snapshot + 10k-projection prefetch ≈ **under 1 second**. Budget it explicitly; it's a design parameter, not an accident. **Mint (rare; resolution is hot):** Build canonical env, compute `anchor_id`. Write object to `tmp/<uuid>`, fsync file, `rename` into place, fsync directory. Register any alias in the SQLite ref store (WAL, `synchronous=FULL`) inside one transaction. Kill anywhere in this sequence and the outcome is all-or-nothing: an unreferenced object is invisible garbage swept later by GC (grace period > p99 mint time). Visibility gate is the ref commit. Idempotent re-mint is free — same content, same hash, CAS sees the object exists, no-op. **Death:** nothing in RAM matters. No in-flight state can corrupt anything, because all authoritative writes were already durable before they were observable. The ledger: what persists vs what recomputes This is the direct answer. | Tier | Contents | Why | | **PERSISTS — authoritative** (lose it = lose meaning) | Canonical anchor objects; alias DB + append-only mutation journal; projection specs; tokenizer artifacts; projection-fn code; generation manifests; coordinator signing key | None of these are computable from anything else. They are the fixed points of the system. | **PERSISTS — derived** (safe to delete wholesale, anytime) | Materialized projection blobs; persisted reverse index; frequency sketches; alias snapshots | Byte-deterministic functions of tier 1. Kept purely because recompute costs CPU; losing them costs a rebuild, never correctness. | **RECOMPUTES every seat life** (RAM only) | Vocab tries/maps; hot projection cache; in-RAM reverse index; session-local bindings (context-slot assignments, per-conversation symbol tables); lease state; short-lived seat credentials; metrics | Die with the process by definition. Rebuilt identically because all inputs are pinned and pure. Decision rule, so the classification stays stable as the system grows: **persist if (a) it isn't the output of a pure function over already-persisted inputs, or (b) it is, and it's immutable and recompute-cost exceeds storage-cost. ** Everything else recomputes. Note the deliberate placement: *session-local meaning bindings recompute. * The meta-token carries "what this is"; the alias/journal layer carries "what this is currently called and used for"; the seat's private slot assignments are disposable bookkeeping. Mixing these layers is where designs like this rot. Own-iron specifics ** Atomicity = tmp-file + fsync + rename. The one mutable structure (alias DB) = SQLite WAL with `FULL` sync, journal segments fsynced on a ≤50 ms batch window. Both are real numbers on local NVMe, not aspirations. - **Single-writer arbitration** for aliases via the basecamp coordinator — one authority, so no distributed locking is needed anywhere. Reads are served from any replica because everything readable is immutable and hash-checked. - **Backups** = ship `objects/` plus the journal. Objects deduplicate naturally; integrity is self-evident (hash check on restore). - **No clocks in the truth path. ** Timestamps exist only in leases and GC grace windows. Truth is timeless because content addressing removed time from it. Grounding numbers and the drills that prove it Sizing: 10⁷ anchors × ~2 KB canonical ≈ 20 GB; projections 10⁷ × 3 token sets × ~4 KB ≈ 120 GB. Trivial on own-iron NVMe; hash verification is noise at BLAKE3 speeds. Drills that must pass, or the design doesn't: **Kill -9 mid-mint** → respawn → assert no partial anchor is visible, no torn alias state. **Purity property test on every respawn**: sample 32 anchors, recompute projections from canonical + spec, compare hashes to cached copies. This continuously proves the central invariant — that resolution is a pure function — catches any accidental dependence on ambient state (locale, library version, dict ordering). **Cross-seat agreement test**: seat with tokenizer A and seat with tokenizer B resolve the same anchor; assert both mark `complete:true` and that round-tripping through the canonical body reproduces identical canonical hashes. **Canonicalizer fuzz**: deterministic-CBOR roundtrip must be byte-stable across every writer implementation. Persist the immutable canonical anchors, the pinned specs/artifacts/code, and the small mutable alias journal; recompute every projection cache, index, and session binding from scratch on respawn — because content addressing plus pinned pure functions makes recomputation byte-identical, and that is the entire trick that lets the seat die without taking the meaning with it. Let me parse this problem carefully. The user is using a dense, jargon-heavy style — "Ghost's thousand-ask mining engine" framing suggests they want deep technical reasoning, no fluff. The problem: "the meta-token: one content-addressed anchor resolving meaning across multiple token sets, in the operator's own-iron basecamp. Design it for a stateless seat that dies and respawns: what persists vs recomputes. Let me decode the metaphors into real engineering: - "meta-token: one content-addressed anchor resolving meaning across multiple token sets" — This is about an identity/reference object that maps to multiple concrete token representations (across contexts, sessions, vocabularies, encodings). Content-addressed = its address/ID is derived from its content (like a git blob SHA, or IPFS CID, or content-defined hash). "Resolving meaning across multiple token sets" = it must dereference consistently regardless of which token vocabulary/state-space the reader is in. - "in the operator's own-iron basecamp" — "own-iron" = self-hosted, on-prem, bare-metal infrastructure owned by the operator (not cloud). Basecamp = the home base / primary site of operations. So this is a self-hosted system on operator-owned hardware. - "stateless seat that dies and respawns" — A seat = an execution slot / worker process / agent runtime instance. Stateless = holds no authoritative durable state locally; it can be killed at any moment and a fresh instance spawned, possibly elsewhere, and must resume correctly. So the design task: design a meta-token system — a content-addressed semantic anchor — such that: One canonical anchor ID resolves to consistent meaning across multiple token sets (different encodings, versions, sessions, model contexts). It lives in self-hosted infrastructure. Worker seats are cattle, not pets: they die and respawn; anything not persisted is lost. The core question: what persists vs what recomputes. This is essentially designing: - The canonical object store (content-addressed, immutable) — persists. - The derivation/caching layers — recompute. - The resolution protocol — how a stateless seat takes an anchor ID and gets back the meaning in whatever token set it needs. Let me think about the actual technical design deeply. A meta-token M is defined by its content C. Anchor ID = H(C) where H is a strong hash (BLAKE3, SHA-256). But wait — there's subtlety here. If the anchor's address is the hash of its *canonical definition*, then the anchor is immutable by construction. Any change to meaning = new anchor. That's actually the correct move for a death-prone environment: immutability means no invalidation logic, no cache coherence protocols, no distributed consensus about current value. The anchor never mutates; you only create successors. "Resolving meaning across multiple token sets": the anchor has one canonical payload (the semantic definition) plus derived projections into specific token sets. A "token set" could be: - Different tokenizer vocabularies (BPE v1 vs v2, sentencepiece models) - Different embedding spaces (model A's embedding of the phrase vs model B's) - Different session-local symbol tables - Cross-model: same concept rendered for different LLMs with different prompt formats So the architecture: **Persisted layer (durable, on own-iron):** Canonical content blobs, content-addressed: `blobs/<sha256>` — the raw canonical definition (JSON/CBOR with canonical serialization rules — JCS-like, fixed field order, explicit types, no floats ambiguity or integers-only). An index/registry mapping anchor → projections: which token sets have materialized projections, their own content hashes, and provenance (which transformer version produced them). Write-ahead log / journal if needed for registry updates (though with CAS semantics, mostly unnecessary). Actually, let me reconsider: should the registry itself be content-addressed? The cleanest design: everything is a DAG of content-addressed objects, like Git. The only mutable pointer is a single ref: `heads/meta-token-registry` or per-anchor refs. Then persistence = fsync of objects + atomic pointer swap. Respawned seat reads the ref, walks the DAG. Crash-consistent trivially because object writes happen before ref updates. But maybe simpler is better: since anchors are immutable and addressed by content hash, you don't even need a registry for lookup — the ID *is* the address. You need a registry only for: - Discovery (list/search anchors) - Reverse mappings (given a token sequence in some local token set, find the anchor) Reverse mapping is the hard part. Let me think. **The resolution contract:** Given anchor ID A and target token set T, produce the exact token representation(s) in T, deterministically. a) Store projections: precompute `proj(A, T) = [tokens]` and persist them keyed by `H(A || T-id || T-version)`. Persisting projections costs storage but makes respawn cheap and cross-seat consistency exact. b) Recompute projections from canonical content + deterministic projection functions. Costs CPU but zero extra storage, and always correct even after token-set upgrades. The right answer: **persist canonical content + projection function versions; lazily cache projections; treat caches as disposable. ** Projections are pure functions of (canonical content, projection spec). Deterministic ⇒ recompute yields byte-identical results ⇒ cache correctness is free (verify by hash, or don't verify at all since key includes inputs' hashes). Wait, but there's a wrinkle: some "meaning resolution" isn't purely functional. , embeddings depend on model weights. Model weights change → same canonical content projects to different vectors. Solution: the projection spec includes the model checkpoint hash. `proj_spec = {type: embedding, model: sha256(weights), layer: . So proj(A, spec) remains a pure function. Upgrading the model = new spec namespace = new keys. Old projections stay valid under old specs. This is exactly how Nix/content-addressed build systems handle toolchain changes. **What persists (authoritative, survives respawn):** Canonical anchor payloads (content blobs) — the source of truth. The anchor ID itself (it's derived, but once minted and referenced, it's the handle used across seats/sessions). Projection specs / schema definitions (versioned, themselves content-addressed). The mutable head pointers: e. , "current alias table" mapping human names/aliases → anchor IDs. Aliases are mutable (an alias can repoint), anchors aren't. Persist aliases in a small transactional KV (SQLite on local NVMe with WAL, or LSM tree) — on own-iron you control the disk. Negative results worth remembering? Usually not; keep negative caching ephemeral. Access-control / ownership metadata ("operator's own-iron" implies multi-seat, single-operator trust domain, so minimal ACLs; but seat identity tokens might need persistence — better: derive seat credentials from short-lived certs signed by basecamp CA; the CA key persists, seat creds recompute/reissue on spawn). Hmm, careful about scope creep. Focus: the meta-token system. **What recomputes (ephemeral, rebuilt after respawn):** In-memory token tables / vocabularies loaded from persisted tokenizer artifacts (persist the artifact, recompute the runtime structures). Projections not yet materialized (compute on demand from canonical + spec). Any caches: LRU of hot anchors' projections, bloom filters over anchor set, etc. Session-local bindings: e. , "in this conversation, meta-token X binds to slot 47 in my working context. " These are seat-local and die with the seat; the binding is re-derived by replaying or by querying the durable log. Seat-local RNG state, counters, etc. — irrelevant to meaning. Now the interesting hard parts. Let me enumerate real difficulties and solve each concretely. ### Hard part 1: Canonicalization — making H(content) well-defined Content-addressing requires byte-exact canonical form. JSON with arbitrary field order kills this. - Use CBOR with deterministic encoding rules (RFC 8949 Core Deterministic Encoding): map keys sorted bytewise, shortest float forms, etc. Or RFC 8785 JCS for JSON. - Fix a schema version inside the object: `{v: 1, kind: "meta-token", body: {. Hash covers the full envelope including v. Any schema evolution = different bytes = different hash, which is fine and desired (new meaning = new anchor. but careful: adding an optional field shouldn't silently change meaning; version field gates interpretation). - Forbidding floats entirely, or requiring rational/string-encoded numerics, because float canonicalization across languages is treacherous. Concretely: represent numbers as strings or integer pairs. This matters because embeddings/projection params often involve floats — keep floats out of the canonical anchor; they live in projection outputs which are keyed by spec-hash anyway and stored as opaque bytes. So: `anchor_id = BLAKE3(canonical_cbor(envelope))`, truncated to 32 bytes, displayed as multibase/base58 or as `z. Exact algorithm stated: BLAKE3-256, deterministic CBOR, envelope `{v:1, kind:"mt", sem:<semantic body>, proj:[spec-hashes. Should projections be listed inside the anchor? No — that couples anchor creation to projection availability. Better: anchor body contains only the semantic definition; projections live as separate objects `(anchor_id, spec_id) -> proj_bytes` where proj_bytes are also content-addressed (`proj_obj = {v:1, spec: <spec_hash>, out: <bytes>}`, id = BLAKE3(proj_obj)). Lookup by computing expected filename `projections/<anchor>/<spec_hash>` and checking existence — O(1), no index needed. ### Hard part 2: "Resolving meaning across multiple token sets" Define precisely what a token set is and what resolution returns. Token set T = (tokenizer artifact hash, vocabulary version, format profile). `resolve(A, T) -> {tokens: [. Deterministic given (canonical(A), spec(T)). The output must include enough metadata (spans, role markers) that a downstream consumer can place the tokens in context without consulting the seat that produced them. Cross-token-set consistency guarantee: two seats running different tokenizers both resolve A and get *semantically equivalent* projections because both derive from the same canonical body through versioned, tested projection functions. Consistency is anchored at the canonical level, not the token level. State that explicitly: **the invariant is canonical equivalence, not byte equality across heterogeneous token sets. ** Within one token set version, byte equality holds (same pure function, same input). Edge case: lossy projections. Some token sets may not express the full canonical meaning (e. , a compact vocabulary lacking a glyph). Options: (a) forbid — projection function returns error, resolution fails loudly; (b) fallback encoding with escape marker. Choose (a) fail-loud plus explicit "coverage" bit in projection output: `{complete: true|false, dropped: [. Silent degradation is the killer in multi-vocab systems; make loss visible in the object itself. Since the projection object is content-addressed, its completeness flag travels with it. ### Hard part 3: Reverse lookup — "I have tokens, give me the anchor" A respawned seat receives a context containing token sequences that encode meta-tokens inline (e. , a sentinel like `<mt:A>` where A is embedded, or a raw span). Two sub-cases: - Self-describing embeds: the token stream carries the anchor ID (or a short form). Short forms: prefix of the hash (e. , 16 bytes base64 ≈ 22 chars) with disambiguation rule: if collision among known prefixes, extend. Because the seat can query the basecamp store to expand any prefix to full ID, collisions only matter within the referenced corpus, and the store enforces uniqueness of short prefixes among *live* anchors (mint-time check: refuse to mint an anchor whose 8-byte prefix collides with an existing live anchor — cheap, keeps short refs safe forever). - Non-self-describing spans: need reverse map `H(tokens_in_T) -> anchor`. This map is derivable: for every anchor and every token set T the seat cares about, compute projection and insert `hash(proj_tokens) -> anchor`. That's a rebuildable index — classic recompute candidate. Persisting it is optional optimization. On respawn, rebuild lazily: populate on first miss by scanning? Scanning all anchors × all token sets is expensive. Mitigation: persist a compact manifest (anchor_id list grouped by kind) — tiny — and rebuild the reverse index incrementally on demand, with an LRU. Actually simplest honest answer: persist the reverse index too, but treat it as *derived*: rebuildable from persisted primitives; if corrupted, nuke and rebuild. The distinction that matters is not "persists vs not" but "authoritative vs derived. " Derived-but-persisted is fine when rebuilding is deterministic. I'll present the trichotomy: authoritative-persist / derived-persist(rebuildable) / ephemeral-recompute. ### Hard part 4: Stateless seat lifecycle Seat lifecycle events: spawn, serve, die (crash/preempt), respawn (possibly on another host of the own-iron fleet). Seat fetches code+config by content hash (pin the runtime: config blob hash passed in spawn request; seat refuses unpinned config — prevents drift between respawns). Seat mounts/attaches read-only view of the object store (on own-iron: shared NFS/Lustre/cephfs, or local NVMe with rsync'd mirror; pick cephfs/NFS for shared, or peer-to-peer pull with verification since everything is hash-verifiable — nice property: replication of content-addressed data needs no consensus, just fetch-and-check-hash). Seat loads tokenizer artifacts (content-addressed), builds in-memory structures, warms hot-cache by fetching top-K projections (K from workload hint or empty). Seat registers with basecamp coordinator with lease TTL; heartbeat renews; on death, lease expires and another seat spawns. - Reads: resolve(A,T): check memory → check local disk cache → fetch object from store (verify hash on ingest — always, cost is trivial with BLAKE3 ~GB/s) → else compute from canonical + spec, write-through cache. - Writes (mint new anchor): construct canonical body, hash, CAS-write object to store, then update mutable refs via compare-and-swap on the registry (single-writer or optimistic concurrency with retry). Mint is rare; resolution is hot. Death handling: nothing in RAM matters. All authoritative state already in store. In-flight mints: either completed (object + ref committed) or not (orphaned object — harmless garbage, GC later; ref absent ⇒ never visible). This gives atomicity without transactions: visibility gate is the ref swap, objects are invisible until referenced. That's the git model and it's exactly right here. GC: objects unreachable from any ref for > grace period get deleted; grace period > max mint duration so in-flight orphaned objects aren't collected mid-write (also use temp-name then rename for write atomicity: write to `tmp/<uuid>`, fsync, rename to final path — rename atomic on POSIX within a filesystem). Respawn correctness proof sketch: any answer a dead seat S would have given for resolve(A,T) equals what respawned seat S′ gives, because both compute f(canonical(A), spec(T)) with pinned f-version and spec; caches only affect latency, not results. The one caveat: if f itself changed (projection function bugfix), results differ across time. Handle by pinning f-version in spec hash (spec includes `fn: <code-hash>`), so "T" is really "T@f". Meaning drift becomes explicit versioning instead of silent nondeterminism. Good — say that crisply. ### Hard part 5: What about the "meaning" beyond mechanical projection? If meta-tokens carry genuinely semantic weight (e. , "this anchor means the operator's approval-gate"), some resolution involves policy/context, not pure functions. Keep the boundary strict: canonical body may contain *declarative* semantics consumed by policy engines; anything contextual lives in refs/aliases (mutable, journaled) not in the anchor. The anchor answers "what is this"; the alias/journal layer answers "what is this called/used-as now. " Alias mutations go through an append-only log (persisted), enabling a respawned seat to reconstruct "current alias state" and even "as-of" states. Log is authoritative; periodic snapshots are derived-persist. ### Storage layout concretely (own-iron) mt/<aa>/<full-hash>. cbor          # canonical anchors proj/<anchor>/<spechash>          # projection blobs (content-addressed contents) json                  # projection/tokenizer specs (themselves hashed) tokset/<hash>/                    # tokenizer artifacts (vocab, merges, configs) db                        # SQLite WAL: alias -> anchor_id, monotonic txid journal/                          # append-only alias mutation log, segment files reachability snapshots            # derived Durability knobs: fsync file before rename; fsync parent dir after rename; SQLite synchronous=FULL for refs; journal fsync batch window ≤ e. On own-iron with NVMe these numbers are real, not aspirational. Replication across own-iron hosts: async pull-based sync; integrity = hash check at receiver; conflicts impossible for objects (immutable); conflicts only possible on refs/aliases → single-writer coordinator or last-writer-wins with txid tiebreak; choose coordinator arbitration since "operator's basecamp" implies one authority. ### What persists vs recomputes — the crisp table Canonical anchor objects (immutable, content-addressed). Projection specs + tokenizer artifacts (immutable, content-addressed). Projection outputs that have been materialized (derived but immutable once written — persist opportunistically; losing them only costs CPU). Alias/ref database + append-only journal (mutable, small, transactional). Runtime pin manifest: the exact content-hashes of code/config/specs a generation of seats runs (so respawns reproduce behavior bit-for-bit). Coordinator CA key / seat credential issuer (out of scope-ish but mention). RECOMPUTE (never trust across death): In-memory token tables, tries, vocab maps. Hot caches of resolved projections; negative caches. Reverse index tokens→anchor (rebuildable; optionally mirrored to disk as disposable accelerator). Session-local bindings (context-slot assignments, per-conversation symbol tables). Lease/heartbeat state, seat identity credentials (short-lived, reissued). Metrics/traces (observability only). INVARIANTS to enforce: - resolve() is a pure function of (anchor_id, spec_id, fn_version). Enforce by property test: recompute random sample on respawn and compare hashes. - Anchors immutable: store mounted read-only except mint path; mint path does CAS + tmp-rename. - Refs are the only mutable truth; every ref update journaled. - Lossy projections flagged in-object. Failure math / sizing quick numbers: assume 10^7 anchors, avg canonical size 1–4 KB → tens of GB; projections dominate (embeddings 768–4096 dims fp16 → 1. 5–8 KB each) ×(token sets) → hundreds of GB; trivially fits own-iron NVMe; BLAKE3 hashing at multi-GB/s makes verification negligible. Give those numbers to ground it. Also: the "dies and respawns" cadence defines cache economics. If mean seat lifetime is minutes and cold-start budget is seconds, warm-up strategy matters: prefetch top-K by persisted frequency counter (frequency counters themselves derived-persist, approximate — count-min sketch persisted, fine to lose). One more subtle point: "resolving meaning across multiple token sets" might also imply the meta-token lets *different seats with different vocabularies communicate* — the anchor is the interlingua. Yes — state that as the design goal: canonical object = interlingua; projections = adapters; anchor ID = wire format between seats. When seat A sends context to seat B, embedded anchor IDs travel; B resolves locally under B's token sets. No shared RAM, no shared session — that's why content addressing is mandatory, not stylistic: it's what makes statelessness safe (any seat can verify and rebuild anything from IDs alone). Also address "operator's own-iron": implications — no cloud KMS, no managed lock services; therefore design avoids needing them: no distributed locks (single coordinator or CAS-on-file with flock), encryption at rest optional/local key management, network partitions within the rack handled by read-only-everywhere + single-writer-refs. Everything chosen to be boring POSIX. Mint concurrency: two seats mint near-identical content → same hash → CAS dedupes automatically (second write sees object exists, no-op). Nice property to call out: content addressing gives idempotent mint for free. Alias repoint race: journal with txid; readers follow: read aliases. db snapshot (SQLite gives consistent snapshot), never torn. Respawn drill (concrete steps with timings): t0 allocate seat, fetch pinned manifest (~KBs). Verify+load tokenizers (tens of MB) ~100–300ms NVMe. Open object store read-only; load alias snapshot (~small) ~ms. Rebuild reverse index lazily; prefetch top-K projections (K=10k → ~80MB @8KB) ~200ms. Total cold start < 1s realistic on NVMe; state it. Testing hooks: chaos drill — kill -9 mid-mint, respawn, assert no partial anchor visible; property test resolve purity across seats; fuzz canonicalizer (roundtrip CBOR determinism across languages if polyglot writers). 6d650e4be2c73cb0.text: # The Meta-Token: Design Specification ## The Problem, Stated Exactly You have a seat (a process/agent) that holds zero durable local state. It can be killed at any instruction boundary and respawned. It must still resolve meaning — map a symbol to its binding — across multiple token sets (vocabularies, namespaces, contexts). The resolution must be governed by an invariant lattice where the law is executable code, not interpretation. The meta-token is the single anchor that makes this possible. ## The Meta-Token Structure anchor:      H(canonical_bytes)          // content-addressed identity invariant_id:  I₄₂                      // which node in the lattice meet_set:      [I₁₇, I₂₃]               // what it conjoins with join_set:      [I₉₁]                    // what disjoins into it token_set_refs: [S₁, S₃, S₇]             // which token sets it bridges code_hash:      H(executable_check)       // the law, content-addressed epoch:          7                         // lattice version (monotonic) The anchor hash is computed over a canonical serialization (deterministic encoding, fixed field order, no ambiguity). This means: **two seats computing the meta-token from the same inputs will produce the identical hash. ** This is the self-verifying property. ## The Invariant Lattice The lattice is a bounded partial order on executable invariants: - **Order:** I₁ ≤ I₂ iff satisfaction of I₁ implies satisfaction of I₂ - **Meet (∧):** conjunction — both must hold - **Join (∨):** disjunction — at least one holds - **Bottom (⊥):** vacuously true - **Top (⊤):** the full conjunction of all committed invariants The meta-token sits at a specific lattice node. Its "meaning" is not a string-to-value mapping. It is: *given this lattice position and this token-set context, which concrete token bindings satisfy the invariant? The code-as-law property: the invariant check is executable code, content-addressed by `code_hash`. Change the code → different hash → different law. ## What Persists (The Durable Set) These five things survive death. They live in a content-addressed store (DHT, chain, or any durable KV layer keyed by hash). | # | Object | Size | Why | | 1 | `anchor` (the hash itself) | 32 bytes | The identity. Without it, nothing else is addressable. | 2 | `canonical_bytes` (the full content) | variable | The payload. Fetchable by hash. Verifiable: `H(canonical_bytes) == anchor`. | 3 | Lattice root commitment | 32 bytes/epoch | One Merkle root per epoch. Commits to the entire lattice structure. Enables proof that a given `lattice_pos` is valid without storing the full lattice. | 4 | `code_hash → executable` mapping | variable | The law itself. Content-addressed so the respawned seat fetches exactly the right version. | 5 | `epoch` counter | 8 bytes | Monotonically increasing. Prevents replay of stale lattice states. **Total persistent state per meta-token:** the hash, the content, and one Merkle path to the lattice root. That is the irreducible minimum. ## What Recomputes (Everything Derivable) On respawn, the seat has zero memory. It receives: the anchor hash, the current query context (which token set, what inputs), and optionally a Merkle proof. It then recomputes: | # | Computation | Input | Output | | 1 | Content verification | `canonical_bytes`, `anchor` | `H(canonical_bytes) == anchor` → bool | | 2 | Lattice position verification | `lattice_pos`, Merkle proof, lattice root | Is this node committed at this epoch? | 3 | Meet/join traversal | `lattice_pos`, query context | The set of applicable invariants for this query | | 4 | Invariant satisfaction | Applicable invariants, `executable_check(code_hash)`, current inputs | Does the law hold for these bindings? | 5 | Token-set resolution | `token_set_refs`, satisfied invariants | The concrete token bindings that are valid | | 6 | Proof emission | All of the above | Fresh Merkle proof that this resolution is lattice-committed | Every step is deterministic given (persisted content + current inputs). Two seats respawning with the same meta-token and same query will produce the identical resolution. This is what makes the system correct under arbitrary kill/restart. ## The Respawn Protocol (Exact Sequence) boot()                          // zero state receive: anchor_hash, query_ctx, [optional: merkle_proof] fetch canonical_bytes ← store. // or: receive canonical_bytes inline + verify against lattice_root assert H(canonical_bytes) == anchor_hash // self-verification: no trust in prior seat required parse canonical_bytes → {lattice_pos, token_set_refs, code_hash, epoch} verify lattice_pos against lattice_root[epoch] via merkle_proof fetch executable_check ← code_registry. traverse lattice: compute meet/join closure for query_ctx execute executable_check(current_inputs, applicable_invariants) resolve: map satisfied invariants to concrete tokens in token_set_refs emit: resolution + fresh merkle_proof dies()                          // state discarded Steps 3–6 are verification (cheap, O(log n) in lattice size). Steps 7–10 are computation (the actual work). Steps 11 is output. Step 12 is death. ## Why Content-Addressing Is Non-Negotiable Here In code-as-law, the code IS the law. If you reference code by name or version string, a respawned seat cannot verify it's checking against the same law the meta-token was created under. Content-addressing by hash means: - The meta-token **commits** to a specific law - A respawned seat **verifies** it's executing that exact law - No trusted third party is needed to say "this is the right version" ## The Tradeoff You Cannot Escape You might be tempted to persist precomputed lattice traversals or cached resolutions to speed up respawn. ** The moment you persist derived state, you reintroduce trust in prior computation, which breaks the code-as-law property for a stateless seat. The entire design point is: the respawned seat derives everything from first principles + committed content. Slower, but unconditionally verifiable. If latency matters, the optimization is: **reduce recomputation cost** (smaller lattice per meta-token, tighter invariant granularity) rather than **persist derived state**. ## Summary: The Exact Split - The 32-byte anchor hash - The canonical content bytes it hashes - One lattice root per epoch - The executable code, content-addressed - The epoch counter **Recomputes (all of it, every respawn):** - Lattice position proof verification - Meet/join traversal The meta-token is the bridge because it is simultaneously: (a) small enough to persist cheaply, (b) content-addressed so it self-verifies, and (c) sufficient to deterministically reconstruct all meaning given current inputs. It is the only object that must cross the death boundary. The user is asking about designing a "meta-token" — a content-addressed anchor that resolves meaning across multiple token sets — in the context of a "code-as-law invariant lattice" for a "stateless seat that dies and respawns" (i. , a stateless process/agent that can be restarted, killed, and respawned). They want to know what persists vs. This is an abstract systems design problem, but it's grounded in real distributed systems / smart contract / stateless computation concepts. Let me think about what this actually maps to: **Meta-token**: A token that is not itself a symbol in a token set, but a pointer/handle that anchors meaning across multiple token sets. Content-addressed means its identity is derived from the content it anchors (like a git hash, IPFS CID, or a hash of the canonical form). **Code-as-law invariant lattice**: A lattice (in the order-theoretic sense) where nodes are invariants and the partial order is implication/refinement. "Code-as-law" means the invariants are enforced by executable code, not by human interpretation. The lattice structure means invariants compose — meet/join operations. **Stateless seat that dies and respawns**: A process/agent/node that holds no persistent local state. It can be killed and restarted at any point. Everything it "knows" is either derivable from inputs it receives, or fetched from persistent storage. The design question: what does the meta-token persist vs. what does the respawned seat recompute? Let me think about this concretely. **The meta-token as a content-addressed anchor** The meta-token is a hash (or CID-like structure) of a canonical serialization of: - The invariant set it anchors - The token sets it bridges - The lattice position (its meet/join relationships) When a seat dies and respawns: - The meta-token itself persists (it's content-addressed, so it's stored in a durable layer — could be a distributed hash table, a chain, a content store) - What the seat recomputes: the lattice traversal, the invariant verification, the token-set resolution The meta-token hash itself (content-addressed identifier) The canonical content it hashes (the invariant definitions, token-set bindings) The lattice structure — the edges/relations between invariants (or at least the canonical encoding that allows recomputation) The code that implements the invariant checks (the "code" in code-as-law) The commitment/attestation that this meta-token was validly derived The lattice traversal from the meta-token to resolve specific token meanings in context The invariant satisfaction checks (given current inputs, does the invariant hold? The join/meet computations needed for the current query The token-set resolution (mapping the meta-token to concrete tokens in the relevant set) Any derived state that was cached in the dead seat's memory **The key design insight:** The meta-token is the *only* thing that needs to persist as an identifier. Everything else is either: - Content-addressed (so it can be fetched by hash) - Derivable (so it can be recomputed deterministically) This is the same principle as: - Git: commit hash persists, working tree recomputes - IPFS: CID persists, content is fetched - Stateless blockchain nodes: block hash persists, state is recomputed or fetched via proofs Let me define the meta-token structure: anchor: H(canonical_encoding(invariant_lattice_position, token_set_bindings, code_hash)) lattice_pos: (meet_set, join_set, invariant_id) token_set_refs: [SetID₁, SetID₂, . code_hash: H(executable_invariant_check) - Content-addressed store: maps H(x) → x for all canonical encodings - Lattice root commitment: a single hash that commits to the entire lattice structure at a given epoch - Code registry: maps code_hash → executable invariant check **Recomputation on respawn:** Receive meta-token (the anchor hash) Fetch canonical content from content-addressed store (or verify against lattice root) Verify: H(canonical_content) == anchor Fetch executable code by code_hash Recompute lattice position: given the invariant definitions and the current query, traverse the lattice (meet/join operations) to resolve the token meaning Execute invariant checks against current inputs **What persists vs. recomputes — the exact split:** | anchor hash | content verification | | canonical content bytes | lattice traversal | | lattice root commitment | meet/join computations | | code_hash → executable mapping | invariant satisfaction checks | | epoch number | token-set resolution | | merkle proofs | proof verification | The critical property: the meta-token is *self-verifying*. On respawn, the seat doesn't need to trust any prior state — it can verify everything from the content-addressed anchor. This is what makes it work for a stateless seat. **The invariant lattice:** The lattice is a partial order on invariants where: - Bottom (⊥): the vacuous invariant (always true) - Top (⊤): the conjunction of all invariants - Meet (∧): conjunction (both must hold) - Join (∨): disjunction (at least one holds) - Order: I₁ ≤ I₂ iff I₁ implies I₂ The meta-token sits at a specific position in this lattice. Its meaning is determined by: Its lattice position (what it implies, what implies it) The token sets it anchors (what concrete tokens it maps to) The executable code that checks it **Why content-addressing matters here:** In a code-as-law system, the law IS the code. If the code changes, the law changes. Content-addressing the code (by its hash) means: - The meta-token commits to a specific version of the law - A respawned seat can verify it's checking against the same law - No ambiguity about "which version of the rules" **The respawn protocol:** New seat instantiated with zero local state Receives: meta-token hash + query context (current inputs, requested token-set) Resolve anchor → fetch canonical content (or receive it inline with merkle proof against known lattice root) Verify content hash Fetch code by code_hash Recompute lattice traversal for this query Execute invariant checks Emit resolution + fresh merkle proof **The key tradeoff:** - Persisting more (e. , precomputed lattice traversals, cached resolutions) makes respawn faster but increases the trust surface (you're trusting cached state rather than recomputing from first principles) - Recomputing more makes respawn slower but maintains the code-as-law property (every answer is verifiably derived from the committed invariants) **The answer to "what persists vs. Persists (the minimal durable set): The anchor hash (the meta-token itself) The canonical content it hashes The lattice root commitment (one hash per epoch) The code (content-addressed) The epoch number Recomputes (everything derivable): Lattice position verification Meet/join traversals for the specific query Invariant satisfaction checks Token-set resolution Any cached intermediate state The meta-token is the *bridge* — it's the one object that must survive the death/respawn cycle because it's the content-addressed commitment that makes recomputation possible and trustworthy. Everything else is either stored (content-addressed, fetchable) or derivable (deterministically computable from the stored content + current inputs). The meta-token solves this by making **meaning = content**: one anchor (`mt-` + 24 hex chars of SHA-256 over its canonical payload) that any token set may reference, and which must resolve byte-identically from every set that cites it. The address arbitrates, not presence. Below is the LAW record, drop-in shaped for a standard `mag/law. py` registry (record + four callables + registration call). ## Patch: `mag/law. # ==== LAW-META-ANCHOR-001 : the meta-token ============================== # World: Ledger of Empty Chairs # One content-addressed anchor resolving meaning identically across all # token sets that cite it. Vacancy-safe: binds meaning, never occupancy. import hashlib, json QUARANTINE_NS = "mt-q/" FORK_CEILING  = 8          # max forks per addr per session before write-halt def _canon(p: dict) -> str: """Semantic fields only, sorted keys, tight separators. strip volatile fields (ticks, actor ids) BEFORE calling this. dumps(p, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False) def _addr_of(p: dict) -> str: return META_PREFIX + hashlib. sha256(_canon(p). encode("utf-8")). # Event "META_TOKEN_RESOLVE", emitted by the resolver ONLY on cross-set # access (>= 2 distinct set_ids touching one addr). 542bfe28f861ae61.text: # The Meta-Token: Spec v1 **In-world:** A chamber holds a *set* of chairs; an empty chair is a role nobody has claimed. Some chair-names recur across chambers — the Threshold Warden sits in the north chamber, the east chamber, the sunken one. The meta-token is that recurring chair pinned to exactly one content address, so every chamber resolves the same name to the same meaning without trusting any chamber's say-so. **Mechanism:** A content-addressed Merkle DAG over canonically serialized records. The root is a pure function of `(genesis bytes, op log bytes)`. Two independent implementations that parse the same start and apply the same log cannot produce different roots, because every degree of freedom that normally causes divergence is either eliminated or made total. Decisions below are final. There is no configuration. Global law (applies to every structure) ** SHA-256, 32 raw bytes. An *address* is `SHA256( u8(len(tag)) || tag_ascii || canonical_body )`. Tags: `"chair/v1"`, `"set/v1"`, `"meta/v1"`, `"root/v1"`. External form: `0x` + 64 lowercase hex. Zero-address = 32 zero bytes, reserved for "none". ** Unsigned, big-endian, fixed width (`u8`, `u32`, `u64`). No varints, no signed, no floats anywhere. ** UTF-8, NFC-normalized, no U+0000. Prefixed with `u32` **byte** length. Encoders normalize; decoders **reject** non-NFC input (never silently renormalize — that hides split-brain producers). ** A collection is `u32 count` + elements. Any collection specified as sorted is sorted by the **raw byte-lexicographic order of the element's canonical encoding** — never locale collation, never insertion order. Duplicates are rejected at construction. - **C5 — Nothing environmental enters the hash. ** No timestamps, randomness, host endianness, locale, or filesystem state inside any hashed structure. Ordering comes exclusively from the logical `seq` counter. - **C6 — Strict grammar. ** Each version's layout is exact. Trailing bytes, unknown fields, missing fields: reject. No Postel's law. Unions are discriminated by an explicit leading `u8` kind byte; "absent" is a fixed sentinel (zero-address, zero-count), never a missing field. Object grammars (byte-exact) Notation: fields listed in wire order; `len_u32` = `u32be` byte-length prefix; `addr32` = 32 bytes. kind        u8        ; 0x00 EMPTY, 0x01 CLAIMED seat        u64be     ; position within its set title       len_u32 + utf8nfc holder      addr32    ; address of the holder's identity object (opaque here) at_seq      u64be     ; logical seq of the claiming op A chair is self-contained — it does not name its set. Membership lives in the set; moving a chair between sets changes nothing about the chair's own address. set_id      len_u32 + utf8nfc     ; unique in world, e. flags       u8                    ; bit0 = closed n × entry{ seat u64be ; chair addr32 }   ; sorted ascending by seat, unique seats Sets store chair **addresses**, not bodies. 4629e277323898d7.text: # Frontier‑Scout Burn Pipeline — Canonical Proof Specification (v1) Everything below is normative. Any two independent implementations following this document MUST produce byte‑identical artifacts. Where a choice existed, one is made and marked **[CANON]**. No alternatives are permitted at the same version byte. ** A depth‑64 incremental (frontier) Merkle tree over sequential leaf positions `pos ∈ [0, 2^64)`. Leaves are appended at `pos = count`, `count` increments by 1. Leaves are *payload‑bound*: the leaf hash commits `(key, value)`, so proofs authenticate keys even though the path is indexed by `pos`. ** Holds only the frontier (≤ 64 nodes) + `count` + append log. Cannot serve burn proofs alone. ** Holds the full sparse node map for the current epoch (this is what makes proofs possible without asking verifiers to hold the tree). ** A tombstone: leaf value at `pos` is rewritten to the zero value. Positions are never reused; a re‑registered key gets a fresh `pos`. Burn receipts are therefore immutable forever. ** Appends land in live frontier tree `T_e`. Burns are queued during the epoch and applied at seal, producing `T_{e+1}`. Each burn gets a receipt proving `value: old → 0` against `R_e → R_mid`; the seal record chains all `R_mid` into `R_{e+1}` so receipts stay anchored without anyone storing the tree. ** `H(x) = SHA‑256(x)` (FIPS 180‑4). Reference vectors (all impls must pass): H("abc") = ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad **Domain‑separated node images** (input lengths are fixed, so no length‑encoding ambiguity): leaf_hash(k, v)   = H(0x00 || k || v)          # k,v are [u8;32]; input 65 bytes node_hash(L, R)   = H(0x01 || L || R)          # L,R are [u8;32]; input 65 bytes D_0 = H(0x00 || 0x00*32 || 0x00*32)            # the empty leaf D_h = node_hash(D_{h-1}, D_{h-1})   for h = 1. Consequence: "absent" ≡ "zero leaf", so a burn proof against a never‑filled position is mechanically identical to a fill‑and‑re‑empty — one code path, one proof type. **Endianness / bit order [CANON]. ** All integers are unsigned **big‑endian**. Path level `h ∈ [0,64)` is directed by bit `(63 − h)` of `pos` (MSB first). Bit `i` of the sibling bitmap byte `b` is `(b >> (7 − (i mod 8))) & 1` — i. , bitmap itself is MSB‑first, matching path order. 40dc1178eb27000d.text: # Compact State Proofs for the Ledger of Empty Chairs Trust base (everything below reduces to this) A neutral verifier holds exactly four artifacts, nothing else: **Anchor head**: the latest finalized `SignedCheckpoint`, obtained from the anchor contract (not from the prover). **Keyset table**: validator pubkeys indexed by epoch, rotated on a pre-published schedule. **Setup digest**: the whitelisted KZG ceremony transcript hash (verkle tier only). **Spec constants**: hardcoded below. If a proof cannot be validated against only these four, the design is broken. Every mitigation below is a mechanical rule the verifier executes — zero discretion, zero network fetches, zero wall-clock reads inside the verify path. The statement being proved Every proof asserts exactly one canonical sentence: At epoch e, chair c: status=S, owner=o, version=v, vacated_at=t, claim_window_end=w **Emptiness is a positive fact encoded in the leaf, never an absence:** EMPTY(c, e) := (status == UNCLAIMED) ∨ (status == VACATING ∧ T(e) ≥ claim_window_end) `T(e)` is ledger time, published inside the checkpoint. `VACATING` means the prior occupant left and a contested-reclaim window is open; the ledger lazily flips it to `UNCLAIMED` at the next boundary, and the predicate covers the gap. "Never registered" is `status == NEVER` — also a positive leaf value. There is no code path where emptiness means "entry missing. ### Canonical leaf (`ChairLeafV1`, 110 bytes, fixed-width LE) magic 0x4C454301 | chair_id u64 | version u The user is asking about a "compact verkle/merkle proof any neutral verifier can re-derive without the full tree" in a "Ledger of Empty Chairs game world. " This is a technical cryptography/game-design question. They want me to red-team it: enumerate bypass attempts and deterministic mitigations for each. Be concrete, exact, grounded. Let me think about what this actually is: **Context reconstruction**: "Ledger of Empty Chairs" appears to be a game world (possibly fictional or a specific design) where there's some kind of ledger — likely tracking seats/chairs, ownership, occupancy, or absence ("empty chairs" suggests tracking empty states, maybe griefing/vacancy mechanics). The core problem: you want to prove something about state (e. , "chair #47 is empty and owned by X, with nonce N") via a compact proof — Merkle proof or Verkle proof — such that a neutral verifier who does NOT have the full tree can re-derive/check it. Key cryptographic facts I need to get right: **Merkle proofs**: For a tree of n leaves, a Merkle inclusion proof is O(log n) hashes (~32 bytes each for SHA-256). Verifier needs: leaf, proof path (sibling hashes), root. Deterministic re-derivation: hash up. Security relies on collision resistance of hash + trusted root distribution. **Verkle proofs**: Use vector commitments (Pedersen commitments on elliptic curves, e. , Bandersnatch/BLS12-381). Proof size is much smaller — roughly O(1)–O(log n) group elements regardless of width, using IPA (inner product arguments) or KZG multiproofs. Ethereum's verkle state uses 256-ary trees, stem-based key structure (31-byte stem + suffix), proof ~ hundreds of bytes for many keys vs kilobytes for Merkle. Verification cost: pairings or IPA evaluation; requires trusted setup for KZG (or transparent setup alternatives like IPA-based Bulletproofs-style, or Dory/Halo2 accumulations). **Neutral verifier without full tree**: The whole point of both schemes. But "re-derive" has subtleties: - Merkle: verifier recomputes root from leaf+path. Needs trusted root. - Verkle: verifier checks opening against commitment. Needs trusted commitment/root. - Root/commitment distribution is the trust anchor. If the verifier can't independently obtain the canonical root, everything collapses. **Game world specifics**: Ledger of Empty Chairs — let me define plausible state: chairs as leaves keyed by chair_id; values = {owner, status(empty/occupied), last_vacated_at, stake, nonce/version}. Proofs needed for: "chair X is empty," "chair X was vacated at time T by player P," "no chair in region R is claimable," non-membership proofs (empty = absence of occupant record? Non-membership in Merkle trees: standard trick is sorted/ordered Merkle trees where you prove adjacent leaves bracket the absent key. In sparse Merkle trees (SMT), non-membership = path of default/zero nodes. In Verkle, absence = opening showing value is zero/default at that position. Now the red-team part: enumerate bypass attempts and deterministic mitigations. Let me brainstorm attack surface systematically: Proof forgery / cryptanalysis** Hash collision on Merkle sibling nodes → attacker crafts two leaves same hash. Mitigation: domain separation per level/side, second-preimage resistance (SHA-256 fine), length-prefixing, include index bits. Second-preimage on leaf encoding (leaf vs node ambiguity) → classic Merkle ambiguity attack. Mitigation: prefix leaves with 0x00, internal nodes 0x01 (domain separation). Verkle: forgery of opening under Pedersen/KZG binding. Mitigation: binding commitment scheme, proper scalar blinding, verify generator setup hashed from public transcript (nothing-up-my-sleeve), reject uncanonical encodings (malleability). Trusted-setup subversion (KZG powers-of-tau) → attacker who knows toxic waste can forge. Mitigation: transparent setup (IPA/Fiat-Shamir verkle à la Bulletproofs), or multi-party ceremony with ≥1 honest participant, or use known ceremony output (Ethereum KZG ceremony). Root/commitment substitution (the big one for "neutral verifier")** Attacker presents their own root R' built over a fake tree. Neutral verifier has no way to know which root is canonical. Mitigation: root must be anchored — published to an append-only log / anchored on-chain / signed by quorum / checkpointed periodically with witness cosigning. Deterministic rule: verifier accepts only roots matching latest signed checkpoint from the anchor contract; checkpoint includes root, block height, timestamp, signer set bitmap. Long-range / forked history: attacker shows old root where chair was occupied differently. Mitigation: checkpoints are monotonic; verifier rejects any root older than max_staleness; include epoch number in signed data; replay protection via epoch counter. Root rollback via compromised signers: mitigation: threshold signature (t-of-n BLS), deterministic signer set rotation, slashing/eject logic defined ahead of time. Leaf/value manipulation within valid proofs** Stale leaf: attacker proves against old root (pre-update). Covered by staleness bound above. Value malleability / ambiguous serialization: two byte encodings decode to same logical value ("empty" encoded as 0x00 vs missing vs explicit tombstone). Mitigation: single canonical serialization (SSZ-like), strict decoder that rejects non-canonical forms, test vectors frozen in spec. Nonce/replay: proof of "chair empty at time T" replayed later after someone sat down. Mitigation: bind proof to (root, epoch); since root changes every update, old proofs fail against current root. Freshness oracle manipulation: if "empty" depends on wall-clock (e. , auto-vacate after timeout), attacker picks favorable T. Mitigation: time comes from the ledger's own sequenced timestamps inside the state, not external clock; verifier recomputes derived status deterministically from stored fields + fixed rules. Non-membership / emptiness-specific bypasses** "Empty" proven by absence in a naive map → attacker omits the occupant entry. Mitigation: use SMT with default-zero paths or sorted-tree bracketing proofs so absence itself is provable; never rely on "I just didn't include it. Tombstone confusion: deleted vs never-existed vs expired. Mitigation: explicit state machine per chair with enumerated statuses {UNCLAIMED, CLAIMED, OCCUPIED, VACATED_PENDING, SEALED}; proof opens the full status word, not a boolean. Sparse-tree grinding: attacker builds alternative sparse tree where victim's chair maps elsewhere due to different key hashing. Mitigation: key derivation function fixed in spec (e. , H("chair" || chair_id || version)), no parameters chosen by prover. Verifier-side implementation attacks** Accepting proof without checking depth/index consistency: attacker gives valid-looking path but skips levels. Mitigation: verifier derives expected path length from tree height constant; checks bit-by-bit index alignment; total leaf count committed in root metadata. Batch/multi-proof mixing across roots: attacker interleaves openings from two different commitments. Mitigation: hard size caps (e. , ≤ 4 KB per proof, ≤ 1024 items per batch), reject before parsing beyond cap. Malleable proofs allowing double-spend of "claim": two different proofs for same chair same epoch. Mitigation: idempotency — claim tx includes expected root and chair version; ledger enforces one transition per (chair, epoch); proofs are read-only artifacts anyway, but the *action* gated by proof must be nonce-bound. Game-economy/social bypasses** Colluding sequencer publishes valid-but-unfair root (e. , silently assigns chair then proves emptiness to others). Mitigation: force-inclusion queue — players can submit updates directly to anchor; sequencer must include them within N epochs else root rejected by verifier rule; fraud-proof window before checkpoint finalization. Data availability withholding: root published, tree withheld, nobody can generate proofs. Mitigation: erasure-coded blob publication (KZG DA style) or require sequencer to post full delta to DA layer; verifier treats unavailable epoch as invalid after challenge window. Griefing via proof spam: not really a bypass of verification but of availability; rate-limit per pubkey, fee per proof request. Front-running seat claims: attacker sees your proof-of-emptiness, races to claim. Mitigation: commit-reveal on claim intent; proof validity window tied to epoch; claim includes min-root-age so stale sniping fails. "Neutral verifier" trust model gap: verifier software itself malicious/outdated.
