bc0fb5affd457f78.text: # Red-Team: Deniable-yet-Verifiable Comms in the Frontier-Scout Burn Pipeline ## Scope and threat model (fixed, so the attacks below are well-defined) Protocol claims: (1) **Deniability** — covertext is recoverable *only* with the codebook; observers without it learn nothing, including that anything is hidden. (2) **Authorship** — a designated verifier set can prove who sent a recovered message. (3) **Burn** — artifacts are destroyed post-consumption. Attackers: passive observer, active injector, captured scout, partial-material insider, compelled-disclosure adversary, compromised base. Two axioms the whole scheme hangs on. Every bypass below targets a violation of one of them: - **Axiom 1 — Partitioned verifiability. ** Public-verifiable non-repudiation and outsider-deniability are mutually exclusive on the same artifact. Verifier material must be secret and held only by the base. Anything publicly checkable is a beacon. - **Axiom 2 — Fail-closed determinism. ** Every mitigation must be a CI assertion or a runtime invariant, not a guideline. If it isn't machine-enforced, assume it's absent. ## Class A — Detecting the channel (deniability broken without recovery) Statistical embedding fingerprints. ** Naive stego (LSBs, timing jitter, padding choices) shifts the cover distribution; learned steganalysis picks it up without ever recovering content. **Mitigation:** Choice-encoding. Covers are emitted by the *genuine* ambient traffic generator; the payload selects *which* generator output is sent. Every emitted cover is a fully valid sample of the ambient process — KL divergence between emitted and ambient distributions is zero by construction. Where free-form embedding is unavoidable, encode via arithmetic coding under a cover model fitted to live ambient traffic, refreshed weekly. Length/volume correlation. ** Payload size maps to cover size; traffic analysis recovers message size and cadence. **Mitigation:** Quantize every payload to fixed size buckets (next power of two, PRF-padded). Emit constant-volume epochs: idle periods carry PRF-generated decoy covers so total bytes per epoch is load-independent. Enforced by a wire-format invariant: decoder rejects any non-canonical length. Timing correlation / silence-as-signal. ** Send-on-event reveals event times; silence after a major event is itself intelligence. **Mitigation:** Slotted emission. Scouts transmit only at fixed slots (or Poisson with parameters identical to background chatter), buffering real payloads; empty slots carry decoys. Event information lives in content, never in cadence. Runtime invariant: emission timestamps are slot-quantized, independent of event timestamps. Carrier and transport outliers. ** Rare file types, odd ports, non-standard TLS fingerprints flag the scout regardless of content. **Mitigation:** Carrier whitelist restricted to types ≥ threshold frequency in ambient traffic; transport pinned to a mainstream client fingerprint (stock library version, domain-fronted HTTPS). CI test asserts the deployed fingerprint string equals the pinned release. Validity-correlated receiver behavior. ** Receiver ACKs valid messages, silently drops invalid ones → attacker uses the receiver as a forgery-testing oracle. **Mitigation:** Uniform-response policy. ACKs are implicit in the next scheduled traffic stream and statistically identical whether or not a valid message arrived. No observable receiver state change may correlate with validity — asserted by differential testing on the receiver harness. ## Class B — Recovering content without the codebook Keystream/pad reuse. ** Any repeated pad segment turns the channel into running-key cipher: C₁⊕C₂ = P₁⊕P₂. One leaked plaintext strips every overlapping message. **Mitigation:** Information-theoretic one-time pad under a ratchet: Kᵢ = HKDF(Kᵢ₋₁, nonceᵢ, "burn"); Kᵢ₋₁ zeroized on derivation. Nonces strictly monotonic; nonce collision triggers deterministic abort and out-of-band rotation. Deliberate consequence: recorded covertext stays safe against *unbounded* adversaries forever — residual risk collapses to key custody alone. Static codebook table inference. ** A literal lookup-table codebook used repeatedly is recoverable from enough (cover, context) pairs. **Mitigation:** The "codebook" is a keyed PRF family, not a table: encodeᵢ(m) = StegoEnc(HKDF(K_master, i), m). Per-message derived encoding; finite samples don't extrapolate. Hard cap of 2²⁰ messages per master key, deterministic forced rotation, master rotated out-of-band quarterly. Weak RNG on the scout. ** Predictable pads/nonnes = recovery without the codebook. **Mitigation:** Hybrid derivation: nonce = SHA256(TRNG ∥ epoch ∥ counter). TRNG health checks gate transmission — failed health check means deterministic hold, never fallback to software entropy. Min-entropy floor asserted in CI test vectors. Cross-protocol key reuse. ** Codebook material reused elsewhere creates cross-protocol oracles. **Mitigation:** Mandatory domain-separation labels in every HKDF call; distinct label per protocol role. Lint gate rejects any HKDF invocation missing a label; labels registry is closed. ## Class C — Forging or subverting authorship Cut-and-paste re-embedding. ** Attacker lifts a validly signed codeword and re-embeds it in a new carrier/context ("advance to grid X" replayed months later). **Mitigation:** Sign the full context tuple: SHA256(carrier-invariant bytes) ∥ epoch ∥ seq ∥ src-id ∥ dst-id ∥ payload-hash. Carrier hash is defined over the carrier regions *not* used for embedding, computed identically pre/post-embedding — resolves the sign-then-embed ordering circularity. Receiver verifies every field against current expected values; any mismatch → deterministic drop. Splice / truncate / reorder. ** Multi-frame messages disassembled and recombined. **Mitigation:** Per-frame signature covering (epoch, seq, frame-index, total-frames, chunk). Assembly requires complete, contiguous, single-source sets; any gap or duplicate outside the anti-replay window kills the entire message. Codebook-only insider forges. ** Possessing the codebook suffices if auth is a MAC. **Mitigation:** Asymmetric signature (Ed25519) over the encoded payload, then signature+payload jointly encrypted under the codebook-derived pad and embedded. Outsiders see pure cover; insiders recover and verify. Verify keys are provisioned covertly, never published — Axiom 1. Stolen signing key (captured scout). ** Perfect forgeries from the captured device. **Mitigation:** Three stacked deterministic controls: (a) two-man rule — scout signature AND base-session countersignature both required; (b) per-key epoch window and message-count budget enforced by receiver-side monotonic counters; (c) freeze-on-miss — three missed check-ins triggers a covert revocation record (riding the channel as a normal instruction); frozen-key messages rejected unconditionally. Genuine-sender repudiation. ** Real sender later claims "anyone could have built that. **Mitigation:** Proof-of-authorship = signature + base's hash-chained, append-only log entry keyed by (epoch, seq). Log anchors periodically to multiple out-of-band custodians. Combined with secret verify keys, this yields designated-verifier semantics: provable inside, deniable outside. Downgrade / codec confusion. ** Forced negotiation to a weaker legacy mode. **Mitigation:** No negotiable crypto. Version byte pinned at provisioning; any other value → deterministic reject. Handshakes eliminated entirely — all parameters static per deployment, rotated out-of-band (handshakes are covert-channel liabilities anyway). Supply-chain codebook swap. ** Poisoned distribution gives parties mismatched or weakened codebooks. **Mitigation:** Codebook blob digest pinned in a dual-custodian provisioning ceremony; each message carries a codebook-generation byte; mismatch → deterministic drop plus alert on the separate channel. Burn-command forgery. ** Fake "burn everything" to erase evidence selectively or DoS the pipeline. **Mitigation:** Burn requires top-tier signature matching a pre-committed hash revealed at provisioning, confirmed by two consecutive authentic copies from different relays. ## Class D — Burn-pipeline specific bypasses Resurrection via residue. ** "Burned" plaintext persists in page cache, logs, snapshots, swap. **Mitigation:** Decode and verify exclusively in locked pages (mlock); zeroize immediately post-verification; plaintext never touches disk — enforced as a CI grep gate over all serialized/logged forms plus a boot-time invariant. Single atomic deletion routine owns both body and metadata TTLs. ** Scout seized with queued outbound traffic. **Mitigation:** Queue depth ≤ 1; items stored only as covertext; the pad share is deleted locally immediately on transmit-ACK. Exposure window bounded to one slot period by construction. Metadata outliving the body. ** Routing records survive the burn and are the actual target. **Mitigation:** Metadata shares the body's TTL and is deleted by the same atomic routine — no independent retention path may exist (asserted by storage-layer audit). Decoder oracle under injection. ** Crafted covers crash the decoder or produce timing/error differences usable as an oracle. **Mitigation:** Decoder is a total function: every input maps to valid-message or silent-drop, no on-wire error signaling. Constant-work decode — full decode+verify executes regardless of early failure, killing timing oracles. Fuzz gate in CI: zero crashes, branch-uniform timing profile on the adversarial corpus. Replay inside the validity window. ** Context fields still fresh, so attack 10's cousin slips through. **Mitigation:** Per-source sliding-window bitmap over sequence numbers; seen seqs dropped deterministically; window sized to maximum in-flight frames. ## Class E — Compelled disclosure and human layer Subpoena the codebook. ** The sharpest deniability bypass: hand over the codebook and deniability dies, because there's only one decoding. **Mitigation:** Dual-layer OTP by default. Construction: pick decoy P_d (auto-generated, contextually innocuous), random K_d, set C = P_d ⊕ K_d, then K_t = C ⊕ P_t. Distribute K_t to the parties; K_d sits where an adversary will find it. Same covertext decodes to the true message under K_t and a plausible decoy under K_d. Decoy generation is automatic per message — no operator discretion, no forgetting. Voluntary disclosure under capture. **Mitigation:** Duress template — a specific alternate "all-normal" report form whose use signals capture; receiver freezes all keys from that source on sight. Custody sharding: scout holds encode-capable material only, never the full decode side. Local side channels on the verifying device. ** Power/cache observation during verification extracts key state. **Mitigation:** Constant-time verify (no secret-dependent branches or memory access); dudect-style timing tests as a merge-blocking CI gate; secrets in secure element where hardware permits. ## Residual risk ledger (what no mitigation above covers) Stated plainly, because pretending otherwise is how pipelines die: - **Endpoint compromise pre-compose** — malware reading plaintext before encoding defeats everything downstream. Only answer is device hygiene, out of scope here. - **Ambient-baseline drift** — if the cover model lags a shift in real traffic patterns, Class A protections decay. Weekly refresh is a bound, not a guarantee. - **Global traffic analysis across many scouts** — per-message deniability doesn't defeat graph-level correlation over months. Constant-volume epochs blunt it; nothing eliminates it. - **Base compromise** — the base holds verify keys and the log. Hash chaining and HSM custody raise cost; a sufficiently powerful base adversary wins. Two-man rule limits, not prevents. - **Key custody is the whole game** — by design (item 6), confidentiality is information-theoretic, so every remaining attack reduces to stealing key material. Budget accordingly: the threat model collapses to "protect the keys," and every control above should be re-read in that light. Enforcement rule, restated as the deliverable: each numbered mitigation ships as either a CI assertion (fingerprint match, no-plaintext-to-disk grep, fuzz/timing gates, label lint) or a runtime invariant (fail-closed version byte, anti-replay bitmap, ratchet abort, atomic TTL deletion). Anything neither machine-checkable nor runtime-enforced gets cut — prose mitigations are attack surface. Let me parse this carefully. The user is asking about a "deniable-yet-verifiable comms protocol" — meaning a communication protocol where: **Deniable**: The message can only be recovered with the codebook (i. , to an outsider without the codebook, the content looks like noise or innocuous data — plausible deniability about what was transmitted). **Verifiable/Authorship-provable**: The authorship of the message is provable (presumably to the intended recipient or auditor, using some key/signature mechanism). This is in a "frontier-scout burn pipeline" context. Let me think about what that means. "Frontier-scout" suggests reconnaissance/exploration agents at the edge of a network or system — scouts operating in untrusted/hostile territory, sending back intelligence. "Burn pipeline" suggests messages are ephemeral — burned after reading, one-time use, no persistence. So this is like: forward scouts in contested territory send short-lived covert messages back; the pipeline burns them after consumption. The user wants me to red-team this protocol: enumerate bypass attempts (ways an adversary could defeat either the deniability property or the verifiability property) and give deterministic mitigations for each. Let me first formalize the protocol design space so my attack enumeration is grounded: **Protocol components (assumed):** - A codebook K shared between sender and receiver (this is the deniability key — needed to recover plaintext from covertext). - An authorship key S (signing key held by the sender; verification key held by receiver/auditor). - Cover traffic / steganographic embedding: ciphertext embedded into innocuous-looking carrier (e. , timing patterns, image LSBs, header fields, padding, etc. - Burn semantics: after receipt/consumption, artifacts destroyed; possibly keys rotated per-message. - G1 (Deniability/Confidentiality): Without K, an observer cannot distinguish carrier from random/innocuous traffic, nor recover content. - G2 (Authenticity): With verification capability, the receiver can prove a given recovered message came from a specific authorized sender (non-repudiation among insiders), while outsiders see nothing verifiable. - G3 (Burn/Ephemerality): Post-consumption, no residual artifact allows retroactive recovery or forgery. The inherent tension: deniability usually wants repudiability (sender can deny), but here we want *authorship provable* — provable presumably only to those holding the verifier material. This is "undeniable to insider, deniable to outsider. " Classic constructions: designated-verifier proofs, chameleon signatures, MAC-based authentication (MAC gives authenticity to key-holders but is deniable to outsiders since anyone with the MAC key could have forged it). Actually wait — if we want authorship provable, a plain MAC makes it forgeable by any key-holder, which weakens non-repudiation among insiders. The design likely uses asymmetric signature over the codeword, then embeds signature+payload via codebook into cover. Or uses a two-tier scheme: symmetric codebook for recovery/deniability, asymmetric sig for authorship. Now, red-team: enumerate bypass attempts. Let me think adversarially across attacker positions: - A1: Passive network observer (sees all traffic, no keys). - A2: Active network attacker (can inject, replay, modify, drop). - A3: Compromised endpoint (scout captured; has device, maybe partial keys). - A4: Malicious insider with partial material (has codebook but not signing key, or vice versa). - A5: Traffic analyst doing statistical detection (even without recovery, detecting *existence* of covert channel breaks deniability-in-practice). - A6: Insider trying to frame someone (forge authorship). - A7: Legitimate sender trying to repudiate after the fact ("I didn't send that"). - A8: Receiver-side compromise (burn pipeline leaks). Bypass attempts against each goal: **Against deniability (G1):** **Statistical fingerprinting of the embedding channel. ** If the codebook maps bits into cover features (e. , LSBs, timing jitter, field values), naive embeddings leave distributional anomalies: LSB stego shifts histogram; timing channels show bimodal delays; padding lengths show non-uniform distribution. Deterministic mitigation: use a distribution-preserving encoding — map codewords onto cover symbols such that marginal and joint statistics match the natural cover distribution exactly (e. , arithmetic-decoding-based steganography conditioned on a public cover model, or rejection sampling until feature vector matches empirical cover distribution within ε). Concretely: encode via arithmetic coding under a fixed model M trained on legitimate traffic; any bitstring decodes to a cover sample indistinguishable from M's output class. Also enforce uniform padding-length distribution by bucketing. **Codebook reuse across messages → known-plaintext/correlation attacks. ** If the same codebook entry or same keystream segment is reused, XOR-style reuse leaks: C1⊕C2 = P1⊕P2. Observer who obtains even one plaintext (via capture of a scout, or a leaked doc) can strip the pad from all overlapping traffic. Deterministic mitigation: per-message one-time pad derived from a ratchet: K_i = HKDF(K_{i-1}, nonce_i, "burn"), delete K_{i-1} immediately; never reuse any pad byte; nonce monotonic and unique; hard-fail on nonce collision (deterministic abort + key rotation). **Length/volume correlation. ** Message length in cover units correlates with plaintext length → metadata leak (traffic analysis recovers size, timing, cadence even if content hidden). Mitigation: fixed-size frames (constant-rate padding to canonical block sizes, e. , always emit exactly N cover units per epoch, or quantize sizes to a small set matching benign traffic); deterministic: pad every payload to the next power-of-two bucket with PRF output, and add decoy epochs drawn from same PRF so total volume is constant regardless of load. **Timing side channel. ** Send-on-event reveals when events happen. Mitigation: time-sliced transmission — scouts transmit only at fixed slots (or Poisson with parameters identical to background chatter), buffering real payloads; empty slots carry PRF-generated dummy covers. **Carrier selection bias. ** If scouts choose unusual carriers (rare file types, odd ports), the mere choice flags them. Mitigation: restrict carriers to the population baseline — whitelist of carriers whose frequency in ambient traffic ≥ threshold; deterministic mapping from available carriers to this whitelist. **Replay of old cover for correlation. ** Attacker replays previously observed covertext segments to detect whether receivers act on them (behavioral oracle). Mitigation: epoch counters inside authenticated envelope; receiver deterministically drops anything with stale/non-monotonic counter before acting; no observable action on duplicates. **Against verifiability/authorship (G2):** **Signature stripping/re-embedding (cut-and-paste). ** Attacker lifts a validly signed codeword from one cover and re-embeds it into a different cover/context to change apparent meaning (context substitution). , "advance to grid X" signed once, replayed later when X is now wrong/harmful. Mitigation: bind signature to full context: sign (epoch, sequence, source-id, destination-id, carrier-hash, payload-hash). Receiver verifies all fields match current expected values; stale epoch → reject. Deterministic check list, fail-closed. **Forgery via codebook-only possession. ** Insider with codebook but not signing key tries to fabricate a message. If authentication were symmetric (MAC), they succeed. Mitigation: asymmetric signature (Ed25519) over the encoded payload; codebook alone insufficient. But note the tension: raw signatures are self-authenticating to *anyone* who sees them — if the signature is visible in the clear, it breaks deniability (an outsider sees a cryptographic blob proving something exists). Deterministic fix: encrypt the signature under the codebook-derived key along with payload (sign-then-encrypt-inside-cover), so outsiders see only cover; insiders recover both. Verification key distribution must itself be covert (pre-shared during provisioning, not fetched from public infra). **Key-compromise impersonation / stolen signing key. ** Captured scout's signing key lets adversary mint perfect messages. Deterministic mitigations: (a) two-man rule — require signature from scout key AND countersignature from base session key (both needed; capturing one party insufficient); (b) key usage limits: each signing key valid for a bounded epoch window and bounded message count, enforced by monotonic counters checked at receiver; (c) immediate revocation broadcast on loss-of-contact heuristic (scout misses 3 check-ins → its key frozen; frozen-key messages rejected deterministically). Note revocation broadcast itself must be covert — it rides the same channel as a normal instruction. **Repudiation attack by genuine sender (the flip side). ** Because the system promises deniability, a real sender may claim "that wasn't me — anyone could have made it. " If authorship must be provable *among insiders*, need non-repudiation to the verifier set but deniability to outsiders. Deterministic construction: signature verifyable only with private verifier material (designated-verifier style): include in the signed transcript a trapdoor commitment V = Commit(payload, r) where r is chosen so that the verifier can also derive a fake transcript for any payload (DV signatures), OR simpler: keep the verification key secret (only base holds it) — outsiders can't prove anything because they lack both codebook and verify key; insiders can prove because base holds verify key and logs. The deterministic rule: verification keys never published; proof-of-authorship = signature + base's tamper-evident log entry keyed by epoch/seq. **Malleability of the cover codec. ** Some stego codecs allow transforming cover without changing extracted bits (e. , JPEG recompression preserving LSB plane? No—lossy destroys LSBs; but format-transforming malleability: attacker converts PNG→BMP→PNG keeping pixel values, extracting same codeword, then re-signs? They can't re-sign without key, but they can *strip* the outer layer and re-embed the inner signed codeword into a new carrier — that's attack 7 again; covered by context binding including carrier-hash. careful: binding to carrier hash means the signer must know the exact final carrier bytes, which is awkward if embedding happens after signing. Deterministic order: pick carrier first, hash it, then sign (carrier-hash ∥ payload ∥ context), then embed. Embedding must be reversible w. untouched regions — use distortion-free embedding (e. , modify only designated metadata fields whose values don't affect carrier-hash computation. Cleaner: define carrier-hash over the invariant portions of the carrier (the parts not used for embedding), computed identically pre/post embedding. Deterministic spec: H = SHA256(carrier_invariant_bytes); sign(H ∥ ctx ∥ payload); embed into designated fields. **Truncation/splice attacks. ** Attacker truncates a multi-frame message or splices frames from two messages. Legal/process bypass: adversary doesn't break crypto, just gets warrants for the basecamp ISP/backhaul taps and does full-packet capture forever, then waits for a mistake. - Mitigation: assume full passive capture from day one (design goal: capture-everything-safe = forward secrecy + deniable auth + constant-rate cover). Nothing to add beyond above; but explicitly: no PFS violation ever, no renegotiation to non-PFS. Quantum adversary harvesting now, decrypting later ("harvest now, decrypt later") — breaks DH-based FS once CRQC exists. - Mitigation: hybrid PQ: X25519 + ML-KEM-768 in the key exchange; symmetric sizes doubled (256-bit keys); deterministic: hybrid combiner KDF over both shared secrets. Malicious update/poisoned corpus — the cover corpus or codebook update channel is compromised to plant a watermark or backdoor. Clock manipulation — attacker skews basecamp clock to cause nonce reuse or schedule desync revealing patterns. - Mitigation: nonces from counters, not wall clock; schedule anchored to monotonic counter synced via authenticated time only; deterministic: ignore unsigned time sources; drift-tolerant slot windows. Power/event correlation in own-iron — basecamp's own power draw, fan speed, LED activity during crypto ops observable. - Mitigation: dedicated low-power always-on device doing continuous dummy work so load profile is flat; deterministic background workload generator. The "codebook" being recoverable from the messages themselves if embedding uses the codebook as direct keystream (classic misuse). - Mitigation: codebook seeds KDF, never used raw; per-message keys; done above (#21/#31) — I'll merge. Human fallback bypass — under pressure, operator switches to insecure ad-hoc channel ("break glass"), which adversary anticipates. - Mitigation: pre-provisioned emergency procedure that is itself deniable (duress-authenticated decoy channel); deterministic: the ONLY sanctioned alternative is the pre-built decoy path; training + technical enforcement (no other egress allowed by firewall policy). Also structural red-team points: Verifiability-vs-deniability contradiction exploited socially: adversary says "prove you sent it" — if operator can prove authorship to third parties, deniability is void; if only recipient-verifiable, adversary tries to compromise recipient to get verification capability. - Design answer: authorship provable ONLY to holder of recipient private key (MAC-based deniable auth). Third-party proof impossible by construction. Recipient compromise handled by FS (past) + ratchet (future limited window). Deterministic statement: the protocol MUST NOT implement any primitive enabling public verifiability (no bare signatures on wire). Transcript forgery by sender-denial: in deniable auth, sender can deny because receiver could forge — but adversary flips it: receiver's "proof" is worthless, so an impostor can claim the real sender denied. Actually the attack: since MACs are forgeable post-hoc by receiver, a malicious receiver can fabricate messages "from" the sender. That's the cost of deniability. Mitigation if needed: per-message receipt signatures by receiver (kept private), or accept and bound the trust: receiver honesty required. Deterministic mitigation: optional receiver-signed receipts, encrypted to sender, providing sender-side confidence without public verifiability. Partition/split-view: adversary feeds different views to sender and receiver (MITM with two DHs) — prevented by identity binding in MAC (#16) — merged. Traffic analysis via packet size even after padding if padding granularity too coarse relative to message entropy — choose bucket sizes matched to observed marginal distribution of cover channel so padded sizes are indistinguishable from cover size distribution. Deterministic: size buckets = quantiles of empirical cover-size distribution. Embedding capacity mismatch forcing repetition — if payload exceeds cover capacity, system fragments and repeats patterns. - Mitigation: fragmentation with per-fragment fresh nonces and interleaving across covers; deterministic fragment schedule. Cold-start/first-use fingerprint: first-ever transmission stands out (new flow appears). - Mitigation: establish channel long before first real need; warm-up period with pure chaff; deterministic: channel goes live at installation, chaff-only for ≥ D days. Decommissioning leak: teardown leaves artifacts (config remnants, deleted-but-recoverable files). - Mitigation: secure erase procedure, overprovisioned SSD TRIM caveats noted (use crypto-erase: destroy key, data unrecoverable); deterministic: all storage encrypted at rest with per-device key in TPM/secure element; decommission = destroy key. eebfb34ed7f9466a.text: # Red-Team: Deniable-Verifiable Protocol in the Invariant Lattice ## Target model (what I'm attacking) Assumed spec: participants hold long-term Ed25519 identity keys and a shared **codebook** `K_c` (high-entropy symmetric secret driving a keyed codec). Messages are `Encode_{K_c}(payload ‖ metadata)` embedded in a cover medium; outsiders see only cover. Post-decode, metadata carries sender key-ID, epoch, sequence number, and a **tier flag**: tier-0 = Ed25519 signature over canonical bytes (non-repudiable), tier-1 = MAC only (deniable authenticity). Acceptance requires satisfaction of the invariant lattice top element. Every bypass below is paired with a **deterministic** mitigation — a mechanical gate, check, or structural rule, not guidance. ## Group A — Content recovery without the codebook Keystream/nonce reuse → two-time pad. ** Reused `(K_session, nonce)` yields `C₁⊕C₂ = P₁⊕P₂`; codebook never needed. **Mitigation:** Nonce = 64-bit atomic counter + 32-bit direction/channel tag, persisted with the key in one atomic write. Verifier rejects any `(key, nonce)` repeat; counter store is crash-safe (write-ahead). Invariant I-A1: nonce uniqueness is enforced by construction, not discipline. Steganalysis over the message corpus. ** Many embeddings drift cover statistics (histogram, LSB pairs, JPEG coefficient distributions); detector needs no codebook. **Mitigation:** Embedding positions selected by a keyed PRP over cover units; CI gate computes KL-divergence between cover-with-payload and clean-cover distributions on a fixed 10⁶-sample benchmark; merge blocked above pinned threshold ε. Payload density capped at ρ_max per medium. Decoding-oracle probing via the law layer. ** Error messages, logs, or echo endpoints reflect decoded bytes → chosen-ciphertext recovery of codec behavior. **Mitigation:** All decode failures return one constant, length-fixed error blob. Static rule: no code path emits bytes derived from decoded plaintext outside the commit point. Rate-limit decode requests per peer with deterministic penalty ladder. Weak codebook entropy (passphrase-derived). ** Offline guessing against captured covers. **Mitigation:** Argon2id with pinned params (m=1 GiB, t=4, p=parallelism) as the sole KDF; enrollment gate rejects estimated entropy < 80 bits using a fixed estimator; no fallback path exists (coverage test: every codebook-creation call site passes the gate). Side-channel extraction from decoder. ** Table-index timing/cache leakage correlates with `K_c`. **Mitigation:** Bitsliced or constant-time-vectorized table access; pinned crypto library version; CI timing-variance test (fixed workload, assert max−min latency < threshold across secret-dependent branches); runtime attestation binds deployed binary to the pinned hash. ## Group B — Authorship forgery Signing-nonce reuse/bias → private-key recovery. **Mitigation:** Ed25519 only (deterministic nonces by construction); RFC 6979 if ECDSA is unavoidable. Library choice is itself lattice invariant I-B1; no generic-signature interface exposed. Malleability + cross-context replay. ** Second valid signature from `(r,s)` transforms; or a signature valid in channel A replayed in channel B. **Mitigation:** Signed preimage = `H("proto/v" ‖ ctx ‖ channel_id ‖ sender ‖ seq ‖ epoch ‖ body)`; strict canonical encoding enforced at parse (reject non-canonical before verify); per-(sender, channel) monotonic seq with sliding anti-replay window checked atomically at accept. Key-substitution / rogue-key. ** Attacker registers key whose ID collides or substitutes into someone's attribution slot. **Mitigation:** Full `H(pubkey)` bound inside every signed body; registry maps keyID → pubkey with inclusion proof; verifier rejects any body whose embedded key-hash mismatches the resolved registry entry. Proof transferability destroys deniability. ** A standard signature shown to a third party converts a "deniable" tier-1 conversation into attributed evidence retroactively. **Mitigation:** Structural, not cryptographic: two tiers with the tier flag **inside the authenticated region**. Tier-1 uses MAC + key-commitment (any key-holder could have forged → deniable by construction). Tier-0 is explicit opt-in non-repudiation. Verifier rejects any message whose transport framing tier ≠ inner flag tier (downgrade/upgrade forgery fails closed). Designated-verifier proof that isn't simulatable. ** Naive DVS leaks a transcript only the true signer could produce → transferable. **Mitigation:** Chaum–Pedersen DVS with verifier-simulatable transcripts; property test in CI asserts transcript distributions from real signing and verifier simulation are statistically indistinguishable (fixed sample size, fixed test statistic, pinned threshold). ## Group C — Deniability collapse Codebook possession as evidence. ** Seizing the codebook proves participation regardless of message content. **Mitigation:** Codebook derived from passphrase via Argon2id (possession is indistinguishable from holding any secret); at-rest artifacts are uniformly random blobs (encrypted under hidden-volume scheme); organizational codebooks held as t-of-n Shamir shares so no single artifact implicates. Cross-message linkage. ** One confirmed signature lets an adversary attribute the whole epoch history via reused derived keys. **Mitigation:** Per-(epoch, channel) signing subkeys: `sk_e = VRF(master, epoch ‖ channel)`; subkeys never reused across epochs (enforced by derivation API shape — no export path for a subkey outside its epoch). Unlinkability property test: signature distributions under distinct subkeys must pass a fixed independence test. Metadata/timing fingerprinting. ** Content deniable, contact pattern provable. **Mitigation:** Fixed size buckets (pad to next power of two), Poisson-paced cover traffic with pinned rate λ, batching window W. Parameters live in the law; monitors alarm on deviation. Honest limitation: this bounds, does not eliminate, traffic analysis — the deterministic part is that deviations from the pinned profile are detectable alarms, not silent failures. Single confession taints all. ** Legal inference: "he proved authorship once ⇒ he holds the codebook ⇒ all decoded messages are his. **Mitigation:** Per-assertion keys (B2/C2 machinery); no global registry links identity ↔ epochs; where possible, replace signatures with ZK membership proofs (prove "sender ∈ authorized set for this epoch" without naming sender). The tier-0 opt-in is scoped per message, never per identity. ## Group D — Law-layer / lattice bypasses Unsound implication edges. ** Lattice assumes I_x ⇒ I_y; the entailment is false (e. , "MAC unforgeable ⇒ author authentic" fails under shared keys). **Mitigation:** Every edge ships with a machine-checked lemma or a property-test suite exercising exactly that entailment. Fail-closed rule: an edge without a passing proof obligation is deleted from the lattice at build time — the lattice shrinks rather than silently over-trusts. Missing invariant — reachable bad states. ** All checked invariants hold, yet an accepted message violates intent (classic case: validity checked, freshness not). **Mitigation:** Bounded model checker enumerates the accept function's state space up to depth d each release; every counterexample becomes a permanent new invariant + regression test. The loop is mandatory in CI; a release with open counterexamples cannot publish. TOCTOU between verify and act. ** State mutates between signature check and execution; attacker races the gap. **Mitigation:** Verify produces an immutable decision record; the acting stage consumes only that record; static rule bans any I/O or shared-state write inside the verify span (enforced by linter + ownership types). One commit point per message. Forced fallback under load. **Mitigation:** Fail-closed structural rule: no degraded-accept code path exists anywhere. Coverage assertion in CI: every accept site is control-flow-dominated by a successful verify call. That's a feature (dead messages die) and a boundary (archives are lossy by design; anything needing permanent record needs a separate, non-deniable channel — do NOT mix). What must never happen (invariants)** Never derive two members' subkeys to the same value; uniqueness check at issuance and at each rotation. Never reuse an epoch key across epochs, never reuse a nonce under the same key — enforce monotonic counters persisted in a way that survives crashes (write-ahead the counter before sending; a crash between encrypt and send must not allow counter rollback). Never transmit a message whose covertext was generated without consulting the current statistical baseline — i. , never hardcode phrase tables in a way that survives beyond their measured-safe volume; retire tables after N uses. Never send unpadded, length-revealing traffic; length buckets fixed and mandatory. Never let a failed verification be silent: a bad tag must trigger a defined procedure (quarantine, out-of-band challenge), never "ignore and move on" — because systematic tag failures are the signal of either edition skew or active forgery. Never use the codebook channel for content requiring long-term integrity (contracts, chain of custody) — the protocol's deniability means its own records self-destruct evidentially; mixing channels corrupts both. Never respond to a validly-tagged high-stakes instruction without a freshness challenge (replay defense at the operational layer): tag proves origin-era, not now-ness. Never let the anonymity set drop below a floor: if membership falls below k (say 4–5), the protocol must refuse to attribute (fall back to set-wide tags) rather than produce near-unique attributions. Never log plaintexts or decoded frames anywhere persistent; verification happens in ephemeral memory. Never allow enrollment without simultaneous rotation: adding a member must mint a new edition so the newcomer cannot read archived traffic (backward confinement) — otherwise one recruit unwinds history. Also worth specifying detection signals: what failure looks like from inside (tag mismatch clusters, covertext bounce-backs, drop surveillance) and the rule that two independent anomalies = treat book as burned. Format considerations: The user asked for edge cases: failure modes, boundaries, what must never happen. They want concrete, exact, grounded, no fluff. This calls for a fairly long, structured response with headers and tight lists. Markdown appropriate (this will be rendered presumably). I should briefly pin the protocol assumptions (one short section) so the edge cases are grounded in something exact, then deliver the three requested categories. Keep the worldbuilding light but present — Ledger of Empty Chairs flavor: the Registrar as adversary, chairs/occupancy as cover domain, editions of the codebook, marginalia channel. Use in-world terms where they sharpen concreteness. Length: substantial but disciplined. Aim for something thorough — this is a "hard problem" mining request explicitly asking for exhaustive concrete treatment. Maybe 900–1400 words. Dense lists, minimal prose padding. Avoid hedging — make decisions and state them. Let me draft the structure: Grounding: the protocol in six lines (so edge cases attach to something exact). Failure modes (grouped: key material, covertext, replay/state, authorship, metadata, human/operational). Boundaries (exact guarantee statements with limits). Must-never-happen invariants (numbered hard rules). Maybe a short "burn criteria" — when to declare the book dead. Could fold into invariants. Write it tight. Use the world's terms: the Registrar (adversary), editions, epochs, the Circle (holders), drops, marginalia channel, chair-plaque cover genre. One more consideration on the core tension to state crisply: the protocol's proof statement is "written by a holder of edition E during epoch e" — authorship provable inward, deniable outward, and these are the SAME mechanism (shared-key tag), not competing ones. Forgery capability is deliberately distributed: that's the price of deniability and it's why external non-repudiation is exactly zero. State that as a boundary, not a bug. Concrete numbers where possible: epoch = 7 days; length buckets = fixed sizes (e. , 64/256/1024 bytes); entropy budget: embed ≤ 50% of measured per-document headroom; retire encoding tables after ~500 uses or 30 days, whichever first; minimum anonymity set k=5; counter persistence write-ahead. These make it grounded. Edge cases I should make sure to include that are less obvious: - Crash/rollback of counters (nonce reuse via state rewind) — very concrete. - Canonicalization/injective encoding requirement — variant ambiguity. - Edition skew splitting the circle into subgroups — exploitable fork. - Semantic stego failure (covertext claims impossible knowledge) — crypto-perfect, opsec-dead. - Voluntary defection burning deniability — irreducible limit. - Lost book = unrevokable forgery oracle until epoch expiry. - Verification DoS via garbage flooding. - Subkey derivation sensitivity to physical book state (torn page → false forgery accusation). - Archive decay: old messages become undecodable by design — boundary on verifiability over time. - Enrollment without rotation → backward exposure. - Length/timing correlation. - Tag-over-wrong-layer bug: tag must bind decoded frame + epoch + context string; omitting context enables cross-protocol replay (message valid as auction note AND as summons) — cross-context replay. Good one: include "domain separation" invariant. - Two-person collusion shrinking anonymity set below floor. - The "empty chair" specific: messages referencing occupancy states — replaying an old "chair vacant" message is the highest-value attack in this world; hence freshness challenges mandatory for actuation-bearing messages.

66a3b2b5ed89a779.text: # Deniable-Yet-Verifiable Comms on the Git-Bus: Failure Modes, Boundaries, Hard Constraints Before enumerating failures, pin down what the protocol actually is so the edge cases are grounded: - **Payload**: Encrypted with a key derived from the codebook (KDF → AEAD, e. - **Authenticity**: HMAC-SHA256(codebook, canonical_serialization(commit_context ‖ payload_ct)). - **Transport**: Ciphertext+tag embedded in git blob contents or commit message bodies on agreed refs. - **Deniability source**: MAC-based auth means any codebook holder could have produced any valid message. No asymmetric signature exists. Third parties without the codebook see random bytes. - **Attribution scope**: Among codebook holders, a sender-subkey field inside the authenticated region identifies origin. Outside that circle, attribution is impossible. | # | Mode | Mechanism | Consequence | | F01 | Codebook leak | Symmetric key compromise | Total forgery capability, retroactive decryption of all past traffic, no revocation possible | | F02 | Nonce reuse | Counter/IV collision in AEAD | Keystream reuse → XOR of plaintexts leaks; Poly1305 tag forgery becomes tractable | | F03 | Canonicalization mismatch | Two implementations serialize the pre-MAC bytes differently | Valid messages rejected; worse, an attacker exploits the gap to splice headers onto different bodies | | F04 | Truncation attack | Auth covers payload but not parent-commit-hash or ref-name | Attacker lifts an authenticated blob and attaches it to a different commit context | | F05 | Cross-context replay | Message valid on `refs/bus/main` also validates on `refs/bus/emergency` | Old instructions replayed into new operational context | | F06 | KDF weakness | Codebook derived from low-entropy passphrase | Offline brute-force against known ciphertext structure | | F07 | Sub-key enumeration | Sender-ID field inside MAC'd region is guessable | Attacker confirms which sub-keys exist without knowing the codebook by observing length/format patterns | ### Metadata / Traffic Analysis | # | Mode | Mechanism | Consequence | | F08 | Timing correlation | Alice pushes at 0300Z daily; Bob never does | Push timing fingerprints sender despite perfect crypto | | F10 | Ref-creation events | Branch creation visible in reflogs/hooks even if content is opaque | Existence of channel exposed | | F11 | Push-pattern entropy collapse | Cover traffic generated by script; real traffic deviates | Real messages identifiable by deviation from statistical baseline | | # | Mode | Mechanism | Consequence | | F12 | Force-push erasure | History rewritten; authenticated messages vanish | Recipient loses ability to verify past claims; creates dispute window | | F13 | Shallow-fetch truncation | Party fetches depth=5; misses earlier authenticated messages | Gap in message sequence misinterpreted as adversarial deletion | | F14 | Merge-commit ambiguity | Two authenticated streams merge; merge commit itself unauthenticated | Attacker injects malicious merge resolution | | F15 | Ref namespace squatting | Adversary creates `refs/bus/main` before legitimate party | Squatter controls initial state of channel | | F16 | Alternate ODB injection | Malicious alternates file points decoder at attacker-controlled object store | Decoder processes attacker-chosen bytes as if they were bus traffic | | F17 | Hook-side leakage | Server-side post-receive hook logs ref names, sizes, IPs | Transport-layer metadata betrays channel usage | | # | Mode | Mechanism | Consequence | | F18 | Ordering ambiguity | DAG admits multiple topological sorts | Parties disagree on message sequence; state machines desync | | F19 | Missing-gap undetectability | No sequence numbers in authenticated region | Silent message dropping indistinguishable from "no message sent" | | F20 | Codebook rotation race | Old-codebook message arrives after switch | Rejected as invalid → false alarm; or accepted → extends old codebook lifetime indefinitely | | F21 | Multi-party codebook sharing | N>2 parties share one codebook | Any party can forge any other; internal attribution via sub-key is advisory, not binding | | F22 | Selective disclosure cascade | Codebook holder reveals one message to authority | Authority now possesses verification capability for ALL past/future messages on that codebook | | F23 | ACK forgery loop | Both parties can forge ACKs | Delivery confirmation is meaningless; reliability layer cannot distinguish "received" from "fabricated" | | F24 | Forward-secrecy absence | Static codebook | Today's compromise decrypts yesterday's archives permanently | ## BOUNDARIES (What the Protocol Can and Cannot Achieve) - Third party without codebook cannot determine message content. - Third party without codebook cannot attribute authorship cryptographically. - Codebook holder can verify integrity and identify sender sub-key. - Plausible deniability in the sense that verification requires possession of the secret, and possession of the secret undermines exclusive attribution. - Protection against traffic analysis (timing, volume, ref patterns). - Forward secrecy without adding ratcheting (which introduces its own deniability problems: possession of intermediate keys is evidence). - Non-repudiation toward third parties (by design — this is the point). - Resistance to coercion of a codebook holder. - Concealment of the channel's *existence* if observers control the git server infrastructure. - Attribution that survives codebook sharing among multiple parties (sub-key IDs are assertions, not proofs, when the verifier shares forging capability). ## WHAT MUST NEVER HAPPEN These are absolute constraints. Violation of any single item collapses the protocol's guarantees. N01  NEVER place a GPG/SSH/X509 signature on any commit carrying bus traffic. Asymmetric signatures are permanently publicly verifiable. commit destroys deniability for the entire channel retroactively. N02  NEVER derive the codebook from any value present in the repository, its remotes, contributor lists, or commit history. N03  NEVER store the codebook in the same repository, . environment variable in CI, or any location co-located with bus traffic. N04  NEVER authenticate a message without covering: payload ciphertext, sender sub-key, sequence number, target ref name, parent commit OID, and a monotonically-increasing epoch counter. Partial coverage = splicing. N05  NEVER use git author/committer fields as evidence of origin. These are client-controlled strings with zero cryptographic weight. N06  NEVER rely on git timestamps for freshness or ordering. Committer date is arbitrary. Use an authenticated epoch counter instead. N07  NEVER write decoded plaintext back into the object database, even temporarily, even in a detached HEAD, even in a stash. N08  NEVER use deterministic encryption for payloads. Identical inputs must produce different ciphertexts (nonce requirement). N09  NEVER allow the decoder to produce output on malformed input. Parse errors must be silent rejection, not error messages that leak information about the codebook's internal state. N010 NEVER mix deniable (bus) and non-deniable (signed) channels on the same repository without explicit isolation of refs, hooks, and CI. N011 NEVER implement a "verify-only" mode that accepts a message as valid without possessing the full codebook. There is no public verification Verification capability == forgery capability. N012 NEVER log decoded message content, codebook material, or sub-key assignments in application logs, crash dumps, or core files. N013 NEVER allow the protocol to operate over HTTP git transport. HTTPS or SSH only. The transport must not expose object contents in transit even if the payload is encrypted (metadata protection). N014 NEVER permit codebook reuse across separate treaty instances. Each independent bus gets an independently generated codebook. N015 NEVER design the ACK/receipt mechanism to create evidence stronger than the original message. If the original is deniable, the ACK must be equally deniable. Do not create an asymmetry where receipts are more provable than the messages they acknowledge. ## Summary Table: Guarantee vs. | Property | Holds Against | Broken By | | Content confidentiality | Passive observer without codebook | Codebook leak, KDF weakness | | Authorship deniability (external) | Any third party | GPG signature on bus commit (N01) | | Authorship verifiability (internal) | — | Codebook leak, sub-key forgery by co-holder | | Message integrity | Network manipulation | Canonicalization mismatch (F03), partial auth (F04) | | Freshness | Replay of old messages | Missing epoch counter (N06 violation) | | Channel existence concealment | Casual observation | Traffic analysis, server-side hooks (F17) | | Forward secrecy | Future codebook compromise | Static codebook design (F24) | The protocol is sound within its threat model. Every failure above traces to a specific, preventable engineering decision — not to a fundamental flaw in the MAC-based deniable-auth approach itself. The user is asking about a "deniable-yet-verifiable comms protocol" in the context of a "Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty. " This appears to be a fictional or hypothetical system design problem. Let me parse what they're asking: **Deniable-yet-verifiable**: A communication protocol where: - *Deniable*: Messages can be plausibly denied by their author (the author can claim they didn't write it, or that it means something else) - *Verifiable*: But with access to a specific codebook (shared secret), the true authorship and content can be proven **Git-bus treaty**: This seems to be a system where git commits serve as a communication bus — messages are encoded in git objects (commits, blobs, trees) that pass through a shared repository. They want: edge cases, failure modes, boundaries, and what must never happen. Let me think about this as a real cryptographic protocol design problem. The core tension is: - **Deniability** typically requires that signatures are not bound to a specific key in a way that third parties can verify. Standard digital signatures (Ed25519, RSA) provide non-repudiation — anyone with the public key can verify. This is the opposite of deniable. - **Verifiability to a specific party** requires some form of authentication that only the intended recipient can verify. This is essentially the MAC-vs-signature distinction, but more nuanced. Let me think about constructions: ### Possible constructions for deniable-yet-verifiable: **MAC-based authentication**: Use HMAC with a shared secret (the codebook). Only parties with the codebook can verify. Third parties cannot verify authorship. The recipient knows the message is authentic (only someone with the codebook could have produced it), but cannot prove to a third party that the sender wrote it — because the recipient themselves could have forged it. This gives sender deniability against third parties while providing verifiability to the holder of the codebook. **Ring signatures / group signatures**: The signer can prove they're in a set without revealing which member. Deniable because any member could have signed. Verifiable because you know it came from the group. **Designated verifier signatures (DVS)**: A signature that only a specific verifier can check. The verifier cannot convince anyone else because they could have created it themselves. **Chameleon hashes / chameleon signatures**: The signer signs, but the verifier can modify the hash collision parameters after the fact, making the signature appear valid on different messages. This prevents the verifier from proving anything to third parties. **Key-compromise impersonation considerations**: If the codebook is symmetric, both parties can forge each other's messages. In the context of a "git-bus" — using git commits as a transport — the specific mechanics matter: - Git commits have SHA-1/SHA-256 hashes - Commits contain author/committer fields, timestamps, parent references - Git supports GPG signing of commits/tags - The "bus" aspect suggests messages are passed via pushes/pulls to a shared repo Let me think about what "Ghost-AOS" might be — likely a fictional operating system or framework. The "treaty" suggests an agreement between parties about how to use the git bus. Now let me think concretely about the protocol design and its failure modes: Messages are embedded in git objects (commit messages, blob contents, tree structures). Authentication uses a shared codebook (symmetric key or a designated-verifier scheme). The codebook allows recovery of the true message and verification of authorship, but without it, the commit looks like ordinary noise or has plausible alternative interpretations. ### Edge cases and failure modes: Let me be very systematic here: **Codebook compromise → total forgery capability**: If the symmetric codebook leaks, ANYONE who has it can forge messages from either party. There's no asymmetric property to fall back on. This is worse than a private key leak in some ways because there's no revocation mechanism inherent to the design. **Replay attacks**: Git commits are immutable once pushed. An attacker who observes a commit can reference it later. Without freshness guarantees (timestamps aren't trustworthy in git), old messages can be replayed into new contexts. **Truncation/splicing**: If the authentication covers only part of the commit (e. , just the message body but not the metadata), an attacker could take an authenticated message body and attach it to a different commit context. **Key derivation weaknesses**: If the codebook is derived from something guessable (a passphrase, a pattern), brute-force becomes feasible. **Nonce reuse**: If the scheme uses nonces (e. , for stream cipher encryption of the payload), nonce reuse breaks confidentiality AND potentially authenticity. **Malleability**: If the encoding allows bit-flipping that produces valid alternative decodings under the same codebook, an attacker in the middle could modify messages. **Cross-protocol attacks**: If the same codebook is used across multiple channels or contexts, messages from one context might be valid in another. **Deniability boundary violations:** **Metadata leakage**: Even if the message content is deniable, git metadata (author email, timestamp patterns, push timing, branch naming conventions) can create de facto attribution. If Alice always pushes at 3am and Bob never does, timing correlates with identity regardless of cryptographic deniability. **Behavioral fingerprinting**: Commit size distributions, encoding choices, error patterns in the steganographic layer — these can fingerprint the author even if the crypto is perfect. **Selective disclosure paradox**: If the codebook holder reveals a message and its verification, they implicitly reveal the codebook's verification capability. Subsequent messages become suspect (the counterparty knows the codebook has been used for disclosure). **Traffic analysis**: The mere existence of commits on particular branches at particular times, even if content is meaningless, creates a communication pattern that's hard to deny. **Plausible deniability vs. provable denial**: There's a difference between "I didn't send this" being unverifiable-by-third-parties and "I can affirmatively prove I didn't send this. " The former is achievable; the latter generally requires setup assumptions that undermine the whole point. **Git-specific failures:** **Force-push rewrites**: If history is rewritten, previously authenticated messages may disappear or be replaced. **Shallow clones / partial fetches**: If a party fetches only part of the history, they might miss authenticated messages or see them out of order. **Merge conflicts**: When two authenticated streams merge, the merge commit itself needs handling. Is the merge commit part of the authenticated channel? Who "authored" the merge? **Commit hash collisions**: Practically impossible with SHA-256, but the protocol should specify behavior if the object database contains conflicting objects with the same prefix. **Ref namespace squatting**: An attacker creates refs that look like legitimate channel names but point to garbage or attacker-controlled content. **Object injection**: Malicious objects pushed to the bus that parse incorrectly under the codebook but cause crashes or unexpected behavior in the decoder. **Protocol logic failures:** **Ordering ambiguity**: Git DAGs allow multiple valid topological orderings. If message sequence matters, the protocol must specify a canonical ordering, and all parties must agree on it deterministically. **Gap detection**: How do you know you haven't missed a message? If so, how are they authenticated and made deniable simultaneously? **Acknowledgment protocol**: If Bob ACKs receipt, the ACK itself must be deniable-yet-verifiable. But now you have a two-party authenticated channel where each side can forge the other's messages — the ACK proves nothing to third parties but also nothing to Bob himself beyond "someone with the codebook sent this. **Codebook rotation**: When rotating the codebook, there's a window where messages encrypted/authenticated under the old codebook arrive after the switch. Handling requires keeping old codebooks, which increases attack surface. **Multi-party extension**: If more than two parties share the bus, does everyone share one codebook (anyone can forge anyone)? Or pairwise codebooks (combinatorial explosion, and the bus observer can count distinct codebooks)? **Forward secrecy absence**: With a static codebook, compromise of today's codebook decrypts ALL past messages. No forward secrecy unless ratcheting is added, but ratcheting complicates deniability (possession of intermediate keys is evidence). **Backward secrecy**: New codebook holders shouldn't read old messages. But if the codebook is derived from a long-term secret, this fails. **What must NEVER happen:** **NEVER use asymmetric signatures (GPG-signed commits) for the deniable channel**: The moment a commit carries a standard GPG signature, authorship is publicly verifiable forever. This destroys deniability irreversibly. **NEVER log or cache the codebook alongside the messages it authenticates**: If the codebook ends up in the same git repo, config file, or CI logs as the messages, deniability collapses. **NEVER allow the codebook to be derivable from public information**: If the codebook is derived from the repo URL, contributor names, or anything in the public repo, it's compromised. **NEVER rely on git's built-in author fields for authentication**: These are trivially spoofable (`git commit --author`). They carry zero evidentiary weight. **NEVER assume timestamps are trustworthy**: Committer dates are client-controlled. Any freshness or ordering guarantee based on git timestamps alone is broken. **NEVER let the verification path produce output that distinguishes "valid message from Alice" from "valid message from Bob" when both share the codebook**: The entire point is that possession of the codebook makes you indistinguishable from any other codebook holder as a potential author. **NEVER store decoded plaintext in the git object database**: The decoded message, if committed back or stored as a blob, becomes evidence. **NEVER use deterministic encryption for the payload**: Same input + same codebook = same ciphertext = correlation across messages. **NEVER make the presence of the protocol detectable through side channels in the git operations themselves**: If decoding requires special ref names, unusual object types, or distinctive push patterns, the existence of the channel is exposed even if contents remain hidden. **NEVER allow partial verification**: Either the codebook verifies the complete message (content + metadata + context) or it verifies nothing. Partial verification creates malleability. **NEVER trust the network layer for authenticity**: The git remote (GitHub, GitLab, etc. ) can reorder, drop, or inject refs. All authenticity must come from the codebook, not from the transport. **NEVER have a "master" codebook that supersedes per-channel codebooks**: A hierarchy implies a root of trust that, when compromised, destroys everything. **NEVER allow the protocol to function if the codebook holder is coerced**: This is fundamentally impossible to prevent (if you have the codebook, you can be forced to decode), but the protocol must not make it WORSE than necessary — e. , don't include a "prove you received message X" primitive that creates legally actionable evidence. **NEVER mix deniable and non-deniable channels on the same refs**: If some branches carry GPG-signed commits and others carry codebook-authenticated ones, traffic analysis on the signed branches provides cover for attributing the unsigned ones. **NEVER assume the adversary doesn't have a copy of the codebook-verification algorithm**: Security through obscurity of the decoder is not security. The codebook (key) is the only secret. Let me also think about the specific tension between deniability and verifiability more carefully: The fundamental construction is likely: - **Authentication**: HMAC-SHA256(codebook, canonical_message) — only codebook holders can verify - **Encryption**: AEAD (e. , XChaCha20-Poly1305) with the codebook-derived key - **Encoding**: The authenticated ciphertext is embedded in innocuous-looking git objects The deniability comes from: since it's a MAC, the verifier (codebook holder) could have produced the message themselves. So they can't prove to a court that Alice sent it — only that "someone with the codebook sent it. But wait — if BOTH Alice and Bob hold the codebook, then Bob receiving a valid message knows it came from Alice OR Bob. If Bob didn't send it, he infers Alice did. But he can't PROVE it. That's the deniability. If we want stronger properties (Bob can verify Alice specifically but still can't convince others), we need designated verifier signatures or ring signatures. Actually, rethinking: "recoverable only with our codebook" suggests the CONTENT is encrypted and only recoverable with the codebook. "Authorship provable" suggests that with the codebook, you can prove who authored it. But "deniable" means without the codebook, authorship is not provable. So the design is: - Content: encrypted with codebook-derived key - Authorship: authenticated with codebook-derived MAC - To outsiders: looks like noise; no way to attribute - To codebook holders: full recovery + attribution But the attribution question: if it's a shared symmetric codebook, "attribution" means "this came from one of us" not "this came from Alice specifically. So it's still deniable. a0a2a5ed6e0858ad.text: # Deniable-Yet-Verifiable Comms in Sovereign Swarm/Flock Consensus ## Grounding: The Core Construction Before enumerating failures, pin down what we're analyzing: - **Authenticity**: MAC-only (HMAC-SHA256, Poly1305) derived from pairwise DH ratchets. No asymmetric signatures anywhere. Either party to a MAC could have produced it → deniable to third parties, provable to holders of the shared secret. - **Confidentiality**: Symmetric encryption keyed from the same ratchet, separated by KDF into distinct subkeys for enc/MAC/ratchet-advance. - **Consensus**: Epidemic gossip with vector-clock ordering, deterministic conflict resolution (highest-CID-hash-wins), no leader, no voting round, probabilistic finality. - **Codebook**: Out-of-band distributed mapping of logical identities → current ratchet roots. Rotation via embedded ratchet advancement, not external signaling. ### FM-1: Consensus Log Becomes Attribution Evidence The flock agrees on an ordered sequence of state transitions. That sequence—stored locally on every node—is a record of *collective action*. Even though each individual message is MAC-deniable, the *fact* that N nodes converged on the same ordering proves coordination occurred. An adversary who captures multiple nodes' stores sees identical ordered histories → infers participation patterns. **Mechanism**: Node capture → extract local consensus log → compare across captured nodes → intersect → identify active set. **Severity**: Fatal to deniability if consensus state is stored in plaintext alongside encrypted messages. ### FM-2: Byzantine Blame Attribution Paradox When a node equivocates (sends conflicting state updates to different peers), the flock needs to detect and isolate it. Detection requires comparing received values across witnesses. Isolation requires identifying the source. Identification requires either: - (a) Signature → destroys deniability permanently, OR - (b) Cross-referencing MAC'd messages → possible only because MAC key is shared pairwise, but now every pair must compare notes, creating a meta-gossip channel whose contents are themselves evidence. If you choose (a), deniability dies. If you choose (b), the comparison process produces logs that say "node X sent value V₁ to me and value V₂ to you"—which, combined, is strong evidence of X's specific behavior. The act of *detecting* Byzantine behavior creates attribution artifacts. ### FM-3: Sybil Capture Under Deniability Because MACs don't prove unique identity, nothing prevents one adversary from spawning 1000 virtual nodes, each with a valid-looking codebook entry (obtained via social engineering, theft, or insider recruitment). In epidemic consensus, majority/quorum logic is broken: the adversary controls apparent majority. **Specific trigger**: New node joins, presents valid MAC'd handshake using a codebook entry obtained from a compromised insider. Existing nodes accept it as peer. Adversary replicates 500×. Now controls >50% of gossip bandwidth. **Why standard defenses fail**: Proof-of-work is attributable (mining pool analysis). Proof-of-stake requires persistent identity (public key = permanent identifier). Web-of-trust vouching creates a graph that, once captured, reveals the entire social topology. ### FM-4: Ratchet Desynchronization Under Partition Two sub-flocks partition. Both continue advancing their ratchet state. - Sub-flock A is at ratchet index 47; sub-flock B is at index 52. - Messages from A encrypted under state(47) arrive at B, which expects ≥52. - Options: reject (lose availability), accept-and-resync (but resync requires exchanging ratchet state, which reveals how far each side advanced → timing/participation metadata), or maintain a sliding window (increases state size, expands attack surface for replay within the window). **Critical detail**: The resync handshake itself—if MAC'd—is deniable, but the *pattern* of resync requests correlates with partition topology, leaking network structure. ### FM-5: Codebook Partial Compromise → Forgery Window Adversary obtains codebook subset covering nodes {A, B, C} but not {D, E}. Can forge messages appearing to originate from A/B/C, accepted by D/E (who verify against the full codebook). Cannot forge D/E→D/E traffic. **Worse**: If codebook is hierarchical (group key → subgroup keys → pairwise keys), compromising the group key compromises everything below it instantly. If flat pairwise, compromise scales linearly but provides no shortcut. **Rotation gap**: During rotation (old codebook → new), both are briefly valid. Adversary holding old codebook can forge during the overlap. If overlap is T seconds, adversary has T-second forgery window per rotation event. ### FM-6: Metadata Correlation Defeats Cryptographic Deniability Every message carries: length, timing interval since previous message from same logical sender, route path (in gossip: which neighbor forwarded it). Over sufficient volume, statistical clustering identifies individual nodes regardless of MAC deniability. **Concrete example**: Node A sends exactly 3 messages every 300±10 seconds. Node B sends bursts of 7-12 messages every 1800±50 seconds. After observing 48 hours of traffic, adversary clusters with near-certainty. Cryptographic deniability is intact; behavioral deniability is destroyed. **Sub-case**: Gossip forwarding pattern. If node A consistently hears node B's updates before hearing node C's, the adversary infers A-B proximity/relationship from propagation delay alone. ### FM-7: Deterministic Conflict Resolution Enables Censorship Rule: "on conflict, highest SHA256(state_hash) wins. " Adversary grinds candidate states offline until finding one with hash higher than the honest state's hash. Injects grinding result into gossip. Honest nodes converge on adversarial state. **Cost**: ~2^k hashes for k-bit advantage. If hash space is 256-bit, grinding is infeasible for full control—but feasible for *targeted* suppression (grind against one specific honest update to ensure it loses). **Mitigation attempt**: Add node-specific salt to hash input. But salt must be known to all verifiers → transmitted in clear → adversary reads it → still grinds. ### FM-8: Insider Selective Disclosure Asymmetry Participant P decides to cooperate with adversary. - Their copy of the codebook (all pairwise secrets involving P) - Their local consensus log - Their observation of received messages P can now demonstrate to adversary: "message M was consistent with the key I shared with Q. " Combined with P's testimony ("Q sent this"), this constitutes practical attribution of Q. **Key asymmetry**: P can prove Q's authorship *without* simultaneously proving P's own authorship, because P simply claims "I received it, didn't send it.
