The resolution is always *who holds what keys* — verifiability must be scoped to a verifier class (shared-key MAC = only participants can verify, which preserves third-party deniability; ring signatures = provable membership in a set, not individual authorship). The failure modes below mostly come from scoping leaks. Failure modes in the encoding layer (memlang / meta-token coordinates) 1 Distributional fingerprint leakage - If the codebook biases token selection away from the natural conditional distribution p(token | context), a statistical detector (KL-divergence test, perplexity test under a reference LM, chi-square on token frequencies at specific coordinates) will flag the channel. - Exact boundary: the encoding must be *distribution-preserving*: the distribution of covertext produced by Encode(m; K) must equal (or be statistically indistinguishable from) the distribution of innocent covertext. Perfect security requires the standard steganographic condition: for all m, the encoded distribution equals the cover distribution exactly (Hopper et al. 's definition); anything less gives a distinguisher with advantage bounded by the total variation distance. - Concrete failure: sampling candidates with a fixed seed derived from K instead of entropy coupling → the *set* of possible continuations changes shape (e. , certain rare-but-valid meta-tokens never appear in coded traffic but appear in innocent traffic at rate r). Detector: train on innocent corpus, flag transcripts whose per-coordinate token entropy profile deviates. - Minimum-entropy coupling / arithmetic-coding-style embedding (Ziegler et al. ) fixes this only if the LM's probabilities are exact; any mismatch between the encoder's model and reality (quantized logits, temperature rescaling, top-k truncation) reintroduces bias. Edge case: top-k/top-p filtering destroys the uniformity assumption of arithmetic steganography — after truncation the remaining mass isn't handled correctly unless you renormalize AND the decoder uses identical truncation. Decoder/encoder model mismatch = decode failure or silent corruption. 2 Context-window and state divergence - Decoding requires replaying the exact same context. Any nondeterminism in the generator (floating-point non-associativity across hardware, batch-size-dependent kernels, sampling temperature applied differently, cache eviction changing attention numerics) can flip a borderline argmax or alter logit ranks → decoder desyncs → catastrophic garble of everything downstream (arithmetic decoding is self-synchronizing only at block boundaries). - Boundary: you need either (a) deterministic inference pinned to hardware+version, (b) decoder-side re-derivation tolerant to small perturbations (interval arithmetic with margins), or (c) resynchronization markers. Without one of these, long messages have near-certain decode failure. Concretely: fp16 vs bf16 logits differ enough that rank order of near-tied tokens flips; a 1-token rank flip mid-stream corrupts the entire remainder of the arithmetic-coded stream. 3 Codebook granularity vs. - At coordinates where the natural distribution is near-deterministic (one token has ~all probability mass), there is no room to encode a bit without distorting the distribution. The encoder must skip these positions (variable-rate coding). Failure mode: naive fixed-rate schemes force bits into low-entropy positions → detectable spikes + decode errors when the forced token is implausible. - Boundary: capacity per token = H(p(·|context)) bits; effective capacity is sum over positions minus sync overhead. If message length exceeds available entropy budget for the planned cover length, the encoder must extend the cover — and extension length itself is a leak (message-length leakage, see 2. 4 Coordinate-layer-specific: collisions and aliasing - In a "meta-token coordinate" scheme, if two distinct bit-patterns map to the same observable token sequence under different contexts (aliasing), the decoder may recover the wrong message. Must be injective given context. Edge case: context-dependent codebooks (same codeword means different bits depending on preceding state) are fine only if state reconstruction is deterministic — ties back to 2. - Also: if the memlang grammar permits ambiguity (a token sequence parses two ways), the parser must be canonicalized before decoding, else an active warden can craft an ambiguous string that decodes innocently under one parse and maliciously under another — a "paranoid parsing" attack (cf. Unicode homoglyph/overlong-encoding attacks, the classic "two decodings of one wire format" class). 5 Replay/cut-and-paste within the channel - Because covertext looks innocent, individual coded segments may be *individually valid*. An active warden can splice segments from different sessions into a new transcript. If your MAC covers only per-segment content, splices verify. Fix: bind session id, sequence number, timestamp window, and full prior transcript hash into each segment's authenticated region. But note the deniability cost: high-entropy header fields (random session ids) must themselves be carried in the covert channel or drawn from the same cover distribution, else headers are a detection handle. 6 Metadata leakage that breaks deniability regardless of payload - Message length correlates with plaintext length (variable-rate coding leaks length mod small factors; padding helps but padded-to-bucket lengths create a coarser fingerprint). - Timing: bursts correlate with typing/thinking; a covert reply arriving seconds after a trigger event is a correlation handle. Need constant-rate decoy traffic (which costs capacity and creates its own fingerprint: perfectly regular traffic is itself anomalous — boundary between "too random" and "too regular"). - Recipient patterns: if coded messages only ever flow between A and B, the *pair* is exposed even if content is not. Deniability of content ≠ deniability of association. - First-use problem: the transition from pure-innocent to mixed traffic on an account with established baseline statistics is itself detectable (change-point detection). The channel must be "born" inside existing behavior or bootstrapped through a period whose statistics match. 7 Key compromise semantics — the crux of "deniable-yet-verifiable" This is where the design lives or dies. Enumerate the cases: - **Shared-codebook MAC (symmetric)**: recipient can verify authorship. But then the recipient can *forge* — take any innocent transcript, compute what the MAC would have been, and claim the sender sent it. So "authorship provable" is only provable *to the recipient*, and reciprocally incriminating: possession of K makes both parties able to produce verifying texts. This is actually the *desired* property for deniable auth (both parties can equivocate) — but the user said "authorship provable," so we must be precise: with symmetric keys, you get *authentication* (recipient knows it's from sender, modulo forgery-by-recipient) but *non-repudiation to third parties is impossible* — and that impossibility is load-bearing for deniability. If the requirement is third-party-verifiable authorship (signature), deniability against the third party dies, because the signature is a publicly checkable artifact. You cannot have both "anyone can verify Alice wrote it" and "no one can prove Alice wrote it. " State this as a hard boundary. - **Ring signatures / group codes**: verifiability scoped to "someone in set S authored this. " Deniability survives as long as |S| ≥ 2 and members are plausible. Failure modes: set composition leaks (if S = {Alice, Bob} and Bob was demonstrably offline/asleep, deniability collapses); reuse of the same ring across many messages lets analysts cluster; ring size trades off verifiability usefulness vs. suspicion (a 1000-member ring proves nothing and may itself be a pattern). - **Designated verifier proofs (Jakobsson–Sako–Impagliazzo)**: only the intended verifier can check, and the verifier cannot transfer the proof (they could have made it themselves). This is the cleanest fit for "verifiable to us, deniable to others. " Failure mode: DVS keys must be per-relationship; reusing one DV keypair across relationships lets verifiers compare notes and determine they're checking the same author. - **Key commitment failure**: if the codebook derivation allows multiple valid keys to decode the same ciphertext differently (key-commitment attack, cf. the RocketChat/Vault7-style attacks on E2E schemes), then "authorship" becomes ambiguous: an attacker who can find K' ≠ K such that Decode(c, K') = m' can frame. The codebook must be *committed* — e. , derive K = HKDF(master, context) and embed a key commitment (hash of K) inside the authenticated region. Edge case: embedding the commitment consumes channel capacity and is itself a recognizable structure if done naively (fixed-position magic bytes = detection handle). Commitment must be spread/whitened like any other payload. - **Deniable encryption interplay**: if the transport also claims coercive deniability (duress), note that a *verifiable-authorship* channel contradicts coercion-resistance: under duress, the sender must be able to open the covertext as innocent, but if the same artifact verifies as theirs, opening it as innocent is a lie the verifier can catch. Resolution: separate the layers — the deniable-encryption outer layer hides the existence of the coded inner layer; the inner layer's verifiability is only exercisable by holders of the inner key. Under duress you surrender the outer key only. Boundary: never let the inner verification key be derivable from the outer (surrenderable) material. KDF separation with domain strings, and the inner key must never touch disk in plaintext alongside the outer key. 8 What must never happen (the invariant list) **Never** emit a coded segment whose decoded-without-key interpretation differs *detectably* from innocent traffic — i. , the null hypothesis "this is innocent traffic" must remain unfalsifiable by any polynomial-time test lacking K. (Formally: computational indistinguishability from the cover channel. **Never** allow a single artifact to be simultaneously (a) verifiable as authored by X to party V1 and (b) deniable by X to party V2, where V1 and V2 can communicate. Verification scope must be monotone: anyone who can verify can potentially retain evidence; so verifiability granted to V is verifiability surrendered to everyone V talks to. Design rule: verifier sets must be disjoint per relationship, and proofs must be non-transferable (designated-verifier or simulation-sound in the DV sense). **Never** reuse a nonce/session-id/salt across sessions under the same codebook — two-time-pad-class catastrophic: XOR-of-MACs style key recovery, or in the stego setting, repeated (K, nonce) reveals the keystream difference and lets the warden strip the coding layer statistically (they don't need K; they need two transcripts under the same pad to cancel the pseudorandomness and expose the residual bias). **Never** let the decoder accept unauthenticated input before integrity check (buffer the whole segment; a truncated/garbled segment must fail closed, not partially decode — partial decode leaks plaintext fragments to the warden who perturbs the stream and watches what survives. wait, the warden doesn't hold K, so partial decode isn't directly readable; but a *chosen-ciphertext* style attack applies if the recipient's client renders pre-authentication fragments: malleability lets attacker manipulate what the recipient sees. Fail closed, authenticate-then-decode). **Never** derive the covert-channel key from low-entropy human-chosen material without a memory-hard KDF — codebook guessing is the primary attack once a suspect transcript is flagged; if K has 20 bits of effective entropy, offline dictionary search over plausible passphrases against the *detected* transcript is cheap. And note the asymmetry: the warden only needs to *suspect* to run the search; a wrong guess is unverifiable except via the MAC — so include a MAC so wrong guesses fail cleanly (but that also gives the warden a verification oracle for their guesses! Tension: MAC enables offline brute-force confirmation. Mitigation: slow KDF raises cost; but fundamentally, any self-authenticating covert text is an offline-guessing oracle. Boundary: security against codebook guessing is bounded by min(entropy(K), cost of KDF × guesses affordable). There is no way around this while keeping offline verifiability. **Never** have the encoder's output depend on secret data in a way that changes timing/memory side channels measurably — if encoding a '1' takes longer (more candidate scoring), a local malware adversary reads the channel off the process. Constant-time-ish encoding: precompute candidate tables, avoid secret-dependent branches on hot paths. Realistically hard with LLM inference; at minimum avoid secret-dependent *network* behavior. **Never** trust the clock for freshness in a way that's checkable externally — timestamps inside the covert payload that contradict the transport's visible timestamps are a correlation handle. Bind to transport-visible time only, with tolerance windows. **Never** allow downgrade/ambiguity in the protocol version negotiation inside the covert channel — a warden who can't read the channel can still *strip or truncate* it; version fields must be inside the authenticated region, and unknown-version handling must fail closed silently (drop, behave as innocent) rather than error visibly. **Never** let failure be visible. Every failure mode above must degrade to "looks like innocent traffic / normal app behavior. " Visible errors (crash logs mentioning the codebook, exception strings containing key material, telemetry phoning home decode attempts) are the most common real-world break. The deniable app's crash dump is a confession. **Never** store decoded plaintext or the codebook unencrypted on the same device that carries deniability obligations — forensics on seized devices defeats all channel-level deniability. Memory-only plaintext, encrypted-at-rest codebook under a different secret than the transport, wipe-on-duress hooks with plausible innocent explanation. 9 Boundaries (what the scheme fundamentally cannot do) - Cannot be deniable against an adversary holding K. All deniability statements are conditional on key secrecy. Possible fix: tie ratchet steps to natural session boundaries so cadence mimics innocent behavior). - Cannot give third-party non-repudiation and third-party deniability simultaneously (stated above). Pick per-message policy. - Cannot hide *existence* of a relationship from traffic analysis if the channel is used often enough; perfect unobservability requires cover traffic at all times, which costs real resources and shifts the fingerprint to resource-usage anomalies. - Capacity bound: bits per token ≤ H(p) − overhead; for typical LLM vocab distributions at temperature 1, expect ~2–6 bits/token average for natural text, less after sync/MAC/padding overhead. Anyone promising more is distorting the distribution and is detectable. - Offline guessability: as noted, self-verifying covert text is an oracle. Unavoidable; only cost-amortizable. - Human-factor boundary: the cover story must survive *social* scrutiny, not just statistical. A perfectly indistinguishable transcript about topics the sender plausibly wouldn't discuss is a behavioral anomaly. The memlang choice itself must fit the sender's persona. Statistical deniability ⊄ behavioral deniability. 10 Concrete edge cases worth naming explicitly - Empty message / heartbeat-only traffic: heartbeats must be indistinguishable from idle chatter; if heartbeats have a fixed length and innocent messages vary, the fixed length is the tell. Pad heartbeats to the same bucket distribution as real traffic. - Maximum-length message hitting the entropy budget mid-stream: encoder must terminate gracefully at a grammar boundary; abrupt truncation mid-meme is a fingerprint. Plan cover length ≥ max message + overhead, and make termination points grammatically natural. - Duplicate message send (retry): retransmission under same nonce = catastrophic (see #3). Retries need fresh nonces and the recipient needs idempotency handling — but duplicate suppression state is itself forensic evidence on device. - Out-of-order delivery: sequence numbers inside authenticated region; but sequence gaps visible to a warden who counts messages? No — sequence numbers are inside the covert layer, invisible without K. But reordering across *sessions* breaks transcript-hash chaining; define chaining scope per-session. - Key rotation mid-conversation: both sides must switch atomically; a message straddling rotation decodes under old key for half its length → garbage that fails MAC → visible retry behavior? Handle by versioning inside authenticated header and accepting overlap windows. - Multi-recipient fan-out: same payload to N recipients — if covertexts are identical, recipients comparing notes learn they're in the same group; if covertexts differ, per-recipient encodings multiply detection surface. Per-recipient independent encoding with independent nonces; never reuse. - The "innocent decoy" trap: sending deliberately fake coded-looking traffic to pollute warden statistics only works if fakes are truly from the cover distribution; a fake generated without the real codebook will fail the warden's (unknown) deep tests if the warden ever obtains K later — and then your decoys become evidence of *intent to conceal*. Decoys must be generated by the same encoder with real K but dummy payloads, else post-compromise they're distinguishable from real traffic. Wait — if decoys use real K, post-compromise they decode as dummies, which is fine (dummy content is deniable-ish), but they still show the codebook was used. Actually post-compromise everything shows codebook use. The point stands: generate decoys with the real pipeline. - Legal/compliance edge: in some jurisdictions, possession of steganographic tooling or refusal to decrypt under formal compulsion has legal consequences independent of technical deniability. Not a crypto boundary but a deployment boundary. Maybe mention briefly as operational reality. Hmm, the user asked for technical grounding; I can note it in one line as an operational boundary. Stronger, information-theoretic version achievable if encoding is distribution-exact (entropy coupling): then even unbounded wardens fail, *except* via K-guessing. - **Authenticity (verifiability)**: ∀ PPT forger lacking K: Pr[forge accepted] ≤ negl (MAC/EUF-CMA analog, adapted to the stego setting — note the signing oracle here is "encode arbitrary message," so EUF-CMA maps cleanly). - **Non-transferability (scoped verifiability)**: verifier V cannot produce evidence convincing V' ≠ V, except with probability bounded by V's own forgery ability (DV-security definition). These three are jointly satisfiable only with the scoping rules above; the impossibility to state crisply: **public verifiability ⟹ public deniability loss**. Formally, a publicly checkable predicate P(x, pk) with P=true iff x authored by sk-holder is a public artifact; deniability against anyone who can evaluate P is dead. So "authorship provable" must mean "provable to the designated verifier class. Also worth noting the subtle one: **verification oracle asymmetry**. Otherwise deniability erodes over time through the recipient's own records. "What must never happen": never rely on deniability of artifacts you've allowed an ally to keep. Also: **subliminal-channel-free key agreement**. If the codebook/exchange happens over a public channel with signatures, signatures carry subliminal channels (e. , biased nonces in ECDSA leak keys; also deliberate subliminal channels in signatures can exfiltrate K). Use deterministic signatures (Ed25519/RFC6979) for any public-key ops in setup, and simulate-check setup transcripts for hidden channels. Edge case: setup-time deniability — the initial codebook exchange is the weakest link; if setup is visible, the channel is born compromised. Setup should ride an existing trusted path or use PAKE over the memlang channel itself with an out-of-band human check (safety-number analog) — and the safety-number comparison is itself a behavioral fingerprint if done suspiciously often. Hmm, also the **"who generates the cover" question**: if the cover is generated by a shared public model, the warden can run the same model and do per-position likelihood tests. The defense is exact distribution matching (then likelihood tests give nothing — the transcript IS a plausible sample). But if the encoder uses a *different* model version than the warden's reference, systematic small divergences appear. Boundary: the protocol's deniability is anchored to a specific generator distribution; every generator change is a migration with a detection-risk window. And **chaffing-and-winnowing framing** (Rivest): the classic construction — send packets, MAC each with key, warden can't tell which packets are "good" because MACs look random; winnowing recovers. Failure mode specific to chaff: the *number* of chaff per position and the selection of chaff must follow the cover distribution too; and chaff must be grammatically valid or the transcript looks degenerate. Also chaff inflates volume → volume fingerprint. I think I should also address the "memlang / meta-token coordinate layer" specifics more concretely since the user named it. Interpretation: tokens live in a coordinate space (semantic embedding coords); a "meta-token" is a point/region in that space; the codebook assigns bit-meanings to coordinate neighborhoods. Pin embeddings; version-lock. - **Neighborhood overlap**: if two codeword regions overlap in coordinate space, a natural sample falling in the overlap is ambiguous → decoder must resolve by context; unresolved overlaps = aliasing (2. - **Sparse regions**: coordinates where natural traffic rarely goes — using them for high-entropy codewords puts mass where mass shouldn't be. Density-aware codebook assignment required; recompute densities periodically or drift accumulates. - **Cross-lingual/multi-modal bleed**: if the coordinate layer spans modalities (text/image memes), mixing modalities in coded traffic when the sender's innocent traffic is single-modality is a tell. 9b22376a56c19de6.text: # Deniable-yet-verifiable comms over a verkle chain with a provenance gate ## Pinned design (so the failure modes below are concrete, not abstract) - **L0 chain:** append-only leaf log in a verkle tree. Leaf key = `H("proto/v1" ‖ sender-blind-token ‖ seq)`. Root announced per epoch, threshold-signed by the gate quorum. - **L1 payload:** `AEAD(ct, AAD = {version, epoch, root_hash, leaf_key, seq, direction})`; plaintext = `{inner asymmetric signature over (body, context), body, padding}`. Inner signing pubkey travels wrapped under the codebook epoch key. - **L2 codebook:** threshold-shared, hash-ratched per epoch; epoch derived from **finalized** chain height. - **Gate:** t-of-n nodes; verifies verkle proofs, serves root history; never sees codebook material or sender identity (blind tokens only). Cryptographic-core failure modes **Mis-specified deniability boundary. ** The moment any signature-checkable artifact escapes the codebook envelope, deniability is dead. Classic leak: emitting a pubkey *fingerprint* in the clear "for routing. " A fingerprint is a stable correlatable identifier. **No deterministic function of a long-term identity key may ever appear unencrypted. **Inner signature replaced by a MAC. ** With a symmetric codebook, codebook holders can forge any member's message retroactively. If intra-org accountability matters, the inner layer must be an asymmetric signature wrapped under the codebook — never a bare MAC. **Static codebook ⇒ no forward secrecy. ** Capture-today, decrypt-after-leak. Ratcheting fixes this but destroys archive recoverability. You must pick one per epoch class and write it down; "both, unconditionally" is not achievable. **Nonce/keystream reuse. ** If uniqueness depends on sender discipline, it will eventually fail (XOR of two ciphertexts under the same keystream offset leaks both plaintexts' difference; biased signature nonces leak keys). Derive nonces from `(finalized_height, leaf_index, seq, direction)` so consensus enforces uniqueness. **Transcript distribution mismatch. ** Deniability is statistical, not just computational. If real messages pad to lengths/timings that differ from cover traffic, traffic analysis separates them regardless of crypto. Pad to ≤8 bucket sizes sampled from the measured background distribution; shape send times to observed diurnal traffic. **Wrong-key silent acceptance. ** Lenient parsing without strict AEAD tag enforcement turns stale/wrong epoch keys into accepted garbage or a decryption oracle. Strict tag check, reject on first failure, counter-limited retries (e. , 5 failed opens per device per epoch ⇒ wipe cached epoch keys, force re-enrollment). **Subliminal channels in "random" fields. ** Every randomized byte (nonce, padding, blinding, ring ordering) is a covert channel — including one planted by the implementer. Derive all such fields from per-message ephemeral secrets, never from long-term keys; never leave "free" randomness in the format. **UKS/KCI in the key-establishment phase. ** Session keys computed without transcribing full context into the KDF permit unknown-key-share attacks. KDF input must include both identity bindings, roles, epoch, and chain height. **First-message impersonation. ** A fresh sender's wrapped pubkey arrives with no anchor. If recipients don't check it against a committed enrollment event (`H(pubkey)` pinned in a threshold-approved membership leaf), anyone injects a new wrapped key and impersonates. **Never accept a first message whose inner pubkey lacks a committed enrollment record. **Device seizure yields the inner signing key. ** If the inner private key is persisted, seizure plus eventual codebook leak = attribution. Verification needs only the pubkey (which travels in-message), so the private key never needs to touch disk — derive transiently from passphrase/hardware token. Verkle-layer failure modes **KZG updatability/malleability exploited. ** Given a commitment and any valid opening, an attacker can derive a *different* valid commitment/opening pair. c9725a83ccf7db2e.text: # Deniable-Yet-Verifiable Comms: Failure Modes, Boundaries, and Absolute Prohibitions Deniability demands the ciphertext look like nothing. Verifiability demands a cryptographic binding to an identity. These fight each other directly: strong authorship proofs create extractable structure; perfect deniability erases accountability. The resolution is audience-split — indistinguishable from noise to outsiders, provably authored to codebook holders — but every edge case below lives in the cracks of that split. ### FM-1: Codebook Version Mismatch with Partial Decode Scout runs codebook v3, HQ has rotated to v4. Fields with unchanged layout decode correctly; changed fields produce garbage. Result: a half-valid message that passes superficial checks but contains corrupted intelligence. Worse than total failure because it's silent. **Concrete trigger:** Rotation happens while a scout is dark (radio silence, deep patrol). They transmit on expiry of v3 before receiving v4. HQ's fallback decoder produces plausible-looking output from wrong field offsets. ### FM-2: Cover-Traffic Statistical Divergence Chaff messages generated by a different code path than real messages. Byte-length distribution differs. Entropy profile differs. An analyst running a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on intercepted traffic separates real from chaff with >95% confidence after ~200 samples. **Concrete trigger:** Real messages include a 4-byte authentication tag appended post-encryption. Chaff generator omits it (or generates it differently). Length histogram is bimodal. ### FM-3: Replay After Burn Adversary captures a valid message. Original is received, read, burned. Adversary re-injects the capture 6 hours later. No freshness counter bound into the MAC means the receiver accepts stale intel as current. In a burn pipeline, the replayed copy may be the *only* surviving copy — no cross-reference possible. ### FM-4: Truncation via Unauthenticated Metadata Message format: `[encrypted_payload][MAC][routing_priority_byte]`. Priority byte sits outside MAC coverage. Adversary flips it from `0x01` (routine) to `0x04` (emergency) on a routine message. Payload verifies fine. HQ diverts resources based on a forged priority flag. **Generalization:** Any field outside MAC coverage is attacker-writable. Audit every byte. ### FM-5: Shared-Codebook Forgery Two scouts share a codebook. Either can produce messages verifiable as the other. "Authorship provable" collapses to "codebook-holder provable. " Under coercion, one scout frames another. **Boundary:** Per-author sub-keys inside the codebook solve forgery but create a mapping table. Capturing one codebook reveals the organizational chart. ### FM-6: Flash Wear-Leveling Ghost Copies Software "burn" deletes the logical file. Flash controller's wear-leveling already wrote the data to physical block 0x4A20 during an earlier write cycle. Logical deletion marks block 0x7B10 as free. Physical block 0x4A20 retains the full plaintext until overwritten by chance. **Concrete trigger:** Any consumer-grade flash storage (SD card, eMMC, NAND). Software-level zeroization is insufficient. Requires hardware-level secure erase or self-destructing storage. ### FM-7: Timing Oracle in Decoder Valid message: decoder runs full MAC verification (~2ms). Invalid message: decoder exits early on length check (~0. **Fix:** Constant-time decode path regardless of input validity. Pad all operations to worst-case latency. ### FM-8: Coercion Collapse at Human Layer Crypto is sound. Courier carries a memorized codebook. Under interrogation, courier claims ignorance. Interrogator says "recite your codebook entries. " Courier can't produce them without revealing knowledge. Deniability dies at the flesh level, not the math level. **Boundary:** True deniability requires the codebook to be derivable from something innocuous (a book, a song, environmental features) rather than stored or memorized as an obvious artifact. ### FM-9: Clock Skew Exceeding Validity Window Anti-replay uses timestamp windows (±60 seconds). Scout's crystal oscillator drifts 40ppm. Over 48 hours: 3. Over 30 days: 104 seconds. Day 12 onward, all messages fail freshness checks. Scout interprets this as "I'm blown" and goes permanently dark. ### FM-10: Known-Plaintext Structure Leakage Report template: `[GRID_REF: 8 bytes][STATUS: 1 of 4 values][PRIORITY: 1 of 3 values]`. Adversary knows the template. Each message leaks 2 bits of status + 1. 58 bits of priority = constrained plaintext space. Over 500 messages, this dramatically narrows keyspace search for the cipher. ### FM-11: Rotation Signal Intercepted on Compromised Channel Codebook rotation order transmitted via outgoing codebook N. Codebook N was compromised last week. Adversary learns exact activation time of codebook N+1. Pre-positions recording infrastructure. When N+1 activates, adversary has clean before/after traffic for cryptanalysis. ### FM-12: Error Differentiation Oracle Decoder returns distinct error codes: `ERR_PADDING` vs `ERR_MAC` vs `ERR_LENGTH`. Adversary submits modified ciphertexts, observes which error fires, uses this as a padding oracle to decrypt byte-by-byte without the codebook. **Fix:** Single opaque failure output. Identical observable behavior for all invalid inputs. ### FM-13: ACK Confirms Real Traffic HQ sends acknowledgment: "MSG 47 received. " Adversary monitoring both endpoints sees that message #47 (of 60 transmitted, 55 being chaff) got an ACK. Now knows #47 was real. Chaff camouflage broken retroactively for the entire session. ### What the protocol guarantees: | Content confidentiality | Only codebook holders recover plaintext | | Authorship | Provable to codebook holders via MAC/signature | | Outsider view | Statistically indistinguishable from noise | | Post-burn secrecy | Local copies unrecoverable (with hardware enforcement) | ### What the protocol does NOT guarantee: | Property | Why it fails | | Traffic-analysis resistance | Volume, timing, and directionality still visible | | Pre-burn forward secrecy | Static codebook = captured key decrypts archives | | Human-layer deniability | Possession/knowledge of codebook is incriminating | | Implementation correctness | Bugs undermine mathematical guarantees | | Endpoint security | Compromised endpoint sees plaintext pre-encryption | ### Hard theoretical limit: You cannot simultaneously achieve "anyone could have authored this" (deniability) and "only Alice authored this" (non-repudiation) for the same verifier. The protocol resolves this by splitting audiences, but the split itself creates a detectable asymmetry if the adversary can observe both audiences' behavior. ## WHAT MUST NEVER HAPPEN | # | Prohibition | Consequence if violated | | N-1 | Never reuse OTP segments | XOR of two ciphertexts leaks both plaintexts | | N-2 | Never co-locate codebook and messages on same device | Single capture yields both | | N-3 | Never send ACKs that confirm decryption success | Reveals which messages are real | | N-4 | Never implement burn as software-only deletion | Flash ghosts persist | | N-5 | Never fall back to unauthenticated decode on verification failure | Creates decryption oracle | | N-6 | Never distribute codebooks over the monitored channel | Bootstrap compromise | | N-7 | Never use different code paths for chaff vs. real | Statistical separation | | N-8 | Never assume protocol format is secret | Kerckhoffs violation | | N-9 | Never allow partial burns | Fragments reconstructable | | N-10 | Never double-purpose auth tag as routing data | Malleability attack surface | | N-11 | Never use static keys across epochs | No forward secrecy; archive decryption | | N-12 | Never expose distinct error types externally | Oracle attacks | ## Summary of Critical Design Constraints **Single code path** for chaff and real messages — byte-identical distributions. **Constant-time everything** — no early exits, no data-dependent branches in decode. **MAC covers every byte** — no unauthenticated fields, period. **Hardware-enforced burn** — fuse, secure element, or physical destruction. **Ratcheting key evolution** — each message advances key state; past captures don't decrypt future traffic. **Opaque failure mode** — one error output, indistinguishable across all failure causes. **Per-author sub-keys** — but the mapping must not be stored alongside the codebook. **Out-of-band bootstrap** — codebook distribution never touches the comms channel. **Generous clock tolerance** — validity windows measured in hours, not seconds, with monotonic counters as primary anti-replay. **Silent discard** — failed verification produces zero observable response. No NACK, no retry request, no log entry readable by adversary. The user is asking about a deniable-yet-verifiable comms protocol in a "frontier-scout burn pipeline" context. Let me parse what this actually means: **Deniable-yet-verifiable**: A protocol where messages can only be recovered with a specific codebook (so to outsiders, the traffic looks like noise or innocuous content — deniability), but authorship is provable (verifiability). This is essentially steganography + authentication. **Frontier-scout burn pipeline**: This sounds like an operational context where scouts at the edge of a network/territory send reports back, and there's a "burn" mechanism (messages are destroyed after reading, or the pipeline itself has destructive properties). Let me think about this as a real cryptographic/operational problem and enumerate edge cases, failure modes, boundaries, and "never happen" constraints. Let me structure this properly: **Core tension**: Deniability vs. These pull against each other: - Deniability: you want plausible deniability that you sent anything meaningful. The ciphertext should look like noise or cover traffic. - Verifiability: you want to prove *who* authored it, but only to those with the codebook. This is essentially: authenticated encryption with deniable authentication, or a MAC-based scheme where the MAC doubles as part of the cover text. **Key design elements I should address**: **Codebook management** — how it's distributed, rotated, versioned **Cover traffic generation** — what the message looks like without the codebook **Authentication tag placement** — where the proof of authorship lives **Burn semantics** — what happens after read, key destruction, forward secrecy **Clock/timing issues** **Partial recovery / truncation attacks** **Codebook compromise cascade** Let me be very concrete and systematic. Codebook version mismatch (the most common operational failure) - Scout has codebook v3, HQ has rolled to v4. Message encrypted under v3 arrives; HQ tries v4 first, fails, falls back. or doesn't. - Edge case: partial overlap between versions. Some fields decode correctly under both versions, others don't. You get a "half-decoded" message that looks valid but is garbage. This is worse than total failure because it's silent corruption. - Mitigation boundary: you need a version epoch embedded in a way that's itself deniable (e. , encoded in timing, or in a header field that looks like padding). Cover-traffic statistical leakage - If your cover is "random bytes," but your actual encrypted payload has different entropy characteristics than random (e. , MAC tags have specific length, headers have fixed positions), a traffic analyst can distinguish "real" messages from chaff. - Concrete failure: you generate chaff messages to hide real ones, but chaff messages are generated by a different code path than real ones → different byte-length distribution → trivially distinguishable. - Boundary: the cover generator and the real-message wrapper must be the same code path, same distribution. - Adversary captures a valid message, re-injects it later. Without sequence numbers or timestamps bound into the MAC, the receiver accepts it as fresh. - In a burn pipeline this is especially bad: if the original was already burned (read and destroyed), a replay might be the *only* copy the receiver sees, and they can't tell it's stale intel. - Must-have: monotonically increasing counter bound into the authentication tag, with a replay window. Truncation/cut-and-paste - If the message format allows variable-length payloads, an adversary who captures multiple messages can splice segments. If the MAC covers the whole message, this fails — but if any field is outside MAC coverage (e. , a "priority" flag, a routing hint), it can be flipped. - Concrete: adversary flips one bit in a non-authenticated field → message decodes differently → scout's report says "clear" instead of "compromised. Key-compromise cascade - One scout's codebook is captured. Does it decrypt other scouts' traffic? If codebooks are shared across a unit, yes → total compromise. - Boundary: per-scout codebooks, or per-pairwise-channel codebooks. But then codebook distribution becomes the weak point. Burn failure — the message that didn't burn - Receiver reads message, burn command issued, but storage isn't actually zeroized (e. , flash wear-leveling means old data persists in unmapped blocks). - Concrete: on flash storage, "delete" just marks blocks as free. Wear-leveling may have written the message to multiple physical locations. Zeroizing the logical file leaves physical copies. - This is a hardware-level failure mode that software "burn" commands don't address. Timing side-channels in decoding - If decoding a valid message takes measurably longer than rejecting an invalid one (e. , early-exit on MAC check), an adversary with timing information can infer which messages are real. - Must be constant-time across all paths. Deniability collapse under coercion - The whole point of deniability is that under interrogation, the carrier can claim "I didn't know this was anything. " But if the codebook is on their person, or if possession of the codebook itself is incriminating, deniability fails at the human layer regardless of crypto. - Boundary: the codebook must not be stored with the courier/scout. It must be memorized, or derived from something innocuous. Authorship forgery when codebook is shared - If two operators share a codebook, either can forge the other's messages. "Authorship provable" requires per-author keys within the codebook framework. - But per-author keys create a metadata trail: if the codebook reveals *which* sub-key was used, and sub-keys map to individuals, then capturing the codebook reveals the org chart. Clock skew in time-bounded validity - If messages have a validity window (to prevent replay), clock drift between scout and HQ causes false rejection. - Concrete: scout's clock drifts 90 seconds over 48 hours in the field. Validity window is ±60 seconds. Messages start failing after day 2. Scout doesn't know why. Falls back to plaintext or goes dark. Chaff-to-real ratio leakage - If you send 10 chaff for every real message, and the adversary knows the ratio, they can do frequency analysis. If the ratio changes based on operational tempo (more real messages during active ops), the change itself is a signal. Codebook rotation gap - During rotation from codebook N to N+1, there's a window where some nodes have N, some have N+1. Messages sent during this window may be undecodable by parts of the network. - Worse: if the rotation signal itself is sent via the old codebook, and the old codebook is compromised, the adversary learns the new codebook's activation time and can prepare. Padding oracle analog - If the decoder returns different errors for "bad padding" vs. "bad MAC," an adversary can use error differentiation to decrypt without the codebook. - Must return identical observable behavior for all failure types. Forward secrecy absence - If today's codebook is captured, yesterday's (already-burned) messages can be decrypted from archived traffic captures. - In a burn pipeline, the *point* is that burned messages are gone. But if the adversary recorded RF traffic or network captures, burning the local copy doesn't help unless keys provide forward secrecy. - Boundary: you need ratchet-style key evolution, not static codebooks. The "known-plaintext" problem with structured reports - Scout reports follow templates ("GRID REF: ___, STATUS: ___"). Template structure is known to adversary. - Concrete: if status field has only 4 possible values, that's 2 bits of known structure per message. Over many messages, this constrains the keyspace search. ### What the protocol CAN guarantee: - Only codebook holders can recover content - Authorship is provable to codebook holders - Non-holders see statistically indistinguishable-from-noise traffic ### What the protocol CANNOT guarantee: - That the codebook holder won't defect - That physical capture won't yield the codebook - That traffic analysis won't reveal *that* communication is happening (volume, timing patterns) - That the cover story survives behavioral scrutiny (a scout who suddenly sends 10x normal volume is suspicious regardless of content) - That implementation bugs won't undermine the math - Deniability and non-repudiation are in direct tension. You cannot have both "anyone could have written this" and "only Alice could have written this" simultaneously for the same audience. The resolution is audience-dependent: deniable to outsiders, provable to insiders. But this means the *insider* proof material must not be extractable by outsiders even with the full ciphertext. ## WHAT MUST NEVER HAPPEN **Never reuse a one-time pad segment. ** If the codebook includes OTP material, reuse enables XOR-of-two-ciphertexts attacks that leak both plaintexts. **Never store the codebook and the messages on the same device. ** Capture of one device yields both. **Never acknowledge receipt in a way that confirms decryption. ** An ACK that says "message received and understood" tells the adversary which messages were real (vs. chaff) if they're watching both ends. **Never let the burn be advisory. ** Burn must be enforced at the storage layer (hardware zeroization, fuse-blowing), not a software suggestion. **Never allow the system to fall back to unauthenticated mode. ** If codebook verification fails, the message must be discarded, not "decoded best-effort. " Best-effort decoding is an attack surface. **Never transmit the codebook over the same channel as the messages. ** Bootstrap problem: you need a secure side channel for initial codebook distribution. **Never make the chaff generator distinguishable from the real-message generator. ** Same code path, same entropy source, same length distribution. **Never rely on obscurity of the protocol format alone. ** Assume the adversary knows the protocol completely (Kerckhoffs's principle); security must reside entirely in the codebook/key material. **Never allow partial burns. ** Either the entire message state is destroyed or none of it is. Partial burns leave fragments that can be reconstructed. **Never let the authentication tag serve double duty as routing metadata. ** If the tag is used for both integrity and addressing, modifying the address modifies the tag, creating a malleability oracle. 31018a19ebd8cacd.text: # Deniable-Yet-Verifiable Comms Protocol: Edge Case Analysis Pure symmetric construction. Shared codebook `K`. Sender produces `nonce ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag` where ciphertext = AE(K_enc, nonce, plaintext) and tag = MAC(K_mac, nonce ‖ seq ‖ len ‖ ciphertext). Output is bit-indistinguishable from random to any party lacking `K`. Correct tag verification under `K` constitutes proof of authorship *within the holder set*. Running on operator-controlled hardware ("own iron"). ### FM-1: Codebook Compromise → Retroactive Total Collapse Single most dangerous mode. Adversary obtains `K` (through endpoint breach, coercion, side-channel, insider): - Decrypts **all previously recorded ciphertext**, forever. - Forges **all future messages** with perfect validity. - Cannot be distinguished from legitimate sender by any holder. No asymmetric separation between read-capability and write-capability. One secret governs both. ** Protocol dies, not degrades. ### FM-2: Nonce Reuse Same `(K, nonce)` pair used twice: - Under CTR-mode: keystream XOR reveals `P₁ ⊕ P₂`, leaking both plaintexts. - Under GCM: authentication key `H` is recovered from two-tag collision. Attacker gains **forgery oracle** for all subsequent messages. **Trigger conditions:** counter reset after reboot without persistence, fork of VM/container restoring old state, race condition in concurrent sends. ### FM-3: Replay Injection Adversary records valid message `M(seq=n)` at time `T`. Replays at time `T+Δ`. Receiver accepts if: - Sequence window is too wide. - Timestamp tolerance exceeds Δ. - No freshness check exists. In command contexts, replaying `"EXECUTE"` or `"ABORT"` hours/days later is operationally devastating. ### FM-4: Truncation / Splicing If MAC coverage omits any field (length prefix, routing header, padding indicator), attacker manipulates uncovered portion: - Truncate ciphertext → receiver decrypts partial plaintext, possibly misinterpreting intent. - Splice ciphertext blocks from two different valid messages → Frankenstein message passes MAC if those blocks were individually covered. **Rule:** MAC must cover every byte the receiver acts upon. ### FM-5: Length / Timing Side Channel Content is protected. Pattern is not: - Burst of 4KB followed by silence ≠ steady 64-byte heartbeat. Observer infers event-driven communication. - Message appears precisely when operator's cover activity has a gap → correlation attack. Deniability of *content* does not confer deniability of *existence*. ### FM-6: Ratchet Desync Per-message key chaining (`K_{n+1} = H(K_n)`) provides forward secrecy. Packet loss at position `n` makes receiver unable to decrypt `n+1, n+2, . Recovery mechanisms (publishing catch-up seed) create a high-value target: single message that unlocks everything after it. ### FM-7: Codebook Bootstrap Exposure Initial `K` distribution: - Sent over same channel → visible to channel observer. - Sent out-of-band → that channel is single point of failure; compromise there compromises everything downstream. - Derived from password → brute-forceable offline if derivation parameters are known. ### FM-8: Error Oracle Receiver rejects invalid messages with distinguishable errors: - `"MAC verification failed"` vs `"malformed header"` vs `"unknown version"`. Attacker submits modified ciphertexts, observes which modification changes the error class. Extracts information byte-by-byte (padding oracle pattern). ### FM-9: Group Attribution Ambiguity Multiple operators share one `K`: - Receiver knows *someone* with `K` sent it. - If individual attribution is required: derive per-sender subkeys `K_i = HKDF(K, "sender-"‖i)`. - If full internal deniability is required: single shared `K` suffices, but compromise of any member compromises all. These goals conflict. Must choose explicitly. ### FM-10: Own-Iron Specific — Supply Chain & Physical Operator controls software stack but likely not silicon: - **Hardware RNG backdoor:** deterministic output seeded by manufacturer. All keys predictable to chip designer. - **Cold boot:** DRAM retains contents for seconds-minutes after power removal. Codebook recoverable from RAM snapshot. - **TEMPEST:** EM emanations from display/CPU leak processing activity. - **Firmware rootkit:** persists below OS, captures keys before encryption, invisible to software audit. ### B-1: Deniability Boundary | Passive network observer | Yes | | Traffic analyst (metadata only) | Partially | | Adversary with recorded traffic, no `K` | Yes | | Adversary with `K` | **No** | | Coerced operator revealing `K` | **No, retroactively** | | Endpoint memory access | **No** | Deniability is conditional on codebook secrecy. It is not an unconditional property. ### B-2: Verifiability Boundary | Verifier | Can verify? | Codebook holder | Yes | | Third-party auditor (no `K`) | **No** | | Court / external party | **Only if `K` surrendered** | Public verifiability and deniability are mutually exclusive. Verification requires the same secret whose possession must be deniable. Choose the audience. ### B-3: Scale Boundary Pre-shared symmetric codebooks scale as O(n²) for pairwise secure channels. Above ~10 participants, key management dominates operational cost. Revocation of a single compromised member requires rekeying all others. Not suitable for: large networks, open enrollment, zero-trust admission. ### B-4: Freshness Window Clock skew between endpoints defines replay acceptance window: - Skew = 0s → window = 0s → any jitter drops valid messages. - Skew = 300s → window = 300s → attacker replays within 5 minutes. Sequence numbers avoid clock dependency but require ordered delivery or windowed acceptance (e. , 64-bit sliding window). Out-of-order arrival beyond window = permanent loss. ### B-5: Availability Under Loss Strict authenticate-before-parse means: - Single flipped bit in transit → entire message discarded. - No partial recovery, no best-effort decode. - Effective reliability = link reliability × MAC pass rate. In high-loss environments (HF radio, congested links), application-layer fragmentation with per-fragment authentication is mandatory. ### B-6: Store-Now-Decrypt-Later All recorded ciphertext is permanently useful to future codebook holder. Without forward secrecy (ratcheting), the storage boundary is infinite: capture today, decrypt in 2035. With ratcheting: forward secrecy bounds exposure to messages after last ratchet step. But adds desync fragility (FM-6). ### B-7: Metadata Resistance Floor Even with perfect content protection: - Source/destination IP (if not torified) - Inter-packet timing - Connection duration/frequency - DNS queries preceding connection These require separate mitigations (cover traffic, mixnets, timing normalization). Content encryption alone provides zero metadata resistance. ## WHAT MUST NEVER HAPPEN ### N-1: Nonce reuse under any key. Not in testing. Not in simulation. " Not after reboot without persistent counter. A single reuse under GCM/CTR hands the attacker a forgery oracle. ### N-2: Codebook transmitted over the operational channel. Bootstrap must occur via physically separate, higher-assurance path. If the only available path is the operational channel, the protocol cannot be safely initialized. ### N-3: Unauthenticated plaintext acted upon. Decrypt-then-parse-then-verify is forbidden. Order must be: verify MAC → then parse → then act. Parsing before verification exposes parser to attacker-controlled input (memory corruption, logic bugs). ### N-4: Distinguishable rejection reasons. All invalid inputs produce identical response: silent drop, fixed-delay, no output difference. No error codes, no timing differences, no log entries distinguishing failure type. ### N-5: Plaintext persisted beyond immediate processing window. Zeroize buffers after use. Disable swap or use encrypted swap with volatile key. No core dumps. No debug logging of decrypted content. No writing plaintext to temp files. ### N-6: Same codebook across protocol versions or contexts. Domain-separate all key derivations: `K_enc = HKDF(K, "enc-v1")`, `K_mac = HKDF(K, "mac-v1")`, `K_ratchet = HKDF(K, "ratchet-v1")`. Cross-protocol use enables reflection and substitution attacks. ### N-7: Fallback to weaker mode on failure. If AES-GCM unavailable → halt, do not fall back to unauthenticated CTR or ECB. A dead link is recoverable; a silently degraded link is not. ### N-8: Acceptance of far-future sequence numbers. Sliding window must reject `seq > highest_seen + window_size`. Accepting arbitrary future sequence numbers enables pre-play: attacker injects message with `seq = 10^9`, causing receiver to reject all legitimate intermediate messages. ### N-9: Multiple copies of codebook in memory. Each additional copy expands attack surface (cold boot, heap spray, swap-out). Maintain exactly one copy in locked memory (`mlock`), reference by pointer, zeroize on shutdown. ### N-10: Custom cryptographic primitives. No custom ciphers, no custom hash functions, no custom MAC constructions, no "improved" padding schemes. Use: AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, HMAC-SHA-256, HKDF-SHA-256. Vetted implementations only (libsodium, monocypher, platform APIs). ### N-11: Reliance on deniability as sole protection layer. Assume codebook compromise is inevitable on a long enough timeline. Design for containment: ratcheting limits blast radius, per-session subkeys limit cross-session exposure, periodic rekey limits temporal exposure. ### N-12: Broadcast to multiple recipients without per-recipient derivation. If `M` is sent to Alice and Bob using same `K`: Bob decrypts Alice's copy. 180e0334d3e736a0.text: # LoEC/1 — Deniable, Verifiable, Stateless Seat Comms Targets and threat model Three properties, taken literally: **Covertness:** an observer holding only the public Ledger sees statistically normal seat behavior. They cannot confirm a message exists, let alone read it. **Private verifiability:** a codebook holder can prove a given Ledger event was authored by a specific member. Proof validity does **not** transfer to non-holders (this is what makes authorship provable *and* deniable simultaneously — we use symmetric MACs, never signatures). **Statelessness:** a seat may die at any instruction boundary and respawn with zero local memory. Everything needed to continue is a pure function of (member secret, public Ledger). Adversary tiers: (a) passive outsider reading the Ledger; (b) active outsider who can write Ledger events subject to the game's deposit cost; (c) a member whose secret leaks (partial tier — see §7 for what this costs us). The Ledger records seat events: claims, vacations, annotations. Each event has fields with **semantically interchangeable variants**: cause-of-vacation phrasing (16 canonically equivalent strings), chair choice within an equivalent set (8), tick placement within a grace window (32 ticks). These are our carrier. Capacity: `log2(16·8·32) = 12 bits` per event. This is a low-rate command channel (~a 200-bit message ≈ 17 events), not bulk transport. Camouflage rule: we never emit uniform bits naively. We map payload bits onto event choices by inverse-transform sampling against the **baseline distribution measured from recent public Ledger history** (estimated fresh each life — see §6). Marginal statistics per seat stay inside the population envelope. Keys: three-tier persistence - **Memorized (never written, never in the seat):** per-member 256-bit secret `s_m`. Held by the operator/player, not the seat instance. - **Persistent public registry (in the Ledger):** at enrollment, member `m` posts `P_m = g^{H(s_m)}` disguised as a routine seat-registration entry. Plus revocation entries ("chair burned"). The roster is *not* stored anywhere — it is recomputed by folding registry entries. - **Derived per epoch, never persisted:** epoch `e = ⌊ledger_height / E⌋`. Public epoch entropy `R_e = H(entry_at_epoch_boundary)`. Pairwise directional keys: x_m      = H(s_m) Z_ij     = H( P_j^{x_i} )                      // static ECDH, direction i→j K_e(i→j) = HKDF(Z_ij, R_e, e, "LOEC/1", i, j)  // fresh per epoch Message format and the encode/verify core Plaintext: `{sender_id, epoch, seq, body, pad}`. Per-slot processing: slot_ctx   = H(sender_seat, event_index, H(prev_ledger_entry))   // position-bound ks         = HKDF(K_e(i→j), slot_ctx, "enc") ct         = body_bits XOR ks                                    // ChaCha20-class stream τ          = Trunc_32( HMAC(K_e(i→j), slot_ctx || ct) ) Embedding: fill the event's choice-space with `ct` bits greedily, then **rejection-sample the final combination** (phrasing × chair × tick) until the combination's hash equals `τ`. Exactly one combination in the class will match with overwhelming probability; that event gets written. Decoding (recipient): enumerate all combinations in the class for that slot, compute each one's implied tag, take the match. The tag match **is** the authorship proof: only a holder of `K_e(i→j)` could have produced an event whose implied tag equals `τ` at that exact `slot_ctx`. Attribution is pairwise (`K_ab ≠ K_ba`) — even other insiders cannot attribute i↔j traffic. A "proof" shown to an outsider is unverifiable by them; sender denial survives. False accepts: 2⁻³² per guess, throttled in-fiction by the chair-deposit cost per Ledger write. Spawn algorithm (entire stateless lifecycle) e        = h div E roster   = fold_registry(from_last_checkpoint_entry)   // pure function of Ledger x        = H(s_memorized) for j in roster: K_e[i→j] = HKDF(H(P_j^x), R_e, e, . baseline = estimate_distributions(last W ledger entries)  // camo recalibration rng      = seeded per-event: HKDF(K_e, slot_ctx)          // no RNG state kept cursor   = next_free_slot(h) - **Dies mid-draft:** the unposted half-encoded event is simply never written. Receivers only accept complete tag matches; unmatched slots read as no-message. Aborted drafts cost nothing and require no recovery logic. - **Dies idle:** nothing was held; nothing lost. - **Respawn continuity:** same `s_m` ⇒ same identity, same keys, seamless. The protocol never notices the death occurred. - **Ledger rollback/fork:** tags bind `H(prev_ledger_entry)`; rolled-back messages self-invalidate. Accept only after depth `D = 6` confirmations. What persists vs. what recomputes — the explicit answer | Item | Disposition | Location / mechanism | | Member secret `s_m` | **Persists**, never in seat | Operator memory | | Registry (`P_m`, burns) | **Persists** | Ledger, permanent entries | | All events / messages | **Persist** | Ledger | | Roster | **Recompute** | Fold registry entries from checkpoint | | `x_m`, all `K_e(i→j)` | **Recompute** | Pure function of `(s_m, Ledger@e)` | | Epoch counter | **Recompute** | `e = ⌊h/E⌋` — ledger height *is* the counter | | Sequence numbers | **Recompute** | Derived from slot positions; `seq` only orders within epoch | | Replay window / seen-tags | **Not needed** | Tags are position-bound; replay structurally impossible | | Camouflage model | **Recompute** | Estimated from last `W` public entries each life | | RNG state | **Not kept** | Deterministic per-event seeding from `slot_ctx` | | Partial drafts, caches | **Deliberately destroyed** | Die with the seat; treated as no-op | Invariant: **the Ledger plus one memorized 256-bit secret fully determines the seat's entire communicative past, present, and capability. ** Nothing else exists anywhere. Anti-traffic-analysis (mandatory, not optional) Bursts correlate with message times, so every seat runs **constant-rate decoy churn**: Poisson(λ₀) baseline events regardless of traffic. Pending messages ride inside the churn budget; idle periods emit all-padding messages (encrypted zeros) so event-count distribution is invariant. Receivers distinguish via tag scan. λ₀ and the baseline distributions are protocol parameters, recalculated per-life from public history — keeping even the camouflage stateless. Guarantees, and the one thing statelessness costs **Provided:** covertness (PRF assumption + statistical camouflage); private authorship verification, pairwise-attributed; structural replay immunity; tamper-evidence via prev-hash binding; instant respawn with zero recovery protocol; clean revocation. **Not provided, stated plainly:** forward secrecy against member-secret compromise. Because every key is deterministically re-derivable (that is the price of statelessness), a leaked `s_m` unlocks that member's entire pairwise past and future. Any design claiming both full statelessness *and* forward secrecy against secret compromise is lying about one of them; this one doesn't. **Parameters (v1):** E = 512 ticks/epoch · 32-bit tags · D = 6 confirmation depth · W = 4096-entry camo window · grace window 32 ticks · λ₀ tuned per-seat-class · version string `"LOEC/1"` in every HKDF info field. 83291096b5ffd61f.text: # Deniable-Yet-Verifiable Comms for a Stateless Seat Property definitions (exact, no vibes) Three properties, stated precisely: - **P1 Confidentiality+Unlinkability (external):** Without the codebook `CB`, a global passive observer sees wire records computationally indistinguishable from random bytes. They cannot recover plaintext, cannot count distinct authors, cannot confirm two records share a channel beyond timing/volume metadata. - **P2 Attribution (internal, scoped):** Any holder of `CB` can decrypt any record and determine which ring member authored it — *under the honesty assumption*. The evidence is simultaneously forgeable by every ring member (see below), so it proves nothing against a denying or coerced insider. - **P3 Forgeability-equals-deniability:** Every member can derive every other member's signing key from `CB`. Therefore any transcript implicating member X is bit-for-bit reproducible by any other member. This is not a bug — it is the deniability mechanism. Verifiability and deniability are the same fact viewed from inside vs. outside the ring. Non-goals, stated once: no protection against `CB` compromise (total loss, past and future), no traffic-analysis resistance without cover traffic, no post-compromise security beyond epoch granularity. **Primitives:** HKDF-SHA-256 for all derivation. XChaCha20-Poly1305 for AEAD (24-byte nonce). Keyed BLAKE3 for the authorship tag and log chain. No signatures anywhere — signatures are non-repudiable and would break P3. **Key schedule (all recomputable, nothing cached):** K_cb      = codebook master secret (external to seat; never persisted) K_E       = HKDF(K_prev_epoch, salt="epoch", info=cb_version)   // forward-chained K_{E,s}   = HKDF(K_E, salt=sender_idx, info="author") K_log,E   = HKDF(K_E, salt="log") K_dev     = HKDF(K_cb, salt="dev-seal")                          // seals persisted blob Epoch keys chain forward (`K_{E+1}` from `K_E`), so old epoch keys are erasable after log compaction — epoch-granularity forward secrecy with ~zero persisted state. **Wire format (constant shape, no authorship metadata on the wire):** offset  size  field 0       2     magic 0x4758 2       1     version = 1 3       1     flags (bit0 compressed, bit1 ack, rest 0) 4       4     ct_len (BE) 8       24    nonce 32      var   AEAD ciphertext (+16B Poly1305 tag) AAD     =     bytes [0. 8) of header 0    8   epoch_ctr (u64 BE) 8    4   seq (u32 BE) 12   1   sender_idx (0xFF = system/broadcast) 13   32  body_hash = BLAKE3(body) 45   var padded_body (bucket-padded: 256/512/1K/2K/4K) +16  auth_tag = BLAKE3(key=K_{E,s}, "auth" || epoch || seq || body_hash || flags)[0. **Nonce:** deterministic — `HKDF(K_E, "nonce" || sender_idx || seq)[0. Unique because `(epoch, sender, seq)` is unique by invariant ι₃ below. Consequence: the seat needs **zero RNG state** on the crypto path. Respawn-safe by construction. **Receive path:** open AEAD under `K_E` (one trial, not n — the group key decrypts), read `sender_idx`, recompute `auth_tag` under that member's `K_{E,s}`, constant-time compare. Mismatch → reject, log the rejection, never deliver. **ACKs:** same format, flags bit1 set, body carries `(acked_epoch, acked_seq, highest_contiguous_seq)`, tagged under the *acker's* `K_{E,s}`. Delivery confirmation is deniable by the same mechanism. The invariant lattice Predicates over protocol state `Σ = (Log, W, E, CB_v)` where `W[s]` is the per-sender watermark. Ordered by enforcement scope; every transition must preserve everything at or below its tier. Tier C (audit-time — probes, fuzz harness, CI) ι₆ Deniability:   wire transcripts simulatable without CB (P1) ι₇ Liveness:      honest send + retry ⇒ eventual accept at all honest seats Tier B (respawn/epoch-boundary — validator run) ι₂ Causality:     per-sender seqs strictly increase; gaps permitted but logged ι₅ Reconstruct:   Σ_respawn = F(CB, Log) — deterministic, total function Tier A (every transition, inline asserts — microseconds) ι₀ Secrecy:       nothing leaves the process unencrypted under K_E ι₁ Origin:        accept(m) ⇒ auth_tag valid under some member's K_{E,s} ι₃ Anti-replay:   (E, s, seq) unique in Log; duplicates rejected ι₄ Durability:    transmit ⇒ record fsynced first; accept ⇒ record fsynced first Meet/join semantics: the meet `∧(Tier A)` must hold at *every intermediate step* of every transition — no torn states. Log appends are atomic framed records; a torn tail is detected by the MAC chain and truncated. The join is respawn itself: `checkpoint ⊔ log-tail-replay = Σ`, well-defined *because* ι₅ makes reconstruction deterministic. Code-as-law means: the validator is the sole arbiter, seats fail closed on any Tier A/B violation, and there is no human override path. | Codebook / `K_cb` | **Never** | External; supplied at spawn | | All keys (`K_E`, `K_{E,s}`, `K_log,E`, `K_dev`) | **Never** | HKDF from `K_cb` + counters | | Nonces | **Never** | Deterministic KDF | | Sealed state blob | Yes | `{cb_version, epoch_ctr, self_idx, checkpoint, pinned_epochs}` sealed under `K_dev` | | Log | Yes | Append-only, sealed per-segment under `K_log,E`, BLAKE3 MAC-chained | | Checkpoint | Yes | Every 4096 records: `{rec_no, W[·] snapshot, mac_tail}` | | Watermarks `W[·]` | Checkpoint only | Full rebuild = replay ≤4096 records | | Sent-unacked queue | **Never** | Log scan: records flagged sent ∧ ¬acked | | `epoch_ctr` | Fast path | Ground truth = `max(log. | `self_idx` | Sealed | Recompute path: manifest lookup at spawn | | RNG state | **Never** | OS entropy at spawn; used only for padding jitter, never crypto | | Membership | **Never** | Codebook manifest, hash-pinned in state | Total persistent footprint: one sealed blob (~200B + watermarks) plus the sealed log. Everything else is a pure function of `CB` and the log. Death and respawn (exact) **Death:** nothing happens. The single critical ordering rule is ι₄: `fsync(log. append(record))` **before** `transmit(record)`. This guarantees no sent-but-unlogged message exists, which is what makes idempotent retransmission safe. Load sealed blob, open with `K_dev`. Pin codebook: `BLAKE3(CB) == manifest_hash` from state. Codebook drift is a law violation; the seat refuses to run. Seek log to checkpoint offset. Stream records: verify frame length → verify MAC chain → decrypt under `K_log,E` → apply to `W`. Torn tail → truncate, emit warning. Derive working keys lazily per contact. Rebuild resend queue: outbound records after last ACK per destination. Retransmit with **identical** `(epoch, seq)` — receivers dedup via ι₃, so retransmission is free of side effects. Run the Tier B validator over reconstructed `Σ`. Any assertion failure → fail closed, emit no traffic. Concurrent respawn of two seats is a non-event: each seat owns its private log; cross-seat consistency flows through protocol messages, never through shared storage. Edge cases nailed down - **No wall-clock anywhere. ** Epochs advance on message count (rotate at 2²⁴, far below the u32 seq ceiling) or explicit rotate command. Timestamps appear only as advisory payload fields. - **Compaction & forward secrecy:** background job re-encrypts log segments older than grace period `G` under the current `K_log,E`; only then are old epoch keys unpinned and erasable. Uncompacted segments pin their epoch keys via the `pinned_epochs` list in the checkpoint (usually empty — a few bytes). - **Late joiners** with a fresh codebook can derive only the current epoch forward — they read compacted history onward. - **Large messages:** fragment at 4 KiB buckets; `(frag_total, frag_idx)` rides in the plaintext header extension; each fragment is independently AEAD'd with its own seq. - **Multi-codebook history:** log segments carry `cb_version`; respawn loads the pinned versions from external storage to read across rotations. Validator (code-as-law, executable) def validate(log, cb): W, seen, mac = defaultdict(int), set(), ZERO for rec in log. stream():                      # ι₅ entry point assert framing_ok(rec)                    # torn-tail detection mac = blake3(key=K_log(rec. e), prev=mac, msg=rec) pt = aead_open(K_E(rec. e), rec)           # ι₀ upstream guarantee e, seq, s, bh, body, tag = parse(pt) assert (e, s, seq) not in seen            # ι₃ add((e, s, seq)) exp = blake3(key=K_author(cb, e, s), msg=b"auth" + pack(e, seq, bh))[:16] assert ct_eq(tag, exp)                    # ι₁ W[s] = max(W[s], seq)                     # ι₂ return W                                      # feeds checkpoint CI runs this on every code change against golden transcripts; the respawn path runs it against live state; a periodic probe injects mutated records (flipped bits, replayed seqs, stripped tags) and asserts rejection. f124aeeaa09f4f09.text: # Ghost-AOS Git-Bus Treaty — Protocol GBUS/1 **Deniable, attributable, deterministic messaging over a git branch. Threat model and goals (exact) Parties **Alpha** and **Beta** share one 64-byte secret, the **Codebook** `M`, exchanged once out-of-band. The bus is a linear git branch. - **G1 Confidentiality:** ciphertext in the repo is useless without `M`. - **G2 Attribution-to-peer:** each envelope's origin is provable to the receiving party. - **G3 Repudiability:** no third party — forensics, hoster, or an adversary who later captures `M` — can obtain a *transferable* proof that either party authored anything. - **G4 Determinism:** given the same Codebook and the same accepted envelope stream, two independent implementations produce byte-identical blobs, byte-identical commit chains, and byte-identical roots. Non-goal: forward secrecy against compromise of the current `M` (see §9). Non-goal: hiding bus existence from someone with repo read access (mitigated, not solved, by chaff — §6). No algorithm agility. Implementations MUST use exactly: | Hash | SHA-256, FIPS 180-4 | | AEAD | XChaCha20-Poly1305 (24-byte nonce, 16-byte tag), draft-irtf-cfrg-xchacha | | KDF | HKDF-SHA-256, RFC 5869 | | Git objects | `git init --object-format=sha256` | All integers unsigned, **big-endian**, fixed width. All hex lowercase. All protocol literals ASCII. Bodies are opaque bytes. Codebook and key schedule Per epoch `e` (u32, starts 0): M_0 = Codebook (64 bytes) prk_e   = HKDF-Extract(salt = "GBUS/v1/epoch" || u32be(e),  IKM = M_e) K_a2b_e = HKDF-Expand(prk_e, "key a2b", 32)     // Alpha→Beta AEAD key K_b2a_e = HKDF-Expand(prk_e, "key b2a", 32)     // Beta→Alpha AEAD key N_d(s)  = HKDF-Expand(prk_e, "nonce " || d || u64be(s), 24)   // d = sender byte M_{e+1} = HKDF-Expand(prk_e, "master next", 64) // deterministic ratchet Label concatenation is unambiguous because every field has fixed width. Stronger operational form: every honest worker's computed payload is byte-identical to every other's, so quorum equality always holds at attempt 0. - **S4 Bounded termination** — every task reaches `SEALED` or `DEAD` within `MAX_ATTEMPTS`. Core invariant that makes this possible: **the answer is a pure function of the spec. ** Workers contribute only attestations; nobody ever "chooses" a value. Retries re-sample the environment, never redefine the answer. No wall-clock term ever enters a decision variable — timestamps are observability-only and excluded from every hash. Substrate contract (only 3 primitives required) Any store providing these suffices (Postgres, Redis, FoundationDB, S3+conditional puts): | `PUT_IF_ABSENT(k, bytes)` | Linearizable create-if-not-exists. Returns win/lose. | `CAS(k, new_bytes, expect_version)` | Linearizable single-key compare-and-swap. | `LIST(prefix)` | **Linearizable within a shard** (repeatable snapshot for the duration of one seal call). Every state transition below is **exactly one CAS on one key**. There are no multi-key transactions anywhere; crash-safety falls out of that. CANON — the canonical encoding (anti-drift core) All payloads, specs, and records are encoded in CANON before hashing or storage. Representation freedom is where drift lives; CANON removes all of it. Tag   Type     Encoding 0x00  NIL      (empty) 0x01  FALSE    (empty) 0x02  TRUE     (empty) 0x03  U64      8 bytes, big-endian 0x04  I64      8 bytes, big-endian two's-complement 0x05  F64      8 bytes, big-endian IEEE-754 bits. 0 normalized to +0. 0x06  BYTES    u32 BE length + raw 0x07  STR      u32 BE byte-length + NFC-normalized UTF-8 0x08  ARR      u32 BE count + elements in produced order 0x09  MAP      u32 BE count + entries sorted by raw CANON bytes of key; duplicate keys forbidden 0x0A  HASH     32-byte SHA-256 pointer **Forbidden inside any payload:** wall-clock time, hostnames, PIDs/TIDs, memory addresses, ambient RNG output, locale strings, non-NFC Unicode, NaN/Inf, −0. Metrics are `U64` scaled integers (e. , score = `micros`), never floats, unless bit-exactness is separately proven. Map iteration order in the host language is irrelevant because CANON sorts at encode time. Hash function everywhere: `SHA-256` over CANON bytes. The classic approaches: **Deterministic execution**: If all workers run the same deterministic function on the same input, they get identical output. Every bypass targets exactly one clause. Catalog follows, grouped by target. ## Class A — Attacks on Purity Ambient entropy injection. ** Worker calls `Math. random()` or reads wall-clock mid-execution; two machines diverge silently. **Fix:** Executor runs a whitelisted opcode set only; any syscall outside it makes the block *invalid* (validation is itself a pure simulation). Randomness enters exclusively as a ledger field: `seed_h = H(seed_{h−1} ‖ VRF_output(proposer_h))`. No seed in ledger → no randomness exists. Runtime assertion in the serializer: unsorted → crash the worker, not the consensus. ** Workers on v1. 0 vs v1. 1 reduce the same prefix differently. **Fix:** Ruleset version byte in every block header; every worker compiles a dispatch table `RuleSet[v]`. Tx ID = `H(canonical_bytes)`; every tx carries `(chain_id, account_nonce, expiry_height)`; duplicate IDs under a processed prefix are no-ops by nonce-sequence rule. External-input reordering. ** Player actions arrive in different orders at different workers. **Fix:** Workers never touch raw external input.
