406e248b3cec9b29.text: # Red-Team: Semantic-Anchor Checkpoints in the Ledger of Empty Chairs ## What's being attacked (exact spec) The context is a canonical byte stream of ordered records `R[0. n)` (UTF-8 NFC, fixed field order, LF-delimited). The ledger engine mints **anchors** `A_i = {seq_i, chain_id, rec_idx_i, prefix_root_i, prev_anchor_id_i, engine_sig_i}` — automatically, at record boundaries, every K records and at structural seals (chair vacate/refill commits, chapter close). `prefix_root_i` is an order-committed Merkle root over `R[0. rec_idx_i)`, domain-separated SHA-256. KV-cache segments span `[rec_idx_i, rec_idx_{i+1})` with a rolling hash chaining each segment to the previous. - **I1 (Correctness):** the reused prefix is byte-identical to what a full prefill of the current context yields. - **I2 (Cost):** fresh prefill touches only tokens after the deepest valid anchor. - **I3 (Freshness):** no superseded checkpoint is ever served as current. Threat model: adversarial content flows through the ledger; agents control their own edit requests; the engine and its signing key are trusted; SHA-256 is unbroken. ### Class A — Anchor authenticity and freshness Self-minted anchor (forged checkpoint ribbon). *Vector:* a seated agent writes its own anchor record claiming the ledger stands at a favorable position. *Skin:* Vess staples a homemade bookmark into the Ledger. *Breaks:* I1, I3. *Mitigation:* anchors exist only in the engine-signed registry embedded in the ledger itself. Validator accepts an anchor iff `verify(engine_key, record)` succeeds **and** the record appears in the registry at `seq ≤ head`. Any anchor absent from the registry is not an anchor; it's payload text. Checkpoint replay / empty-chair resurrection. *Vector:* serve an older *valid* anchor against a newer head. *Skin:* Chair 6 was vacated at rec 412; replaying the rec-380 checkpoint puts Vess back in the chair inside the agent's context while the world says empty. *Breaks:* I3, I1. *Mitigation:* selection rule is deterministic — take the **maximum-seq** anchor passing validation, never merely "a" valid one. Cache lookup keys are `(agent_id, chain_id, anchor_id, head_seq_at_load)`; commit requires CAS on `head_seq`. Head moved → discard the prefilled suffix, redo. Stale segments are unreachable by construction, not by policy. Cross-chain splice. *Vector:* two sessions share a genesis prologue (same house rules); graft Table B's deep anchor onto Table A's prefix to skip A's unique middle chapters. *Mitigation:* `chain_id` is folded into every hash input: `H("LoEC-anchor-v1" || chain_id || . Root recomputation over A's bytes can never equal B's stored root. Strict equality check on `chain_id` at load; mismatch → treat as invalid, step back. ### Class B — Prefix integrity *Vector:* hash computed over write-time serialization; validation re-serializes differently (key order, whitespace, Unicode form). Attacker substitutes raw bytes that normalize identically but differ in meaning-bearing bytes. *Mitigation:* canonicalize once at ingestion; **store the canonical bytes content-addressed**; validation compares stored bytes to current prefix bytes directly — never re-serializes. Non-canonical input is rejected at the door, not coerced. Rule: `hash(stored_bytes) == stored_hash ∧ stored_bytes == current_prefix[0:len]`, else invalidate to previous anchor. Order-blind hashing (chair-history swap). *Vector:* per-chunk hashes computed position-independently; attacker swaps the occupancy histories of Chairs 3 and 7 — same hash multiset, different truth. *Mitigation:* Merkle internal nodes commit to child order (`H(left || right)`, asymmetric); the root binds the sequence. Any permutation changes the root. No multiset comparisons anywhere in the codebase. Second-preimage on a weak/truncated digest. *Vector:* rewrite "Chair 9: occupied by Vess" → "Chair 9: occupied by Mora" under a colliding or truncated hash. *Mitigation:* full-width SHA-256, domain-separated per record type, with length committed alongside (`H(type || len || bytes)`) to kill length-extension. Digests are compared full-width; no prefix matching. Mutable history behind valid anchors (retcon scrub). *Vector:* edit records at or before the deepest valid anchor without advancing the head — scrub Chair 2's vacancy record directly. All anchors stay "valid"; the prefix is now a lie. *Breaks:* I1, I3. *Mitigation:* records `≤ deepest_valid. rec_idx` are **write-once**. Corrections are forward-only amendment/tombstone records appended to the stream. Enforcement: any write targeting a record index below the deepest valid anchor triggers **physical invalidation** of every anchor at or above that index (cache segments deleted) *before* the write commits. No soft flags. ### Class C — Seam and boundary Mid-record anchor placement. *Vector:* an edit lands so the trusted prefix terminates inside a record — prefix ends at `"Chair 5 is occ|"` and the "new suffix" begins `upied by an unlisted guest. *Mitigation:* anchors are minted only at record boundaries, and the validator asserts `is_record_boundary(prefix_len)` before accepting any anchor. Assertion fails → step back one anchor. Fail-closed, no rounding. Segment splicing at seams. *Vector:* mix a segment from revision t with a segment from revision t+1; each passes a local spot-check, but the concatenation was never a real state. *Mitigation:* rolling hash chains segments (`seg_i` carries `H(last_block(seg_{i-1}) || seg_i)`), and validation always runs **root-to-head in one pass** — no per-segment spot checks, ever. A spliced pair breaks the chain deterministically. ### Class D — Cost-invariant erosion Byte-zero touch (full-refill tax). *Vector:* edit the Ledger's title page; every prefix root breaks; every turn pays a full re-prefill. *Breaks:* I2 permanently. *Mitigation:* rule 7 already forbids this — the preamble is write-once; changes are appended amendments, leaving old anchors valid and the amendment as ordinary suffix. Belt-and-braces: mandatory re-anchor cadence (every K records / T tokens, whichever first) caps worst-case blast radius at K records regardless of where an edit lands. Delta-expansion laundering. *Vector:* report a 3-token suffix ("the bell rings"); the template layer expands it into a 400-line guest manifest at prefill time. Cost accounting and anchor geometry diverge. *Mitigation:* anchors are stamped **post-expansion**, on the final token stream. Deltas are measured in expanded tokens only. During any long prefill, the engine mints intermediate anchors on the fly, so even a laundered suffix gets subdivided for next time. Cadence is uniform — no discretion, no exceptions. Anchor suppression / flooding. *Vector:* a writer class requests "no anchors tonight" (every edit becomes a full refill — slow bleed) or demands one per token (metadata bloat, tiny stale segments inviting seam attacks). *Mitigation:* minting is **engine-side and structural only**. Writer requests to add, suppress, or reschedule anchors are parsed as ordinary text and ignored. Cadence parameters live in engine config, not in anything the stream can influence. ### Class E — Concurrency and lifecycle TOCTOU between validation and prefill. *Vector:* ledger appends after anchor validation but before KV-load; the loaded prefix is stale relative to head. *Mitigation:* single-writer discipline: read `head_seq` → validate → prefill → CAS on `head_seq` at commit. CAS failure → discard suffix, revalidate, redo. Advisory locks prohibited; the CAS is the only gate. Reported-offset desync. *Vector:* writer reports suffix length/offsets that drift from reality; next delta computes from the wrong offset, silently duplicating or dropping records at the seam. *Mitigation:* offsets are **derived, never reported**: `next_offset` = position of the deepest sealed anchor, recomputed by scanning the canonical artifact each cycle. Writer-supplied numbers are treated as comments. Arithmetic edge cases. *Vector:* crafted negative or overflowing lengths make the validator compare empty slices and pass. *Mitigation:* unsigned 64-bit checked arithmetic throughout; any `len < 0`, overflow, or `start + len > total` aborts validation and drops to the previous anchor. Fail-closed on anomaly, always. ## The deterministic core (what makes all fifteen close) **Engine-only, structural, non-discretionary anchor minting** at fixed cadence and record boundaries. **Content-addressed canonical bytes**; order-committed Merkle roots; domain-separated, length-bound SHA-256 with `chain_id` in every input. **Deepest-max-seq selection**, boundary assertion, and full root-to-head chain verification in one pass. **Write-once history, forward-only amendments**; any below-anchor mutation force-invalidates upward before committing. **CAS-gated lifecycle, derived offsets, fail-closed arithmetic. Every mitigation above is a mechanical rule with a single enforcement point — no heuristics, no anomaly scores, no "probably fine. **Explicitly out of model:** compromise of the engine signing key (mitigated operationally: HSM residency, rotation schedule, registry counters) and breakage of SHA-256. Within the stated threat model, the fifteen vectors above are closed deterministically; outside it, they're closed by the key ceremony, not by the checkpoint design. 18396615bde07930.text: # Red-Team: Semantic-Anchor Checkpoints / Suffix-Only Re-Prefill (Ghost-AOS Git-Bus Treaty) The invariant under attack State it precisely, because every bypass below is an attack on one clause of it: > **INVARIANT:** For any served request, the KV blocks reused must have been prefilled from a token stream that is *token-for-token identical* to the current request's prefix `[0. a)` as committed at anchor `a`, under the same unbroken anchor-parent chain and generation counter. Only tokens `[a. n)` — the suffix — may be freshly prefilled. Anything else is a violation. Threat model: adversarial agent process, compromised tool returning hostile content, malicious co-tenant on shared serving infra, buggy/malicious middleware between bus and serving layer. The kernel and signing keys are trusted; nothing else is. Content-integrity layer 1 Retro-edit of committed prefix. *Bypass:* Agent (or injected tool output interpreted as an edit op) issues a mutation targeting span `< a` — e. , rewriting an early standing instruction. If the editor holds write handles to committed segments, the "immutable" prefix changes while caches built on the old bytes remain live. *Mitigation:* Content-addressed storage. Every committed segment is stored at `addr = SHA-256(canonical_token_ids ‖ role ‖ position_base)`; anchors reference addresses, never buffers. Write ops carry a target address; the bus rejects any write whose target address exists in the committed set. Mutation of history is structurally impossible, not policy-forbidden. 2 Canonicalization aliasing. *Bypass:* Same "content," different bytes — Unicode NFD vs NFC, JSON key order, whitespace, role-string casing. Attacker claims prefix-continuity while the actual token stream differs, smuggling altered tokens into the "reused" region without tripping invalidation. *Mitigation:* The hash is computed over **tokenizer output (token IDs), never raw text**, after kernel-owned tokenization. One canonical serializer is normative in the treaty (NFC, sorted keys, fixed role vocabulary). Non-conforming input is rejected at ingest, before it ever reaches a hash. 3 Hash truncation / collision forgery. *Bypass:* Short display hashes (12-hex-char "commit ids") used in comparisons somewhere in the pipeline; attacker grinds a colliding replacement segment. *Mitigation:* Full 256-bit digests everywhere, including logs and UIs. Comparison code paths take the full digest type; no string-truncated equality exists in the codebase. Collision-resistance assumption is stated in the treaty as load-bearing. 4 In-band anchor spoofing. *Bypass:* Tool returns text containing `<ANCHOR id=". A parser that scans the token stream for markers accepts a forged checkpoint boundary, splitting the context so poisoned content sits "before" a fake anchor and inherits cache trust. *Mitigation:* Anchors are **out-of-band only** — they live in the signed bus envelope, never in the token stream. The in-band marker grammar is stripped/escaped by the sanitizer pre-tokenization, and the anchor parser reads exclusively from the envelope channel. In-band occurrences are inert bytes. 5 Compression-codec confusion. *Bypass:* Segments stored compressed; hash taken over the compressed blob. Two valid decompressions of one blob (codec ambiguity, version drift) yield different token streams with identical stored hashes. *Mitigation:* Hash binds the **decompressed canonical token IDs**. Codec ID + version is a field inside the hashed record. Every read does decompress-then-verify; a stored hash is never trusted without recomputation over materialized tokens. Boundary-correctness layer 1 Token-boundary desync. *Bypass:* Editor computes the edit point in characters/bytes; the server works in tokens. Off-by-N lands the "suffix start" mid-token, silently mutating the final prefix token — the worst case, because one corrupted token sits inside nominally cached territory. *Mitigation:* Kernel owns tokenization; all boundaries are token indices minted by the kernel. Editors submit byte ranges; the kernel maps them to token boundaries atomically and assigns any straddling partial token to the *earlier* segment. Any edit adjacent to a boundary forces re-anchoring of the boundary token. 2 Suffix reorder / set-semantics laundering. *Bypass:* Any dedup or similarity shortcut that treats the suffix as a bag lets an attacker permute suffix tokens — same multiset, different meaning — while skipping re-prefill. *Mitigation:* Position-indexed hashing throughout: suffix block hashes include absolute offset relative to the anchor base. There is no set, bag, or similarity comparison anywhere in the validity path; equality is bitwise on ordered token IDs. 3 Anchor-chain truncation and ID reuse. *Bypass:* Serve a chain claiming depth `m` when edits exist at depths `(m, n]` — i. , skip intermediate anchors — or reuse a human-readable anchor ID across branches with different content, so a cache keyed on the ID collides across divergent histories. *Mitigation:* Each anchor commits `parent_hash`; the serving layer walks parents to genesis before granting any reuse; a broken link ⇒ full re-prefill. Cache/block keys are `(content_hash, chain_position, generation)` — derived values only. Human-assigned IDs never enter a key. KV-cache layer 1 Cross-tenant block poisoning. *Bypass:* Shared prefix-cache pool; co-tenant prefills blocks that your agent then reuses because the first N tokens happen to match. *Mitigation:* Block identity is namespaced: `block_id = H(tenant_id ‖ agent_id ‖ chain_head_hash ‖ [pos_lo, pos_hi))`. Cross-tenant reuse is unrepresentable in the key space. Global prefix pools are prohibited by the treaty for anchored contexts. 2 Stale-generation replay. *Bypass:* After a rollback or branch switch, the serving layer serves blocks from the abandoned generation — old suffix bytes grafted onto a new logical context. *Mitigation:* Monotonic kernel-issued generation counter stamped into every block; every request carries its expected generation; mismatch ⇒ reject and full re-prefill. Rollback creates a *new* generation; old ones are never resurrected. 3 Partial-hit stitching. *Bypass:* Memory pressure evicts middle blocks; the layer "helpfully" stitches a hit-run + recomputed middle + hit-run. Partial runs are not eligible for reuse. Hit/miss decisions are logged with the chain digest for audit. 4 Speculative-token promotion. *Bypass:* Draft/speculative decoding writes candidate tokens into cache beyond the confirmed suffix; a racing commit promotes rejected speculation into the anchored stream. *Mitigation:* Speculative blocks are born tagged `speculative=true`, allocated from a separate pool, invisible to anchored-region lookups. Promotion requires an explicit kernel commit that re-hashes the materialized tokens; anything else is freed at step end. 5 GC use-after-free spray. *Bypass:* Race the collector: free blocks still referenced by an in-flight request, then spray allocations to land attacker-shaped activations in that physical memory. *Mitigation:* Refcount + epoch fencing: blocks are pinned by the generations of all in-flight requests; release requires fence advance past every holder. Freed blocks enter a quarantine of `Q` generations before physical reuse. Wrap-around-free 128-bit refcounts. 6 Chunked-vs-monolithic numeric drift. *Bypass:* "Equivalent" prefill done in different chunk sizes or kernel paths produces slightly different hidden states; an attacker argues equivalence while the reused blocks encode a different computation than a clean run would. *Mitigation:* The treaty pins numerics per generation: chunk size, kernel selection, and reduction order are recorded in the anchor commit metadata and are mandatory for any reuse. Re-prefill of a suffix is bit-reproducible within a declared hardware class; cross-class reuse is disallowed. Bus / protocol layer 1 Commit forgery and replay. *Bypass:* Inject fabricated `COMMIT` frames (fake anchors) onto the bus, or replay captured old commits to rewind the head behind applied edits. *Mitigation:* Commits are Ed25519-signed by kernel-held keys only; agents have no signing capability. Strictly increasing sequence numbers with a zero-size replay window (each seq accepted once, ever). Periodic signed Merkle roots over the log let any replica detect tampering in O(log n). 2 Split-brain fork-merge. *Bypass:* Two bus replicas diverge; agent is fed different prefixes on each; a merge concatenates both while caches on each side believe their half is shared prefix. *Mitigation:* Single-writer with fenced epochs: only the current leader epoch emits commits; stale-epoch frames are discarded on arrival. A merge is a *branch point*, not a continuation — the merged context opens a new anchor chain at generation `g+1`, forcing deterministic full re-prefill of the merged region. 3 Treaty downgrade. *Bypass:* Component negotiates a "best-effort anchoring" profile at handshake, unlocking whole-context mutation on a technicality. *Mitigation:* No negotiation. One mandatory profile; capability flags are advisory. Handshake pins a protocol version; unknown version ⇒ fail-closed session rejection. There is no code path that relaxes anchor enforcement. 4 Bus-view ≠ served-view desync. *Bypass:* Middleware mutates the request in transit; the bus's Merkle root describes context X while the model actually receives Y — cache validity is checked against a stream that was never sent. *Mitigation:* End-to-end integrity: the request envelope carries the chain root; the serving layer recomputes the root over the received token stream immediately before cache lookup. Mismatch ⇒ reject, full re-prefill, security event. Transport is mutually authenticated; the root check catches anything transport misses. 5 Clock-skew causality inversion. *Bypass:* Wall-clock timestamps on anchors; skewed clock reorders apparent causality so a later edit masquerades as pre-anchor content. *Mitigation:* Ordering derives exclusively from kernel sequence numbers (logical clock). Timestamps are informational fields outside the hash and outside any decision path. Lifecycle / concurrency layer 1 TOCTOU edit race. *Bypass:* Read head anchor `h`, build suffix against it; a concurrent edit advances head to `h'`; the write lands, stitching a suffix authored for `h` onto `h'`. *Mitigation:* Optimistic concurrency with CAS: every edit request carries `base_anchor_hash`; the kernel applies it iff head == base, else rejects with the current head. All mutation funnels through the single kernel writer — no distributed write path exists. 2 Rollback cache resurrection. *Bypass:* Agent rolls back to retry, but the failed branch's suffix blocks survive and get matched by prefix similarity against the retried request. *Mitigation:* Rollback = checkout into a *fresh* generation; abandoned-branch blocks drop to refcount zero and are freed immediately (no grace), and branch ID is baked into block keys so they can't match anything again. 3 Compaction abuse. *Bypass:* Compaction/summarization necessarily rewrites the middle. Attacker spams compaction triggers to (a) force perpetual full re-prefills — cost DoS — or (b) exploit a sloppy implementation that keeps old cache mappings across the rewrite. *Mitigation:* Compaction is formally a branch point: new chain, generation bump, unconditional invalidation of all ancestor-region blocks. Compaction events are rate-limited and budget-charged to the requesting component, so spamming is self-limiting economically. 4 Counter wraparound. *Bypass:* After 2⁶⁴ generation increments, wraparound makes ancient blocks compare "current. *Mitigation:* 128-bit counters; any observed decrease or wrap condition is a fatal session error (fail-closed), not a modular comparison. Comparisons use wrap-detecting subtraction that traps on anomaly. Economic / availability layer 1 Anchor starvation and anchor flood. *Bypass:* Agent never emits anchors ⇒ suffix grows unbounded ⇒ every edit re-prefills everything (the optimization is dead). Inverse: one anchor per token ⇒ Merkle/signing overhead dominates throughput. *Mitigation:* Cadence is kernel-enforced, not agent-enforced: hard ceiling of `S_max` suffix tokens triggers a forced anchor; a floor interval suppresses flooding. Because the kernel, not the model, owns the trigger, agent behavior cannot move it. 2 Dirty-suffix churn. *Bypass:* Flood the bus with micro-edits so the suffix is perpetually dirty and re-prefill fires constantly. *Mitigation:* Edits queue to anchor boundaries and are coalesced within a fixed window into one re-prefill; per-component edit budgets (`K` edits per interval) with overage rejected. Worst-case re-prefill volume per interval is therefore a treaty constant, not attacker-controlled. 3 Prefill-latency side channel. *Bypass:* Time responses to infer whether an edit touched the prefix (TTFT delta reveals cache hit/miss ⇒ probes another tenant's or a prior session's context shape). *Mitigation:* Deterministic bucketing: scheduled prefill work is padded to fixed token-count buckets (e. , multiples of 256) plus fixed jitter drawn from a seeded per-session PRNG; hit/miss is not observable below bucket granularity. Residual risk is documented, not hand-waved. Semantics / inference layer 1 Hot-suffix injection. *Bypass:* The structural consequence of suffix-only re-prefill is that the suffix is always the freshest, highest-salience region — adversaries aim prompt injections there deliberately, knowing recency bias amplifies them. *Mitigation:* Provenance masking: every suffix span carries a kernel-assigned source tag (`user | tool | system | kernel`); tool-derived spans are wrapped in delimiters emitted *post*-tokenization by the kernel (unforgeable, since they're inserted after the tool's bytes are hashed). At decode, an attention mask bars tool-tagged spans from contributing to instruction-following heads. Deterministic mask, no classifier in the loop. 2 Anchor-metadata smuggling. *Bypass:* Anchor records carry summaries/notes; attacker plants instructions in free-text metadata fields that get rendered back into context during reconstruction from checkpoints. *Mitigation:* Frozen protobuf schema for anchor records: opaque fields reserved, no free-text slots; reconstruction renders *only* hash-referenced token-stream content. Metadata is control-plane and provably never enters the data plane. ## Closing note on residual risk Two items are mitigated to "deterministic and auditable" rather than "impossible": **3. 6** (numeric reproducibility is pinned per hardware class, not universal) and **6. 3** (latency leakage is reduced below bucket granularity, not eliminated). Everything above is enforceable by construction — hash-addressed storage, kernel-owned tokenization and cadence, signed single-writer commits, generation-fenced namespaced cache keys, CAS mutation, fail-closed versioning — such that each bypass either cannot be expressed in the protocol or collapses to a detected fault with full re-prefill as the safe fallback. If an agent edits its context (e. , rewrites a memory block, reorders sections, injects new tool results), naive systems invalidate the whole cache. The design goal: structure the context as an append-mostly log with immutable prefix segments ("semantic anchors") and a mutable suffix, so edits only touch the suffix and only the suffix gets re-prefilled. **Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: Checkpoints that mark stable semantic boundaries — e. , after each completed task step, tool call batch, or reasoning segment — where the content up to that anchor is frozen/hashed/committed. Like git commits on a bus. **Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty**: A protocol/treaty between components (the Ghost runtime? the AOS kernel? the model server? ) governing how context mutations are published to a bus, versioned like git commits, with rules about what can be mutated, when anchors are created, and how cache invalidation propagates. Protocol/treaty-level attacks:** **Treaty downgrade**: Malicious component negotiates a weaker mode ("best-effort anchoring") enabling whole-context mutation. - Mitigation: No negotiation: single mandatory profile; capability flags are advisory-only; kernel rejects sessions lacking the anchor profile. 72025613b7e4c4d6.text: # Red-Team: Semantic-Anchor Checkpoint Reuse (Suffix-Only Re-Prefill) ## Framing: the oracle and the trap Correctness has exactly one oracle: **a reuse-path forward pass must be numerically identical to a cold full prefill over the same rendered token stream. ** Every bypass below is a way to break that identity while making the validator believe it held. The trap in the name: the moment "semantic" enters the *acceptance predicate* (embedding similarity, LLM-judged equivalence, paraphrase tolerance), you lose. Transformers are not invariant to token perturbation — one changed token invalidates all downstream attention. Anchors may sit at *semantically meaningful boundaries*, but acceptance must be **byte/token-exact**. That single rule kills the largest attack family. ## Invariants (every mitigation enforces one of these) - **I1 Token-exactness:** KV for span `[0,k)` is reusable iff `token_ids[0:k]` are element-wise identical to the IDs that produced it, under identical `(model_rev, tokenizer_rev, rope_cfg, kv_dtype, kernel_regime)`. - **I2 Position continuity:** suffix prefill starts at `pos = k`; positional config identical. - **I3 Render-boundary authority:** all equality decisions on the fully rendered stream (post pointer-resolution, post template, post truncation). No upper layer grants reuse. - **I4 Validator independence:** reuse length is computed by the validator from hashes over live data; editors, logs, and memlang claims are advisory. - **I5 Whole-block atomicity:** reuse granularity = whole KV block; any changed token kills its block and all successors. - **I6 Lineage scoping:** reuse only along the ancestor path of the current context version in the version DAG. - **I7 No fuzzy path:** the accept predicate is pure equality on token IDs + binding metadata. Nothing else exists in the code path. ## Family 1 — Forge the anchor (make false equality hold) Weak-digest collision. ** Segment hashes over truncated digests (CRC32, 32-bit truncations) let crafted replacement content collide with the original, reusing KV computed over different tokens. → **Mitigation:** BLAKE3/SHA-256 over `tokenizer_ver ‖ token_ids(span) ‖ len(span)` plus binding tuple. On any hit, re-verify by comparing raw token IDs before assembly. Verification is O(span); prefill is O(span · layers · d_model) — always cheaper. Tokenizer/model revision skew. ** Same bytes, new tokenizer ⇒ different token IDs; byte-level hashes match, KV is for a different sequence. → **Mitigation:** hash token IDs, never bytes (bytes allowed only as fast pre-filter). Bind `model_rev` and `tokenizer_rev` into the segment key. Mismatch ⇒ miss, never fuzzy-match. Structural-token spoofing. ** Untrusted content contains `<|im_end|>`-class strings, bending segmentation to create fake anchor alignments or hide edits in "boilerplate" regions. → **Mitigation:** reserved tokens are emitted *only* by the trusted template renderer; the renderer rejects any occurrence of reserved token strings inside content fields. Anchors are minted exclusively at template-emitted boundaries; content-internal candidates are ignored. Coordinate aliasing in memlang. ** Duplicate/alias coordinates resolve to unequal spans; the differ compares alias-to-alias and masks a change. → **Mitigation:** closed coordinate namespace — coordinates are minted only by the render pass as `(render_pass_id, span_id)`; no plugin/user alias creation. Comparison is on canonical span IDs only. Coordinates are indexes, not evidence. Forged checkpoint log. ** Compromised plugin appends a checkpoint claiming "append-only" over what was a rewrite. → **Mitigation:** checkpoints are Merkle-chained: each commits `H(prev_ckpt ‖ rendered_root)`, root = Merkle over segment hashes. Validator recomputes the root from the live stream every turn; forged entries fail root recomputation. Log accelerates multi-hop reuse; live diff is truth. ## Family 2 — Hide the change (make true inequality invisible) Editor lies about the change point. ** Buggy or malicious diff reports "suffix-only" while an edit landed mid-context. → **Mitigation:** validator ignores the claim entirely. It hashes every segment of the incoming context and computes the first mismatch itself: `reuse_segs = LCP(new_seg_hashes, prev_seg_hashes)`. Inside the first mismatching segment, a direct token-array scan finds the exact first differing token. Producer claims are advisory, always. Indirect-reference mutation. ** Context text holds a pointer ("see slot M7"); text is unchanged, resolved content changed. Diffing at the pointer layer sees nothing. → **Mitigation:** I3, absolutely: diff/hash/validate only the post-resolution rendered stream. Pointer-layer equality grants zero reuse. "No reuse above the render boundary" is a hard architectural rule. Out-of-band raw-store write. ** Something edits the token store directly, bypassing the memlang API; coordinates and committed roots go stale. → **Mitigation:** raw store is immutable; all writes through the transactional context API. Every validation recomputes the rendered root and compares to the committed root; mismatch ⇒ epoch bump ⇒ full re-prefill. Coarse anchors cost reuse efficiency at worst, never correctness. Post-anchor truncation. ** Middle-out truncation drops tokens after anchors were computed; stale KV for dropped tokens is still attended to. → **Mitigation:** anchoring runs strictly after final truncation; any truncation event bumps the epoch ⇒ zero reuse across it. Truncation is rare; full re-prefill is the cheap deterministic answer. ## Family 3 — Corrupt the geometry Partial-block aliasing. ** Reuse boundary falls mid-block; naive code rounds and reuses a partially-valid block. → **Mitigation:** I5 as executable assertions: `invalid_from_block = first_diff // BLOCK`; assert `first_reused_block_end ≤ first_diff`; assert `blocks[blk-1]. end_pos == blk·BLOCK − 1` (contiguity). Unit-test invariants, not conventions. Position/RoPE forgery or drift. ** Suffix prefilled at pos 0 instead of k; or rope config (scaling, base) changed since the cached blocks were written. → **Mitigation:** blocks carry `rope_cfg_hash` and `base_position_offset`; validator asserts `suffix_start_pos == last_reused_block. end_pos + 1` and config-hash equality. Evicting caches are simply ineligible. Branch/rollback confusion. ** Retry/branch rewinds to checkpoint T₁ then diverges; latest-keyed cache hands back sibling-branch segments. → **Mitigation:** version DAG. Cache keyed by `(lineage_id, ckpt_seq)`; child lineage id = `H(parent_lineage ‖ branch_point ‖ nonce)`. Worst-case validator work is O(context_len) hashes — bounded and orders of magnitude below prefill. Timing side channel. ** Early-exit hashing reveals where edits landed (edit-structure disclosure). → **Mitigation:** validator always performs the full hash pass over all segments regardless of early match; bucket the reuse-decision latency. Constant-shape work, deterministically. Sampler-state carryover. ** Decode-side: repetition windows, n-gram bans, last-logits state reused across the edit boundary influence generation with tokens no longer present. → **Mitigation:** sampler state is derived solely from the post-edit visible context, rebuilt at the reuse boundary. No cross-boundary sampler state survives. ## Enforcement kernel (what actually runs) stream = render(ctx_new)                      # post-resolution, post-template, post-truncation = committed_root: bump_epoch(); full_prefill()          # B8 if epoch_changed(prev, cur):      bump_epoch(); full_prefill()          # B2,B10,B12 segs = segment(stream)                        # template boundaries only             # B3 h    = [H(tok_ver ‖ ids(s) ‖ len(s)) for s in segs] j    = LCP(h, prev. h)                         # validator-computed                   # B5,B6 d    = first_differing_token(segs[j], prev. segs[j])   # exact scan, if j < len blk  = d // BLOCK assert blocks[0. bindings == BINDINGS_NOW        # model,tok,rope,dtype,regime,lineage  # B1,B12,B13,B15 assert blocks[blk-1]. end_pos == blk*BLOCK - 1                                                 # B11 kv = blocks[0. blk]; prefill(stream[blk*BLOCK :], start_pos = blk*BLOCK)                      # I2,I5 version); commit seg_hashes Two kill-switch rules dominate: **(a)** acceptance is token-exact equality or nothing (I7 — dead-code-eliminate every fuzzy path, then fuzz the accept function to prove none remains); **(b)** the reuse length is always validator-computed from live data (I4 — no input from editors, logs, or the coordinate layer is ever load-bearing). ## Ground-truth tests (lock these in CI) - **Differential oracle:** reuse-path logits ≡ cold-full-prefill logits, bitwise, under deterministic kernels. This single test detects every bypass above. - **Mutation property test:** flip any token anywhere; assert reuse length drops to exactly `floor(diff/BLOCK)·BLOCK`. - **Fault injection:** forged checkpoints (B5), lying diffs (B6), aliased coordinates (B4), mid-validate edits (B16) — assert output equals the full-prefill baseline in all cases. - **Concurrency stress:** randomized interleaved edits/requests; assert the pin invariant never breaks. Every bypass resolves to attempting to smuggle a non-equality past one of those gates; every mitigation is the gate, asserted, not requested. Verification and inference run on different objects. 2):** Cache key IS the verkle root over the exact token-id sequence at anchor time. Stored alongside cached KV: the root it was computed from. " They want a red-team analysis: enumerate bypass attempts and deterministic mitigations for each. They want concrete, exact, grounded answers. These anchors are hash-chained. **Context edit re-prefill only the new suffix**: When an edit occurs to the agent's context (e. , a tool result is appended, or an earlier segment is revised), instead of re-prefilling (re-encoding/re-processing) the entire context into the model, the system only processes the *new suffix* — the delta since the last anchor. So the architecture: context = sequence of segments. Each segment has provenance metadata (source, signature/hash, timestamp, anchor index). Checkpoints are verkle roots over the segment set. On edit, the system computes a new root, produces a witness showing exactly which leaf indices differ from the previous root, and re-prefills only those leaves' content plus the cached prefix's KV state. Deterministic mitigation: Every checkpoint header includes monotonically increasing sequence number and a forward-linked hash: root_k commits to H(root_{k−1} || seq_k || timestamp_bucket). Gate accepts only root_k where seq_k == local_seq + 1 and H-chain verifies back to genesis pinned in the gate's immutable config. Timestamp bucketing (e. , 30s buckets) with rejection of roots whose bucket < max_seen_bucket − 1 bounds rollback even against a compromised sequencer. Additionally, revocations/grants are recorded as leaves in the tree itself, so rolling back the tree rolls back the revocation — hence the seq/bucket binding is the load-bearing control; make revocation entries also mirrored in an append-only log outside the tree whose head is checked (dual-commitment: tree root AND log head must both advance together; mismatch ⇒ halt). Fork / equivocation (two valid chains)** Attack: Compromised or malicious chain-builder emits two divergent checkpoint sequences, both internally consistent, feeding different views to different components (verifier sees chain A, inference sees chain B) — split-view. Or within one component, presenting different roots at different times to launder a mutation through a "legitimate" re-anchor. Deterministic mitigation: Single-writer discipline enforced by hardware-backed monotonic counter (TPM/secure-element NV counter incremented per checkpoint; roots are signed along with counter value; verifier rejects any root whose counter ≤ max observed, and rejects two roots sharing a counter value — equivocation is then detectable and fatal: on detection, gate enters fail-closed halt, requires out-of-band operator reset). Where hardware counters aren't available: threshold signatures (2-of-3 independent signers on each root) make undetected forks require compromising 2 signers — still deterministic in the sense that the check is binary. Also gossip/audit: every emitted root is written to an append-only WAL fsynced before use; recovery replays WAL; divergence between WAL and live state = halt. Anchor-placement gaming (timing attacks on anchoring)** (a) **Anchor-starvation DoS**: attacker floods edits so that no stable anchor ever forms, forcing either perpetual full re-prefill (cost attack) or indefinite deferral of commitment (freshness attack — context runs long stretches uncommitted, expanding the window for B1/B5-style tricks). (b) **Anchor-hugging concealment**: attacker times a mutation immediately AFTER an anchor is taken, so the mutated segment sits deep inside the "new suffix" and rides through multiple turns under suffix-only prefill, never individually committed until the next anchor — maximizing the blast radius of any single forged suffix and delaying detection. Deterministic mitigations: Anchoring is forced by budget, not by stability heuristics: hard rule — a checkpoint MUST occur at least every N tokens of suffix growth (N fixed, e. , 4096) and at most M seconds (M fixed); violation = gate halts the session (fail-closed), not "try again later. " Anchor points are chosen deterministically from the stream: anchor whenever suffix length hits N, or at tier-boundary transitions, whichever first — no discretionary timing for anyone to game. For (b): suffix segments carry a TTL: any segment older than one anchor interval without inclusion in a committed root is evicted from the prefill entirely (deterministic eviction, not flagging) — so concealed mutations self-destruct rather than linger. And every prefill must reference the latest committed root; prefilling against a suffix that extends > N tokens beyond the last root is rejected outright. Provenance-spoofing at the gate (confused deputy)** Attack: The gate trusts metadata fields (source_id, tier, signature) delivered alongside content. Bypasses: (a) downgrade attack — strip a tool response's wrapper so it arrives looking like a user message (tier escalation from 3→2? actually user is lower than tool? depends; the real target is making untrusted content look like tier 0/1); (b) signature stripping/re-attachment — take a legitimately signed benign payload, swap the body, keep the signature envelope if the signature covers metadata but not body (signing-scope bug); (c) key-confusion — cross-protocol: use a key certified for purpose X (e. , logging signer) in the provenance role because the gate doesn't check key-usage attributes; (d) replay of a signed provenance record onto different content (signature covers content hash, but attacker finds two contents colliding in the hash — only viable if hash is weak; or replays the whole record+content pair in a different session where it wasn't intended); (e) SSRF-style: gate fetches verification material (trust roots, revocation lists) from URLs supplied inside the message. Deterministic mitigations: (a) tier is assigned by the transport listener, never read from payload: inbound socket/channel identity (mTLS client cert, unix peer creds, namespace) maps 1:1 to tier via static config table; payload-declared tier is ignored unconditionally. (b) Signature scope is fixed by schema: sig covers H(tier || source_id || seq || content_hash || prev_record_hash); verification recomputes over exactly these fields extracted post-parse of the canonical form; any extra/missing field = reject. (c) Keys carry mandatory purpose OIDs/extensions; gate pins allowed key fingerprints per role — no dynamic trust discovery. (e) No network fetches during verification: trust anchors and revocation state are compiled into the gate image, updated only via the same signed checkpoint channel (and revocation via B5's dual log). All five are closed-form checks. KV-cache desync / speculative-prefix poisoning** Attack: The optimization assumes cached KV states correspond exactly to the committed prefix. Bypasses: (a) quantization drift — cache stored in fp8/int4, recomputation path uses bf16; attacker engineers conditions where the degraded cache materially shifts behavior (e. , sensitive tokens whose activations flip under quantization), while hashes match because hashing is over text, not activations; (b) cache-slot reuse across sessions with partial invalidation bugs (evict-by-LRU touches shared pages; copy-on-write prefix trees leave stale branches); (c) deliberate GPU memory pressure induced by attacker-controlled long suffixes to trigger cache eviction + silent fallback to a wrong-length prefix (off-by-one on token boundaries — tokenizer boundary effects: cached prefix ends mid-token-pair; suffix starts with a continuation byte that merges differently when concatenated than when encoded standalone — the classic "token healing" problem: encode(prefix)+encode(suffix) ≠ encode(prefix||suffix)). Deterministic mitigations: (a) cache fidelity is part of the commitment: store H(config || dtype || kernel_version || token_ids) with the cache entry; gate pins exact dtype/kernel; any mismatch = full recompute (deterministic fallback). Better: hash the token-id sequence, not text. (b) Cache entries are immutable and copy-on-write at segment granularity; a slot is either exactly reusable (root match) or discarded — no partial reuse path exists in the code; enforce by construction: reuse decision is `stored_root == current_root` single comparison. (c) Token-boundary rule: suffix encoding always begins at a segment boundary that was itself a token boundary at anchor time; the anchor procedure records the tokenizer's absolute token offset; suffix decode resumes from that offset with the constraint that the first suffix token must not be a merge-continuation of the last prefix token — if the raw bytes would merge, the runtime inserts the already-committed tokenization of the boundary (store the exact token ids at anchor time; suffix prefill consumes stored ids, never re-tokenizes the junction). Concretely: at anchor, freeze `token_ids[0. k]`; suffix is tokenized as `tokenize(bytes[k:])` but with a guard: if `tokenize(bytes[k-δ:k+ε])` differs from the frozen tail, splice using frozen ids — deterministic splice rule, checked by comparing `H(frozen_tail_ids)` at every prefill. Verkle-specific: sparse-tree / empty-subtree exploits** Attack: (a) Injecting massive numbers of empty/degenerate leaves to bloat witness size or trigger slow paths (DoS via proof-size blowup — verkle multiproofs are compact normally, but adversarial key distributions can degrade IPA/KZG multiproof performance); (b) exploiting the sparse "absence proof": proving a leaf does NOT exist to convince a component that a safety filter leaf is absent (e. , "prove there's no revocation at this index") — absence proofs are legitimate, but attacker flips usage: presents absence-of-malware-scan-record as evidence scanning isn't required; (c) commitment to a subtree replaced by direct leaf injection at a depth the verifier doesn't re-derive (stem/extension-node confusion in verkle trie structures — inserting at stem level vs leaf level inconsistently). Deterministic mitigations: (a) Fixed tree arity and fixed depth with padding rules defined upfront: every leaf slot exists in the commitment whether populated or not (dense indexing by segment ordinal, not sparse keying) — witness size becomes O(1)-bounded per proof regardless of content; no sparse-path performance cliff. (b) Absence claims are never actionable: the gate's policy checks are positive-presence checks only ("revocation record for key K must exist and say revoked-or-not"); missing record = fail-closed default-deny. Encode the rule: every permission consulted must resolve to an existing leaf; lookup miss ⇒ deny. (c) Depth/stem derivation is a pure function H(domain_tag || leaf_index) with domain tags per level; verifier recomputes stems independently and rejects any proof element whose derived stem mismatches its claimed position — position is never taken from the proof, always recomputed. Edit-semantics laundering (diff-descriptor lying)** Attack: The system computes "only the new suffix" from a diff descriptor (which leaf indices changed). Attacker compromises or spoofs the diff computation to declare a smaller change-set than actual: root updates correctly (so chain stays consistent), but the re-prefill only ingests the declared subset — the remaining mutated segments enter inference via stale cache (ties to B1) or are silently skipped. Variant: declare a change as "append-only" when it's actually a modify-in-place; append-only edits skip re-validation of touched interior nodes. Deterministic mitigation: Never trust a diff descriptor. Compute the change-set deterministically from the two roots themselves: walk both trees level by level comparing child commitments; descend only where commitments differ; the differing leaf set is derived, not declared. Cost is bounded (verkle gives shallow descent). Then require: re-prefill set == derived differing set exactly (bitwise equality of index sets); if the declared set ⊂ derived set ⇒ halt and mark the chain-builder hostile (this is tamper-evidence, escalate). Append-only claims are validated by checking derived set == {k. n} contiguous tail; otherwise the "append" is rejected and treated as general edit requiring full interior re-validation. Cross-session / cross-agent contamination** Attack: Shared prefix caches across agents/sessions: agent A's committed prefix (containing attacker-influenced content A was tricked into accepting) is reused as a warm-start for agent B with different privileges — B inherits A's poisoned context while B's own provenance gate never saw those segments. The root matches because the cache is keyed by content root alone, ignoring session identity. Equality requires all four; content-root equality alone never suffices. Genesis/trust-bootstrap attack** Attack: Poison the very first anchor: if genesis root or the initial trust config (allowed signers, sentinel definitions, tier table) is supplied at runtime or fetched, attacker substitutes their own genesis — everything downstream verifies perfectly against the wrong root of trust. Variants: supply-chain compromise of the gate binary itself (mitigation moves out of scope of the protocol but must be stated), TOFU (trust-on-first-use) interception on first connection. Deterministic mitigation: Genesis root, signer set, sentinel byte sequences, tier table, and gate code measurement are pinned in read-only storage / measured boot (TPM attestation or signed firmware); the gate refuses to initialize unless measured values match pinned expectations; no runtime overrides exist — no API, no env var, no file that can change them (enforced by mounting config read-only + verifying at every startup, not just first). TOFU is banned: first-use failures are halts, not learning opportunities. Sentinel/delimiter forging via encoding tricks** Attack: The data fences from B2 rely on sentinel byte sequences. Attacker crafts content that, after the pipeline's transformations (case folding, entity decoding, template expansion, second-pass rendering in the UI, log-and-replay, summarization round-trips), yields the sentinel bytes — escaping the fence at a later stage than the ingestion-time scan. Classic second-order injection: safe at intake, dangerous after transformation T. Deterministic mitigation: The ingestion scan operates on the FINAL bytes that will enter the prefill, computed after ALL transformations — i. , transformations happen first, then canonicalization C(), then sentinel scan, then hashing, then storage; prefill consumes the scanned bytes. Rule: no transformation may occur after the scan point; any component needing transformed content must re-submit it through the gate as a new segment (which re-runs the full pipeline). Scan is exact byte matching for the complete sentinel set including all escape-encoded forms the runtime itself could emit; on hit: reject (not escape) — rejection is simpler to prove correct than escaping. Summarization/compression outputs are new untrusted segments (tier of their source, marked derived=true) and re-enter through the gate. Anchor-grinding via semantic-anchor definition** If "semantic anchor" involves any notion of embedding similarity or model-judged stability, attacker games the judge: craft near-duplicate content that flutters around the similarity threshold to manipulate when anchors fire (feeding B7), or craft content that forces premature anchoring mid-instruction, splitting a coherent directive across an anchor so the suffix-only prefill processes a fragment lacking its governing antecedent (fragmentation attack — the model sees "…do X" in suffix with the qualifying conditions stranded pre-anchor and now served from cache in a way the attacker can no longer influence but ALSO the fragment gets interpreted standalone). Deterministic mitigation: Remove judgment from anchor selection entirely — anchors are purely positional/counters (every N tokens, tier boundaries, tool-call boundaries), never semantic-similarity-triggered. If fragmentation is a concern, add the deterministic rule: a suffix may not begin mid-document-segment; pending segments are buffered until a segment boundary coincides with the anchor cadence (bounded delay by construction since segments have max length L_max < N). Interpretation risk of fragments is then bounded to whole segments, and whole segments carry their tier/fence protection from B2/B14. Resource-exhaustion on the gate itself** Attack: The gate is the chokepoint; attacker sends pathological inputs to make verification slow/unavailable, then exploits timeout-fail-open behavior (many systems default to allowing on verifier timeout to preserve liveness): giant multiproofs, deeply nested canonical structures causing quadratic parsing, decompression bombs inside tool payloads (gate must decompress to scan sentinels), regex-based checks with catastrophic backtracking. Deterministic mitigations: Hard resource ceilings enforced before any parsing: max bytes, max nesting depth, max proof elements, fixed-size buffers, no regex anywhere in the gate (byte-exact comparisons and linear scans only), streaming decompression with output cap (reject at cap, don't truncate), and — the critical one — **fail-closed on all timeouts**: verification timeout ⇒ segment rejected and session flagged; liveness is preserved by rejecting, not by admitting. Every limit is a constant in the pinned config (B13). Memory allocation is pre-computed from declared sizes with declared-vs-actual consistency checks (declared length must equal actual consumed bytes exactly). Re-prefill ordering / attention-position forgery** Attack: Within the suffix, attacker influences the ORDER of assembled segments (multiple tool results arriving concurrently; race conditions in the assembler) so that their content occupies positions with maximal recency/proximity to the generation point, crowding out the trusted trailer or displacing a competing benign tool result that would have contradicted them. Not a cryptographic break — a scheduling attack on assembly. Position of the trusted trailer is fixed at the terminal index by construction (B2). No component may reorder after assembly; the assembled byte string is hashed and that hash is what the checkpoint commits to — so any post-assembly touch invalidates the root. Hash-function / commitment downgrade** Attack: Negotiate or degrade the hash/commitment parameters: MD5/SHA1 acceptance via legacy flags, shortened truncations ("128-bit is enough"), alternative commitment schemes with weaker binding injected via version negotiation, or algorithm-substitution attacks (rogue-but-valid-looking parameters in a signed update). Deterministic mitigation: Algorithm identifiers removed from the wire entirely — the gate speaks exactly one suite, hardcoded in pinned config; no negotiation exists (absence of a mechanism is the strongest mitigation); version upgrades are new gate binaries subject to B13 measurement. Truncation forbidden: full-length digests compared with constant-time memcmp; any length mismatch = reject. Also worth covering: Side-channel on the "suffix-only" optimization itself** Attack: The optimization leaks which parts were re-prefilled via timing/power/cache-side-channels; attacker infers context contents incrementally across turns (each turn reveals a bit about what changed). In multi-tenant settings, cross-request cache-timing on shared accelerators leaks suffix lengths/content classes. Deterministic mitigation: Full mitigation is expensive; deterministic partial: pad every re-prefill to fixed bucket sizes (next power-of-two token count) and constant-time-ish batching (fixed batch composition windows) — this converts leakage to coarse buckets only; document residual risk honestly. If the threat model includes physical co-tenancy, the deterministic answer is: no shared accelerators across trust domains, period (allocation rule, not a crypto fix). Update-channel compromise for the chain software itself** Signed-update substitution: attacker doesn't break the protocol, they ship a "patched" gate/chain-builder that subtly mis-implements one check above (e. , skips the derived-vs-declared diff comparison in B11). Deterministic mitigation: reproducible builds, signed binaries measured at boot (B13), dual-vendor signing, and canary assertions: embedded self-tests at startup that feed known attack vectors (crafted proofs from B3, malleable serializations from B4) through the gate and require rejection — a deterministic test-vector battery executed on every cold start; failure = refuse service. That's comprehensive. Now organize the answer. Format considerations: This is a deep technical red-team request. The user wants enumeration + deterministic mitigation per item, concrete and exact. A structured list format with headers per attack, mechanics, and mitigation is right. Should be thorough but not bloated — each item tight. Use numbered attacks with names, "Mechanics" and "Mitigation" sub-parts. Maybe group by layer: (I) commitment-layer attacks (verkle/witness/root), (II) cache/prefill-layer attacks, (III) content/admission-layer attacks (provenance gate, sentinels, tiers), (IV) lifecycle/liveness attacks (anchors, rollback, forks, DoS), (V) platform/bootstrap attacks. That grouping aids navigation. Length: this deserves a long answer given "enumerate . be concrete, exact" — but keep each item crisp. Aim for maybe 20 items grouped, each ~4-8 lines. Add a short preamble defining the invariant being defended and assumptions, and a short closing on the load-bearing invariants (the few checks everything reduces to). Avoid fluff per instructions. Proof shows a value at index i by opening the polynomial at ζ_i. Small proofs (~constant size) vs Merkle's log(n) sibling hashes. - Trusted setup: KZG needs structured reference string; toxic waste τ allows forging openings (equivocation) — yes, knowing τ lets you create a commitment that opens to arbitrary values. Mitigations: multi-party ceremony, or IPA-based verkle (no trusted setup) — correct. - Index binding: standard practice derives evaluation points deterministically; binding index into Fiat-Shamir prevents replaying openings across positions — correct. - Subgroup checks: standard for BLS curves — correct. - Multiproofs: KZG multiproof via quotient polynomial / IPA-based multiproofs (Denton's approach) — proof size grows slowly; adversarial inputs mostly affect prover time, but malformed proof handling matters — my mitigation (strict canonical format, size caps) stands. - Token healing / boundary effects: real phenomenon (e. , in guidance/transformers token healing literature) — encode(A)+encode(B) ≠ encode(A+B) at junctions — correct and important here. - JCS RFC 8785 for JSON canonicalization — correct. - Fail-closed timeouts — correct stance. - TPM NV counters / monotonic counters — correct. - mTLS channel-binding for tier assignment — correct approach. Mitigation: the unit of verification must be the final token-id sequence; hash the token ids, commit to token ids, and the prefill consumes exactly the committed id array — render/template steps must occur BEFORE commitment, inside the gated pipeline. This overlaps B14/B4 but is distinct enough (it's about committing to tokens, not bytes) and is arguably THE core invariant. I'll fold it prominently — maybe make it its own item early since it's foundational: "commit to token ids, not source bytes. 7f17ac8fd953ea04.text: # Red-Team: Semantic-Anchored Suffix-Only Re-Prefill ## Assumed mechanism (pinned so mitigations are exact) Context is a token-ID stream. Anchors are sidecar records `{seq, offset a, H = SHA256(token_ids[0:a]), kv_block_refs, model_rev, tokenizer_ver, template_ver, pos_cfg}` chained by HMAC. An edit is valid iff it targets offset ≥ last sealed anchor; then prefix KV is reused and only `tokens[a:len]` is prefilled. Universal rule: **any check fails ⇒ discard chain from that point, full re-prefill, re-seal genesis. Fail closed, never best-effort reuse. ## Class A — Stale-reuse correctness bypasses (wrong KV attached) Truncated-hash collision. ** 64-bit anchor hash → birthday forge at ~2³² edits. → Full SHA-256 over token IDs; no truncation anywhere. Tokenizer/template drift. ** Identical string, different token IDs or chat-template rendering → string hash passes, KV mismatches. → Hash token IDs, never text; bind `tokenizer_ver`, vocab fingerprint, `template_hash` into the anchor key; mismatch ⇒ invalidate. Weight/quant hot-swap under same model name. → `model_rev + dtype + quant_config` in key; mismatch ⇒ global chain invalidation. Length-dependent positional scaling (dynamic NTK/YaRN). ** Changing suffix length changes position mapping for the *entire* sequence — prefix KV is invalid despite identical tokens. Most subtle failure here. → Ban length-dependent positional schemes in the burn pipeline; pin static RoPE config; startup property test: `pos_map(L)[0:m] == pos_map(L')[0:m]` for sampled L, L′. Sliding-window / sink eviction. ** Engine silently evicted blocks inside the anchored span; "reuse" attaches garbage. → Either forbid windowed-attention models in this pipeline or pin anchored blocks against eviction; engine must emit eviction events; any eviction touching `[0,a)` ⇒ deterministically drop anchors above it. Shared radix-tree contamination. ** Another request mutates shared prefix blocks via refcount/COW bug. Batched-kernel nondeterminism ("anchor rot"). ** Recomputed suffix KV ≠ single-pass KV; drift compounds across edits. → Prefer deterministic kernels; regardless, forced full re-prefill every N=32 edits to resync; log drift metric. Seam corruption with no probe. ** Bitrot or buggy block store; hash was correct at write time, blocks since corrupted. → At seal, store `h_seam = SHA256(hidden_state[last_prefix_token])`. On reuse, recompute forward over the final 16 prefix tokens against cached KV and require cosine ≥ 0. 999 to stored seam vector; fail ⇒ invalidate upstream. ## Class B — Invariant violations ("only suffix" silently false, burn explodes) Edits below the seal. ** Insertion/deletion at offset < last anchor forces fallback; repeated early edits = full re-prefill every time while system still reports "anchored. → Edit API is only `apply_edit(anchor_seq, new_suffix)`; server rejects any op referencing offset < last sealed offset with `ERR_BELOW_SEAL`; caller must explicitly re-anchor (one paid full prefill, booked to a visible budget line). ** Volatile spans (tool noise) never sealable → suffix grows unbounded → giant compaction prefill; or seals fire constantly, each costing full prefill. → Deterministic sealer: seal at min(K=2048 tokens, tool-commit boundary); volatile spans hard-capped at V=1024 tokens then mandatory seal. Policy is code, zero LLM discretion. Hidden prefix mutation via intel rotation. ** Rotating "frontier intel" injected into the system region kills every anchor downstream. → System region is anchor level 0; rotations create a new chain branch and may only occur at phase boundaries, each booked as an explicit full-prefill cost. Text-space diffs + retokenization. ** Whitespace/Unicode shifts move boundaries below the anchor while string hash claims "unchanged. → Token-space edits only; NFC-normalize at ingest; assert token-ID equality for claimed-unchanged regions, else fail closed. Tool replay rebuild. ** Restore re-calls tools to reconstruct context; nondeterministic outputs ≠ anchored hash, discovered after prefill spend. → Never rebuild by replay; persist verbatim payloads keyed by anchor; replay only for flags-asserted idempotent reads; hash-verify restored payload before prefill. ** Mid-context summarization is a hidden full rewrite that voids the invariant silently. → Compaction emits `CHAIN_RESET`, costs exactly one full re-prefill, permitted only at task-phase boundaries, forbidden during a burn sprint. ## Class C — Content-adversarial attacks on the anchoring logic In-band anchor forgery. ** Model/tool output emits fake `<<ANCHOR …>>` markers; parser mis-seals at attacker-chosen offset. → Anchors exist only in the HMAC-signed sidecar; marker grammar is reserved; any marker-shaped sequence in model/tool output fails that tool call at ingest — never parsed. ** Content hashed pre-clean; a post-hash cleaner (homoglyph folding, control-char strip) mutates tokens; reuse check passes on the stale hash. → Hash strictly after final normalization, immediately before KV write; content frozen post-hash; any post-hash transform ⇒ new anchor required. Anchor-ID replay/squatting. ** Captured `(anchor_id, hash, block_refs)` replayed into a later session. → `anchor_id = HMAC(session_key, seq ‖ content_hash)`; block refs carry epoch; epoch mismatch ⇒ reject. Provisional-anchor poisoning. ** Seal on unvalidated content, promote later without rehash; poison persists across many cheap edits. No skip path. ** Agent-side tooling writes the sidecar directly. → HMAC chain (`mac_i = HMAC(k_session, mac_{i-1} ‖ seq ‖ offset ‖ H ‖ model_rev ‖ tok_ver ‖ tmpl_ver ‖ pos_cfg)`); store read-only to agent runtime; chain break ⇒ full re-prefill. Concurrent append during seal. ** Stream appends while seal hashes a snapshot → seal covers fewer tokens than KV holds. → Single-writer per context via monotonic version counter; seal is CAS(version); concurrent mutation aborts seal, retries at next boundary. ## Class D — Burn-economics and pipeline attacks Suffix-inflation DoS. ** Every turn appends max-size tool dumps; per-edit cost stays linear in suffix; total burn O(n²) despite anchoring. → Hard suffix cap S_max=4096 tokens/edit; overflow ⇒ truncate with `[TRUNCATED n]` sentinel + scheduled compaction; per-edit suffix metered. Telemetry discount gaming. ** Cheap suffix prefill undercounts context cost; budget enforcer sees headroom and permits runaway loops. → Ledger: `cost = 1. 0 × suffix_tokens + 0. 05 × prefix_hit_tokens`, append-only; circuit breaker trips on ledger totals (B_max/task), never on live gauges. Cold-resume assumes warm KV. ** Node dies; manifest restored, cache gone; code path skips prefill → empty context. → Manifest carries `kv_resident` per anchor; preflight asserts resident blocks ≥ manifest count, else deterministic cold full prefill. Parallel-scout races. ** Shared anchor namespace; one scout's GC reclaims blocks another holds. → Per-scout namespaces; refcounted global allocator; leased blocks with deterministic reclaim order; generation counters make double-free impossible. Cross-model routing. ** Mid-task call routed to a cheaper model reuses model-A anchors. → Model identity in anchor key; cross-model reuse refused; per-model chains. Wall-clock decisions. ** Time-based seal/evict logic diverges across nodes → split-brain anchor state. → Logical clock (edit sequence number) only; wall time for telemetry exclusively. ## Minimum CI suite (blocks regression of every mitigation above) Fuzz: `decode(prefix ∥ suffix) == decode(context)` and `kv_len(prefix) == offset` (kills B1/A-off-by-one; half-open intervals `[0,a)` / `[a,len)` mandated). Positional stability property test (A4). Eviction-event → anchor-drop unit test (A5). COW/gen-counter contention test with two writers (A6, D4). Marker-injection corpus: forged anchors in tool output must fail ingest (C1). Kill -9 mid-sprint, resume: assert cold-path prefill fired (D3). Ledger replay: 10k-edit trace reproduces identical cost series (D2, D6). Net effect: every bypass terminates in one of two deterministic outcomes — reject-and-fail-closed to full re-prefill, or bounded-cost fallback with the spend booked visibly. Nothing degrades silently. The user is asking about a hard problem in agent systems: "semantic-anchor checkpoints so an agent's context edit re-prefills only the new suffix, in the frontier-scout burn pipeline. " They want a red-team exercise: enumerate bypass attempts and deterministic mitigations for each. Concrete, exact, grounded. Let me parse the domain first. This appears to be about: **Semantic-anchor checkpoints**: A mechanism where an agent's context (conversation history / working memory) is checkpointed at "semantic anchors" — points where meaning is stable, e. , after tool call results are committed, after a plan step completes. The idea: when an edit happens to the context (e. , compaction, summarization, truncation, injection of new system content), instead of re-prefilling/re-encoding the entire context from scratch (expensive), you only re-prefill the *new suffix* — the delta since the last anchor. **Re-prefill only the new suffix**: This is a KV-cache-friendly incremental prefill strategy. In LLM serving, if you have a cached prefix (KV cache) and you append tokens, you only need to compute KV for the appended suffix. But if the context is *edited* mid-stream (tokens inserted/removed/rewritten before the end), naive systems invalidate the whole cache and re-prefill everything — expensive. Semantic-anchor checkpoints let you say: "everything up to anchor N is frozen and hash-stable; edits only touch [anchor N+1 . end], so we reuse the KV cache for prefix ≤ N and recompute only the suffix. **Frontier-scout burn pipeline**: This sounds like a specific pipeline name — possibly from a multi-agent research/scouting setup where "scout" agents burn through frontier contexts (expensive long-context calls) and there's a budget ("burn") for compute. The pipeline presumably: scout agent explores, context gets edited frequently (pruning, injecting findings), and each edit triggers re-prefill. The semantic-anchor checkpointing is meant to make edits cheap by anchoring stable prefixes. So the engineering claim being red-teamed: **"With semantic-anchor checkpoints, any context edit causes re-prefill of only the new suffix; the anchored prefix's KV cache is reused. An **anchor** `a_i` is a token offset carrying: - a chained hash `H_i = BLAKE3(H_{i-1} ‖ seg_i)` over segment `(a_{i-1}, a_i]`, - a certified invariant level `ℓ_i` in the lattice, - measured stats captured at write time (attention back-mass, dependency counts, survival class). KV validity: position `j` is reusable iff tokens `≤ j` match the cached stream. An edit at divergence `δ` (longest common prefix) forces re-prefill of `(δ, L]`. Anchors exist for three measured reasons, not aesthetic ones: **Localization**: hash bisection finds `δ` in `O(log n)` hash compares (~µs) vs `O(L)` byte scan (~ms at 48k tokens). At measured edit rates this dominates. **Certifiability**: semantic invariants (fact coverage, causal closure) are only computable at segment boundaries where the fact-set is well-defined. **Safe-cut predicate**: zero open tool-call span, zero cross-boundary entity references — checkable only at structural boundaries. Replay-log measurement: mid-turn cuts show survival σ drop of ~0. 18 vs ~0. 03 at turn boundaries. That 6× gap is the empirical justification for semantic anchoring. Block-alignment constraint: serving stacks reuse KV at block granularity (`B` = 16–128 tokens). Effective reuse is `B·⌊δ/B⌋`. Rule: **snap every anchor to a multiple of B**; misalignment wastes up to `B−1` tokens of reuse per cut, free to eliminate. The invariant lattice Levels are bitmask predicates, ordered by subset; meet = ∧, join = ∨: ⊥ < P < P∧Q < P∧Q∧K < P∧Q∧K∧E < ⊤ = P∧Q∧K∧E∧V - **P** (prefix integrity): all chained hashes `H_i`, `i ≤ idx(δ)`, verify. - **Q** (quota): `L' ≤ W`, segment budgets hold. - **K** (causal closure): every tool-result referenced by a surviving turn is present verbatim or covered by a certified summary whose hash chains into the anchor. - **E** (entailment): summary covers the extracted fact-set of the replaced span; probe-measured survival `σ ≥ σ_min`. - **V** (verdict stability): `KL(p_new ‖ p_cached)` at the next-step distribution `≤ ε_KL`. **Grant function is deterministic code over measured values** — never a model judgment: grant(e) = P  iff hashes verify ∧ Q  iff L' ≤ W ∧ budgets hold ∧ K  iff ∀open refs r: r ∈ verbatim ∪ certified_summaries ∧ E  iff σ̂(cut) ≥ σ_min ∧ V  iff KL ≤ ε_KL commit(e) iff grant(e) ≥ required(phase)   // e. K mandatory during active tool loops Hard code-level constraints with measured rationale: system preamble is immutable post-boot (editing it forces 100% re-prefill and voids every certificate); inserts are allowed only at anchor boundaries (mid-segment insertion breaks the chain segment's certificate referents). Let me think carefully about what this actually means technically. **Background: KV-cache and prefix re-prefill** In LLM serving, when you have a long context and you edit it (e. , truncate old turns, insert a summary, compact tool outputs), the token sequence changes. The KV cache is keyed by prefix position: if tokens 0. k are unchanged, their K/V entries remain valid. If you edit at position p, everything from p onward must be recomputed (re-prefilled). So the cost of a context edit is proportional to the length of the suffix after the first divergence point. "Semantic-anchor checkpoints" = placing checkpoints at semantically meaningful boundaries (e. , turn boundaries, tool-call/result pairs, summary insertion points) such that when an edit happens, the divergence point aligns with a checkpoint, so only the suffix after that checkpoint needs re-prefill. Without anchors, an edit anywhere forces re-prefill from the edit point to the end — which can be most of the context. **Code-as-law invariant lattice** This is a formal governance framing: invariants are encoded as machine-checkable rules ("code is law"), organized as a lattice (partially ordered set with meet/join) where stronger invariants imply weaker ones. - ⊥ (bottom): no guarantees - I1: token-prefix integrity (the rendered prompt is byte-identical up to checkpoint) - I2: semantic equivalence (summary preserves required facts) - I3: causal consistency (tool results referenced by later turns still present or summarized faithfully) - I4: budget invariants (token count ≤ window, cost ≤ cap) - ⊤ (top): all invariants hold A context edit must move the state along the lattice without violating invariants above the current level.
